motrok.lydraedi.1.text: Heimssýn points out that fewer than a quarter of the submissions on the parliamentary resolution supported it unchanged, and that Carl Baudenbacher, former President of the EFTA Court, considered the question misleading because it is not possible to continue talks that broke off a decade ago.
motrok.lydraedi.2.title: An advisory vote with low turnout provides a weak mandate
motrok.lydraedi.2.text: Páll Vilhjálmsson says that since the vote would only be advisory, it invites disputes over interpretation: if turnout were close to 50% and yes won by a narrow majority, the authorities would be basing the talks on the support of a minority of eligible voters — far too weak a mandate for such major changes.
motrok.lydraedi.3.title: No is also a democratic position
motrok.lydraedi.3.text: Erna Bjarnadóttir says that no is a legitimate democratic position that is wrongly dismissed as hostility to information; accession talks are not a neutral fact-finding exercise, and the democratic argument of the YES side assumes that only one answer is “informed”.
motrok.byggd.0.title: Iceland would pay more into EU funds than it would get back
motrok.byggd.0.text: Haraldur Ólafsson, chair of Heimssýn, says that the amounts Iceland might receive from individual funds would be only a small fraction of the contributions the country would have to pay; the EU’s cohesion and regional development funds are intended primarily for poorer states in Southern and Eastern Europe, whereas Iceland is one of the more affluent countries on the continent and would be a net contributor.
motrok.byggd.1.title: Brussels would be an even more distant authority for rural Iceland than Reykjavík
motrok.byggd.1.text: In a submitted opinion piece in Austurfrétt, it is questioned whether EU funding would improve the position of rural Iceland: it asks whether its voice would carry more weight, points out that EU rules such as the ETS emissions trading system, “thoughtlessly incorporated into Icelandic law in 2007”, raise the price of all inputs and production and reduce people’s purchasing power — remote power in Brussels would not remedy the neglect of the authorities in Reykjavík.
motrok.taekifaeri.0.title: The euro is not the solution for young people — an independent currency suits a volatile economy
motrok.taekifaeri.0.text: Kjartan Magnússon, a board member of Ung gegn ESB, acknowledges that high interest rates have led many people, especially young people, to look to the euro as a possible solution, but says an independent currency is the better option because the Icelandic economy is based on volatile industries; Iceland recovered more quickly from economic crisis than the eurozone countries Greece and Spain.
motrok.taekifaeri.1.title: Membership binds future generations to an almost irreversible commitment
motrok.taekifaeri.1.text: Erlendur Magnússon says that the experience of the United Kingdom shows that leaving the EU is “almost impossible” and, for a small country like Iceland, “virtually impossible”; the current generation cannot allow itself “to bind our descendants in the shackles of the European Union for ever and ever” — the opportunity for young people lies in keeping the options open.
motrok.taekifaeri.2.title: Housing problems and youth unemployment are worse within the EU
motrok.taekifaeri.2.text: An article on BB.is points out that young people’s housing difficulties are severe in many parts of the EU despite low interest rates: in many European countries, young people find it harder to buy housing, high rents create rental poverty traps, and youth unemployment within the EU has historically been much higher than in Iceland.
motrok.fullveldi.0.title: Sovereignty lies in the right to negotiate
motrok.fullveldi.0.text: Helga Vala Helgadóttir says that sovereignty lies precisely in a state’s ability to conclude international agreements — sovereign states have always entered into such agreements — and criticizes attempts to stir up fear that Iceland’s sovereignty is at risk merely by entering into negotiations; in any case, the nation will have the final say on the agreement.
motrok.fullveldi.1.title: The EEA arrangement is unbecoming of a sovereign state
motrok.fullveldi.1.text: Magnús Árni Skjöld Magnússon, chair of Evrópuhreyfingin, points out that Iceland already adopts 75–80% of the EU’s internal market rules through the EEA — “rules that we have had no part in making at any stage of the process” — and says that real power over its own regulatory framework comes precisely through membership, not by maintaining the status quo.
motrok.fullveldi.2.title: A right to shape, but no right to decide, today
motrok.fullveldi.2.text: Kristján Vigfússon explains that the EEA states have only a limited right to shape EU legislation at the preparatory stage, but no right to decide — at the drafting and adoption stages they have no formal involvement — and asks whether that arrangement is acceptable for a sovereign nation.
motrok.fullveldi.3.title: Sovereignty lies in an informed choice
motrok.fullveldi.3.text: Jóhannes Finnur Halldórsson writes that Iceland is already in the EEA and Schengen without full influence, and that sovereignty lies in the nation making an informed decision itself — negotiations are a natural continuation of the European cooperation already in place, not a departure from sovereignty.
motrok.sjavarutvegur.0.title: Fishing track record decides — the quota would remain Icelandic
motrok.sjavarutvegur.0.text: Thomas Möller, a board member of Evrópuhreyfingin, points out that fishing rights within the EU are based on historical use (relative stability); no other nations have a fishing track record for the main demersal fish stocks in Icelandic waters, and the quota would therefore continue to belong to Icelanders.
motrok.sjavarutvegur.1.title: Malta obtained special arrangements in fisheries
motrok.sjavarutvegur.1.text: Pawel Bartoszek, chair of the Foreign Affairs Committee, points out that “Malta did in fact get fairly extensive special arrangements in its accession treaty … in the field of fisheries” and that fisheries and agriculture are matters for negotiation — the experience of small states shows that they can be negotiated.
motrok.sjavarutvegur.2.title: Full control over marine resources is a red line
motrok.sjavarutvegur.2.text: Þórður Snær Júlíusson explains that Iceland’s negotiating objectives, according to the opinion of the majority of the Foreign Affairs Committee, stipulate “full control over marine resources, fisheries management, and the sustainable use of fish stocks” — control over the nation’s key resources is defined as a red line in the negotiations.
motrok.spurning.0.title: The question is about negotiations, not accession
motrok.spurning.0.text: Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir says: “The question here is not whether the nation should join, but whether we should enter into negotiations” — a decision on membership will not be taken until the nation has seen a completed agreement and voted on it separately in a second referendum.
motrok.spurning.1.title: The Venice Commission confirms the nature of the vote
motrok.spurning.1.text: Páll Rafnar Þorsteinsson points out that the Venice Commission has confirmed that a yes vote does not automatically lead to EU membership, but only to the opening of accession talks, and that the Commission reiterates that a second referendum on actual membership will be held once negotiations are concluded.
motrok.spurning.2.title: Membership is not on the table
motrok.spurning.2.text: Pawel Bartoszek says the no movement is misleadingly equating negotiations with membership: “Iceland’s membership of the European Union is not on the table” — membership would require negotiations, a completed agreement, the approval of all member states, and a second referendum.
motrok.adlogun.0.title: No adaptation took place in 2009–2013
motrok.adlogun.0.text: Halldór Jörgen Olesen rejects the adaptation arguments by referring to experience: during the 2009–2013 talks, no adaptation took place — neither legislative changes nor institutional changes — as confirmed by the Ministry for Foreign Affairs in May 2026; EU IPA grants went to projects such as ecosystem mapping and translations of the regulatory framework. “A yes is not a yes to the EU. A yes is a yes to negotiate.”
motrok.adlogun.1.title: No systemic changes without a second vote
motrok.adlogun.1.text: Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir says that nothing in Iceland’s system of government will be changed on the basis of the negotiations themselves; the government will sit at the table with clear negotiating objectives, and no changes will take effect until the nation has approved a completed agreement in a second referendum.
motrok.adlogun.2.title: A yes vote only opens the negotiation process
motrok.adlogun.2.text: Páll Rafnar Þorsteinsson refers to the Venice Commission’s opinion that a yes vote leads only to the opening of the negotiation process — neither to membership nor to irreversible changes — and that the authorities must ensure that the final decision is taken in a separate vote on the agreement itself.
motrok.ees.0.title: 75–80% of rules implemented without any influence
motrok.ees.0.text: Magnús Árni Skjöld Magnússon says that Iceland already implements 75–80% of EU internal market legislation through the EEA without having had any say at any stage in drafting those rules — so the EEA only "works" by giving up the influence that full membership would provide.
motrok.ees.1.title: The formal influence of EEA states ends at the preparatory stage
motrok.ees.1.text: Kristján Vigfússon outlines the EU legislative process in three stages and shows that the formal influence of the EEA states already ends at the preparatory stage; at the processing and adoption stages they have no involvement, and with the increased power of the European Parliament the involvement of the EEA states has "become more complex and weakened somewhat".
motrok.ees.2.title: The EEA was a temporary solution
motrok.ees.2.text: Björgvin G. Sigurðsson, a former minister, says that "the supplementary membership through the EEA was a temporary solution" — an excellent outcome at the time, but "not a permanent solution and democratically unacceptable in the long run"; the logical next step is to conclude the negotiations and vote on a completed agreement.
motrok.ees.3.title: Today the voting weight is zero
motrok.ees.3.text: Hjálmar Vilhjálmsson, a board member of SJÁ, calculates using the Banzhaf method that each Icelander’s voting weight in the EU Council of Ministers would be about 37 times that of each German — but in the current EEA arrangement the weight of Icelanders in decisions on the rules they now implement is zero.
motrok.efnahagur.0.title: The image of a stagnant EU is outdated
motrok.efnahagur.0.text: Thomas Möller says opponents rely on an outdated image of Europe: the EU economy grew by 14% in 2008–2023 and is the world’s second-largest economy, euro area growth (1.5%) compares well with the United States, and about 3.5 million companies were established in EU countries in 2023, most of them innovative firms.
motrok.efnahagur.1.title: The hidden cost of the króna is overlooked in the comparison
motrok.efnahagur.1.text: Óðinn Freyr Baldursson points out that Iceland’s success outside the EU carries hidden costs: around 1.000 billion krónur, about 20% of GDP, are tied up in foreign exchange reserves, and Icelandic households and businesses pay more than 100 billion a year in interest costs due to the instability of the króna — a cost that falls heaviest on those least able to bear it.
motrok.efnahagur.2.title: The króna costs around 300 billion a year
motrok.efnahagur.2.text: Björgvin G. Sigurðsson estimates that an independent floating króna costs “a conservatively estimated 300 billion a year, divided equally among households, businesses and the public sector” and says the current currency system is “fully exhausted” — meaning that prosperity outside the EU comes at a higher price than the comparison figures cited by the NO side suggest.
motrok.umbod.0.title: The referendum itself is the search for a mandate
motrok.umbod.0.text: Helga Vala Helgadóttir responds to criticism about a lack of mandate by arguing that parliamentary elections are never about one single issue; a referendum is precisely the right tool for seeking a clear mandate from the nation on major issues between parliamentary elections — democracy is about giving the nation the opportunity to express itself now, not only once every four years.
motrok.umbod.1.title: No blank cheque — the objectives are already clear
motrok.umbod.1.text: Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir says the government is not being given a blank cheque: the negotiating objectives are set out in the opinion of the majority on the Foreign Affairs Committee, with precise conditions regarding fisheries, agriculture and energy, and the nation will have the final say on the outcome in a second vote.
motrok.umbod.2.title: The negotiating objectives have been public since 18 May
motrok.umbod.2.text: Þórður Snær Júlíusson responds to claims that no negotiating objectives exist: they have been publicly available since 18. maí 2026 in the opinion of the majority on the Foreign Affairs Committee, with defined red lines on marine resources, water, energy and agriculture.
motrok.umbod.3.title: A dual democratic process
motrok.umbod.3.text: Ingibjörg Sólrún Gísladóttir, former Minister for Foreign Affairs, says the core of the issue is a dual democratic process: the nation first votes on whether talks should continue and later votes again on the agreement itself — it would be hard to find a stronger democratic mandate for the process.
motrok.undanthagur.0.title: Sweden, Finland and Malta secured special arrangements
motrok.undanthagur.0.text: Pawel Bartoszek notes that Sweden and Finland secured special arrangements in their accession treaties and that Malta obtained “quite extensive special solutions … in the field of fisheries” — experience shows that special solutions for small states are a real part of accession treaties, not wishful thinking.
motrok.undanthagur.1.title: All new member states received agreements tailored to their particular circumstances
motrok.undanthagur.1.text: Thomas Möller claims that the accession treaties of all new member states in recent decades were adapted to each country’s particular circumstances through special provisions, and that Iceland’s negotiating position has improved significantly — Iceland would bring the EU, among other things, about 700 thousand square kilometres of maritime area and a key strategic position in North Atlantic security matters.
motrok.undanthagur.2.title: Special arrangements are the rule, not the exception
motrok.undanthagur.2.text: Thomas Möller argues that special arrangements are “the rule rather than the exception” within the EU, and that the Union has a strong history of tailoring accession treaties to the particular circumstances of island states; moreover, the allocation of fishing rights is based on historical use, which would safeguard Icelandic interests regardless of the wording on permanence.
motrok.evra.0.title: The króna has costs of its own
motrok.evra.0.text: Óðinn Freyr Baldursson points out that maintaining the króna comes at enormous cost: about 1.000 billion krónur, around 20% of GDP, are tied up in foreign exchange reserves; households and businesses pay over 100 billion a year in interest costs because of the króna’s instability and less favourable borrowing terms; and currency exchange cost about 12,4 billion in 2025. The króna also amplifies economic shocks and deters foreign investment.
motrok.evra.1.title: The króna costs around 300 billion a year
motrok.evra.1.text: Björgvin G. Sigurðsson estimates the cost of an independent, floating króna at “a conservatively estimated 300 billion a year, divided equally between households, businesses and the public sector in the form of interest-rate differentials”, and says the current monetary arrangement has been “fully tested” — membership of the monetary union is the most important of the benefits of full membership.
motrok.evra.2.title: The growth comparison is misleading per person
motrok.evra.2.text: Sveinn Agnarsson, professor of economics at HÍ, points out that although total economic growth in 2014–2025 was 2.8% in Iceland compared with 1.5% in the euro area, the picture reverses when looking at GDP per capita: 1.0% annual growth in Iceland versus 1.2% in the euro area — and fluctuations in growth are also much greater in Iceland (standard deviation 4.0 versus 2.8).
motrok.evra.3.title: Usurious interest rates have accompanied the króna for more than a century
motrok.evra.3.text: Dóra Magnúsdóttir says the public and small businesses pay much higher interest rates than comparable nations, and that the interest burden has plagued Icelanders for more than a full century; the euro is the only realistic tool for escaping “interest-rate servitude” — large companies already settle in euros, while small family businesses and households are left behind with króna interest rates.
motrok.hervaeding.0.title: There is no European army — and Iceland would have a veto
motrok.hervaeding.0.text: Óðinn Freyr Baldursson points out that no European army exists; the idea is “the brainchild of one man” rather than EU policy. The creation of a joint military force would require the unanimous approval of all member states, so Iceland alone could block it; defence and security matters remain under the authority of each state under the Lisbon Treaty. Iceland has been without an army within NATO since 1949, without pressure to create one — why should an economic union require what the world’s largest military alliance never did?
motrok.hervaeding.1.title: Similar dire predictions have proved wrong before
motrok.hervaeding.1.text: Guðfinna Jóh. Guðmundsdóttir says claims about militarisation and loss of sovereignty are part of fearmongering against the talks; earlier dire predictions about NATO, EFTA and the EEA all proved wrong, and it is more sensible to see the agreement before passing judgment.
motrok.ahrifaleysi.0.title: Each Icelander’s voting weight would be 37 times that of a German
motrok.ahrifaleysi.0.text: Using the Banzhaf power index, Hjálmar Vilhjálmsson calculates that Germany’s decisive voting weight in the Council of Ministers would be only just under six times that of Iceland, even though Germans are about 209 times more numerous — each Icelander would have about 37 times the weight of each German, equivalent to roughly 15 million Germans. Qualified majority voting (QMV) requires the support of at least 55% of member states and 65% of the population, which ensures weight for small states — and today Iceland’s voting weight is zero.
motrok.ahrifaleysi.1.title: The smallest nations have proportionally the most weight — and are the most satisfied
motrok.ahrifaleysi.1.text: Páll Rafnar Þorsteinsson points out that, relative to population, the smallest nations have many times more representatives than the largest; in addition to parliamentary seats, Iceland would receive a full seat in the Council of Ministers, a commissioner and a judge. Small states measure as the most satisfied with membership in Eurobarometer: Ireland 93%, Luxembourg and Malta 91%. Concerns about lack of influence are "entirely a home-made inferiority complex".
motrok.ahrifaleysi.2.title: Six parliamentary seats are more than the EEA’s zero influence
motrok.ahrifaleysi.2.text: Magnús Árni Skjöld Magnússon points out that Iceland already adopts 75–80% of EU internal market rules through the EEA without any voting rights; the current situation is unworthy of a sovereign state, and full membership would provide real power instead of today’s complete lack of influence.
motrok.kostnadur.0.title: Membership fees are outweighed by savings in the tens or hundreds of billions
motrok.kostnadur.0.text: Magnús Árni Skjöld Magnússon acknowledges that direct membership fees would increase, but says that extra cost would quickly be offset by savings that would "run to tens, even hundreds of billions per year" from eliminating the costs of maintaining foreign exchange reserves, tariffs and the krona’s excessive interest rates. In addition, EU regional development funds spend each year about five times more than the entire Icelandic state budget allocates to such projects.
motrok.kostnadur.1.title: Net contribution would be closer to 2–7 billion than 30
motrok.kostnadur.1.text: According to the information website jaedanei.is, Iceland’s annual net contribution after accession would be around 2–7 billion krónur per year (about 0.2–0.3% of GDP based on the Finnish precedent), since the EEA contributions, about 8 billion per year, would cease — and in addition the roughly 1.4 billion in annual tariffs on seafood products to the EU would disappear within the customs union.
motrok.kostnadur.2.title: The króna costs many times more than membership
motrok.kostnadur.2.text: Björgvin G. Sigurðsson says the cost to the national economy of an independent, floating króna is conservatively estimated at around 300 billion a year in the form of an interest-rate differential, divided equally between households, businesses and the public sector — an amount on an entirely different scale from the membership contributions under discussion.
motrok.oafturkraeft.0.title: A YES vote only opens the negotiating table — nothing is settled
motrok.oafturkraeft.0.text: Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir says: “If the result is yes, the door to the negotiating table opens. Nothing else.” Nothing is settled until the process is complete “and then only if the nation itself approves the outcome” in a second referendum on a fully negotiated agreement.
motrok.oafturkraeft.1.title: No legislative changes occurred during the 2009–2013 talks
motrok.oafturkraeft.1.text: Halldór Jörgen Olesen points out that no legislative changes took place during the 2009–2013 negotiation period, and that the Ministry for Foreign Affairs confirmed that no adaptation took place beyond the ordinary obligations of the EEA. A YES vote “opens negotiations. Nothing else” — the nation “keeps all its cards in hand and gets another chance to say no if the agreement is not suitable.”
motrok.oafturkraeft.2.title: Article 50 is a formal exit procedure — Brexit proves that leaving is possible
motrok.oafturkraeft.2.text: According to the information website jaedanei.is, withdrawal from the EU is formally guaranteed in Article 50 of the Treaty of Lisbon — the same process the British used for Brexit — so membership is not irreversible. Before membership could happen, in addition to a second referendum, a constitutional amendment would be required, which two parliaments would have to approve with an election in between.
motrok.landbunadur.0.title: Negotiating objectives: food security, regional settlement and a ban on imports of live animals
motrok.landbunadur.0.text: Þórður Snær Júlíusson says that Iceland would fight for special arrangements in agriculture because of more difficult production conditions: “Production conditions in Iceland are more difficult than in most of Europe. That is why support must ensure food security, regional settlement and continued farming.” The ban on imports of live animals must also remain in place to protect Icelandic livestock breeds.
motrok.landbunadur.1.title: Sweden and Finland secured special arrangements in agriculture
motrok.landbunadur.1.text: Pawel Bartoszek points out that Sweden and Finland obtained a special arrangement in agriculture (northern aid) when they joined the EU, and that Malta received “rather extensive special arrangements in its accession treaty” that still apply — there are therefore precedents for special arrangements for agriculture in northern regions.
motrok.landbunadur.2.title: Opportunities for Icelandic products in larger markets
motrok.landbunadur.2.text: Magnús Árni Skjöld Magnússon says that Icelandic farmers could make use of their distinctive position and expand into larger markets with Icelandic products; he asks whether the state of agriculture is really so good “that it would not be worthwhile for farmers to find out whether there might be, even considerable, opportunities for strengthening it” in negotiations.
motrok.landbunadur.3.title: Food prices could fall by 25–30%
motrok.landbunadur.3.text: Thomas Möller argues, against claims that price reductions are exaggerated, that food prices could fall by 25–30% with membership and interest rates drop from about 9% to about 3%; a NO vote would close the door on these terms for generations.
motrok.nagrannar.0.title: Seven EU states among the top 15 — Norway’s and Switzerland’s prosperity has other explanations
motrok.nagrannar.0.text: Political scientist Elvar Örn Arason points out that seven EU states rank among the top 15 countries on the United Nations standard-of-living index: Denmark, Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Ireland and Finland. The position of Norway and Switzerland is explained by “the exceptional resource wealth of one and the other’s special role as a financial centre — not by their being outside the EU”. Iceland and Norway base their prosperity on close ties to the internal market and are “almost associate members of the Union” without a seat at the table where the legislation is drafted.
motrok.nagrannar.1.title: Most of the old EFTA states joined and are well satisfied with their lot
motrok.nagrannar.1.text: Ingibjörg Sólrún Gísladóttir points out that “most of the states that belonged to EFTA when Iceland became a member have become full members of the EU” and are well satisfied with their situation within the Union; in a more dangerous world, it is important to have friends and allies who can come to one’s aid.
arg.timagluggi.title: An opportunity that will not come again
arg.timagluggi.text: Iceland is said to have an exceptionally strong negotiating position right now — because of a changed global landscape and the EU’s interest in westward enlargement — and that window will close if the United Kingdom moves closer to the union again or Norway joins first.
arg.skyrslan.title: The currency report said to be of no evidentiary value
arg.skyrslan.text: The currency report commissioned by the Ministry of Finance from foreign experts is said to be of no evidentiary value as an argument in the election campaign: the Central Bank is said to have criticised it harshly, and one of its authors is himself opposed to adopting the euro in Norway.
art.119.title: Why am I saying no at the end of August?
art.119.summary: The former chair of VG and minister in the government that applied in 2009 says she will vote no. The experience of the 2009–2013 negotiations shows that the most difficult chapters — fisheries, agriculture and regional policy — never really got underway, and permanent exemptions are a highly unlikely outcome. Iceland is doing well as an independent nation, and stalled negotiations could damage relations with the EU in the longer term.
art.120.title: “The European Union is not a box of chocolates”
art.120.summary: The chair of Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn says the EU is not a box of chocolates where you can pick the best pieces and reject the rest. The government has not clarified its negotiating objectives or red lines, for example on fisheries, and she doubts that permanent exemptions can be secured. The timing of the vote is political and liable to divert attention from economic issues.
art.121.title: Svandís says no
art.121.summary: The former chair of VG and minister says she will vote no at the end of August. Power should lie with citizens rather than distant institutions, and Iceland can play an active part in European cooperation without joining the EU. The position runs counter to the majority of VG voters according to polls.
art.122.title: Jón Sigurðsson’s words do not apply to today’s struggle
art.122.summary: The executive director of Bændasamtakanna likens the EU issue to the struggle for independence: membership would entail transferring a large share of decision-making power in agricultural matters to Brussels. Agriculture would undergo fundamental changes, and the negotiation process itself would create uncertainty for farmers.
art.123.title: Iceland ranks 1st in the world on the UN quality-of-life index — would we really be better off inside the EU?
art.123.summary: Iceland tops the UN quality-of-life index, with lower poverty and lower unemployment than the EU average, so membership is unnecessary for prosperity. Membership would require a transfer of power and constitutional amendments, the Common Fisheries Policy would take over control of the fishing grounds, and net contributions of 10–15 billion a year would divert funds from domestic priorities.
art.124.title: See what exactly?
art.124.summary: The demand to “see the agreement” does not stand up to scrutiny because most of the package was already clear years ago. Iceland would surrender control over fisheries, agriculture, and trade policy while gaining little beyond what the EEA already guarantees; adoption of the euro and permanent exemptions are uncertain outcomes.
art.125.title: Saying yes just to see is out of the question
art.125.summary: The YES side is said to have changed its wording: from open support for membership to wanting to “just see the agreement.” Promises of a 25% price drop and lower interest rates are an illusion because they depend on adopting the euro after a long process of meeting the Maastricht criteria, which Iceland has never fulfilled simultaneously; the króna has enabled the economy to adjust to external shocks.
art.126.title: No safeguards against animal diseases
art.126.summary: A former chief veterinary officer warns that Iceland’s strict import safeguards against animal diseases could be weakened by EU membership without clear guarantees. Icelandic livestock populations have little immunity to European diseases, and the authorities must declare disease prevention a red line in all negotiations.
art.127.title: Reflections on the EU, small states and Switzerland
art.127.summary: Most comparable small states do well outside the EU, and Switzerland shows that bilateral agreements provide market access without surrendering decision-making power. Iceland would be a net contributor to the Union, and the history of disputes over fishing rights suggests that Iceland’s interests are poorly aligned with EU demands.
art.128.title: Warning that foreign parties could gain control over Icelandic fisheries
art.128.summary: Samtök fyrirtækja í sjávarútvegi warn that the 25% cap on foreign ownership in fisheries would fall away with EU membership, and that foreign parties could gain control over catch quotas through subsidiaries and quota hopping, as they say has happened in Denmark and Germany. The association sets out four demands for safeguards that cannot be changed without Iceland’s consent.
art.129.title: Not in Iceland’s interests
art.129.summary: It was a full house when Carl Baudenbacher, former President of the EFTA Court, reviewed the main arguments of EU supporters in eight sections and rejected them. Economic and political developments within the EU are said to be unfavourable to Iceland, the current position in the EEA and EFTA better suited than membership, and the largest states set the direction so Iceland’s influence would be negligible.
art.130.title: Let’s choose to know more
art.130.summary: The Minister of Justice says a deal no one has seen should not be rejected: the vote is about continuing the talks, not about membership. A changed world since 2009–2013 creates new opportunities to defend Iceland’s special interests, and the public should be trusted to gather information and decide for itself.
art.131.title: We should dare to see what an accession treaty might entail
art.131.summary: The chair of Báran says that exploring the option is not the same as approving it: working people are entitled to have economic alternatives examined amid persistent inflation and pressure on purchasing power. The nation should receive full information before a final decision on membership is taken.
art.132.title: An opportunity that will not come again
art.132.summary: A business economist says a national referendum gives the clearest picture of the will of the people, unwarped by the constituency system, which lets vested interests in fisheries, agriculture and finance seize the reins of power. Opponents are deliberately spreading false information, and this democratic opportunity will not come again.
art.133.title: Let’s stop guessing: Let’s get the answers on the table
art.133.summary: The nation deserves to see a completed agreement instead of guessing; a yes vote only opens negotiations, and the outcome can be rejected in a later vote, whereas a no vote closes off the answers. Lower interest rates, currency stability and increased competition would improve conditions for families and young people in the housing market.
art.134.title: A new IMF assessment of euro adoption for Iceland
art.134.summary: A Samfylkingin MP outlines a new IMF assessment in which adopting the euro is described as a clear benefit: lower interest rates and inflation, reduced currency risk and better access to European financial markets. Iceland’s small size and open economy make the stability of the euro desirable, and Iceland can assess the issue from a position of strength.
art.135.title: What is the real threat to Iceland’s sovereignty?
art.135.summary: A professor at HÍ turns the sovereignty arguments around: the real threats facing small nations are tech giants and hostile great powers, and the EU provides collective strength for defence. Iceland would get six parliamentary seats and a representative in the Council of Ministers, and special arrangements in agriculture and fisheries are realistic, as in Northern Sweden and Finland.
art.136.title: Opportunities in value-added processing
art.136.summary: Membership would remove tariffs on processed seafood products so that value-added processing would become competitive domestically instead of moving to Poland, the UK or China; currently only 1.4% of the export value of seafood products is fully processed consumer goods. It is necessary to negotiate clear national control over the fisheries resource, but negotiations provide answers instead of speculation.
art.137.title: Iceland is in the EU
art.137.summary: Iceland is already halfway into the EU through the EEA since 1994, but without any influence over the rules that bind the country. The vote is about gaining clarity on what full membership would entail through formal negotiations — not a commitment to join.
art.138.title: Rósa Björk says yes
art.138.summary: The leader of VG says she will vote yes despite the party’s policy against membership: voters should be allowed to see what kind of agreement is on offer instead of closing the door in advance. Polls show that an overwhelming majority of VG voters intend to vote yes, and environmental protection, agriculture, fisheries, and workers’ pay and conditions should be priorities in the negotiations.
art.139.title: Opponents mislead voters with “nonsense”
art.139.summary: The Minister for Foreign Affairs accuses opponents of the talks of misleading voters with false claims, including about conscription. Iceland should not let the opportunity slip through its fingers, but rather seek a good agreement, and the country’s strong financial position means that Iceland would be among the net contributors, like Germany and France.
art.140.title: Þorsteinn Pálsson writes: One powerful cooperative and another larger one
art.140.summary: Kaupfélag Skagfirðinga shows how borrowing in euros through the European banking system improves the competitiveness of farmers in the region; the whole nation should have direct access to such terms, not just export companies. The EU functions like a large international cooperative, and the current system is unsustainable for agriculture.
art.141.title: Gauti B. Eggertsson: Iceland would carry many times its weight within the EU relative to its size
art.141.summary: A professor of economics at Brown University says in an interview that small states receive proportionally many times the influence within the EU, and that interest rates have fallen sharply in every country that has joined the Union — monthly housing loan payments could fall by more than 100 thousand krónur. High prices are not explained by uniquely Icelandic conditions, and the benefits for households far outweigh the costs of membership.
art.142.title: EU membership would most disadvantage those who currently wield the greatest political and economic influence
art.142.summary: A professor of sociology says direct EU payments to farmers could amount to 3.7–15.6 billion annually and that public support for business, transport and regional development would increase with membership. EU regulations are said to be more transparent and predictable than Icelandic patronage politics, and membership would most disadvantage those who currently have the greatest political and economic clout.
art.143.title: Björgvin G. Sigurðsson writes: Lost power and regained sovereignty
art.143.summary: Iceland implements around 75% of EU legislation through the EEA without democratic participation, and full membership would restore lost power by giving it a seat where the laws are made. The EEA arrangement and the króna cost about 300 billion annually, and the experience of Ireland and Denmark shows that membership does not diminish nationality or identity.
art.144.title: Sigvaldi Einarsson writes: Thirty arguments for, with three against
art.144.summary: Inflation (5.3%) and interest rates (7.75%) in Iceland are far above those in the euro area (2.9% and 2.25%) and place a monthly burden on households. Iceland has unique bargaining chips — green energy, secure data hosting and geothermal expertise — and a YES vote would only authorize negotiations, since the agreement would go to a second referendum.
art.145.title: Óli Rúnar Ástþórsson writes: Within the EU, “Iceland will control fisheries in the North Atlantic”
art.145.summary: Iceland could retain full control over fisheries in the North Atlantic within the EU and negotiate over shared stocks much as it does now. Timing is the key issue: if Iceland waits until the UK moves closer to the Union again and Norway joins, its negotiating position will disappear; a former Commission staff member is quoted as saying the opportunity “will never come again.”
art.146.title: Jóhann Páll Jóhannsson: The blow from Grindavík fell entirely on us – the EU would have come to the aid of a member state
art.146.summary: In an interview, the Minister for the Environment, Energy and Climate says EU solidarity funds would have helped ease Iceland’s burden over Grindavík, which bore the blow alone. Iceland should negotiate from a position of strength at a time of uncertainty in Western defense cooperation, and membership would strengthen sovereignty through collective defense and cybersecurity cooperation.
art.147.title: The Continent XIX: Do small states have a voice within the EU?
art.147.summary: Professor of political science Baldur Þórhallsson is a guest on Evrópuhreyfingin’s podcast and discusses the position and influence of small states within the EU. He believes that Iceland would unquestionably have a voice within the Union.
art.148.title: The Continent XX: A stronger countryside within the EU
art.148.summary: Anna Margréta Guðjónsdóttir, Managing Director of Evris, and Ásta Magnúsdóttir, former executive at EFTA, discuss regional development, support schemes and agriculture. They review opportunities in European funds and markets, not least for start-ups across the country.
art.149.title: The EU seeks the resources of Iceland, Norway and Greenland
art.149.summary: The EU is not self-sufficient in either seafood or energy and has adopted recommendations on the Arctic; its interest in Iceland, Norway and Greenland is explained by the need for food and energy security. Indications of possible exemptions from fisheries management are presented in that light.
art.150.title: Heiðrún Lind and Lilja Alfreðs untangle the knots of information disorder
art.150.summary: It is recounted that Heiðrún Lind Marteinsdóttir, Managing Director of SFS, corrected claims about Norway’s fisheries sector in the 1994 accession negotiations on Spursmál: the EU rejected Norway’s demand that the rule of relative stability be enshrined in the accession treaty and offered only a political declaration.
art.151.title: I fight on horseback . . . reluctantly . . .
art.151.summary: The article discusses a new report by Bændasamtökin on the impact of possible EU membership: Icelandic livestock breeds have been isolated since settlement and are vulnerable to new infectious diseases, and experience shows that permanent exemptions in EU accession agreements are extremely rare.
art.152.title: Would the Norwegian krone pass Iceland’s test?
art.152.summary: The Norwegian economist Hilde C. Bjørnland, one of the authors of the Ministry of Finance’s currency report, believes that Norway should not adopt the euro because of the special characteristics of its economy. The question is how her chapter can then become a central plank in the minister’s argument against the Icelandic króna, especially given that the Central Bank made serious comments on the report.
art.153.title: Til Vinstri við ESB and the coming weeks
art.153.summary: A newsletter on the final stretch of the campaign: the movement has held informational meetings on the militarisation of the EU, fisheries, agriculture and the institutions of the Union, and is announcing, among other things, a meeting on media freedom with Thomas Fazi and Jeffrey Sachs. Members are encouraged to write articles and engage in conversation until the vote; membership is said to entail a transfer of sovereignty and participation in militarisation.
art.154.title: Jón Baldvin Hannibalsson, Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson and Áfram Ísland at Baudenbacher’s meeting
art.154.summary: A report on the well-attended meeting of Carl Baudenbacher, former President of the EFTA Court, at Sjálfstæðishúsið, chaired by Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson. Baudenbacher compared the EFTA Court and the European Court of Justice, which is described as political and powerful, and Jón Baldvin Hannibalsson raised the question of whether common public finances would be the EU’s next step.
art.155.title: Pension liabilities crushing the European Union – Should we pay the pension liabilities of the French, Italians and Germans?
art.155.summary: The pension systems of the largest EU countries are pay-as-you-go systems with unfunded obligations amounting to two to three times GDP in France, Germany and Italy, while Icelandic funded pension schemes are in a strong position. The question is whether Icelanders should take part in bearing those burdens.
art.156.title: Do we want to sacrifice the best living standards in the world to get a seat with no influence in the EU?
art.156.summary: Icelanders enjoy the best living standards in the world according to the United Nations, but the accession and adaptation process would be costly, and contributions to the EU would amount to billions annually. Control over fisheries would shift to Brussels, investment in the fishing industry would be liberalised, and foreign multinationals could buy up companies and export catches from the country unprocessed.
art.157.title: Does Daði Már mean what he says?
art.157.summary: The finance minister’s integrity in the fight against inflation is being called into question, and it is claimed that within Viðreisn it has been said that the only way to get Icelanders to accept the EU process is for the economy here to be in ruins.
art.158.title: Iceland has adopted 13.4% of EU acts - not 75% as Þorgerður Katrín claims
art.158.summary: The foreign minister’s claims that Iceland has adopted 75% of the EU acquis are rejected with reference to answers on kosning.is; the share of acts adopted is said to be closer to 13.4%, and Iceland’s position through the EEA differs from that of other applicant countries.
art.159.title: The secrecy of the euro area central bank
art.159.summary: The European Central Bank does not publish the votes of individual central bank governors on interest-rate decisions, unlike what is customary in most neighbouring countries. Interest-rate decisions are based on average developments in the euro area, where the largest countries carry the most weight.
art.160.title: Tens of billions in contributions to the EU
art.160.summary: Iceland would pay the EU annually 0.7% of GDP, 0.3% of VAT revenues and 75% of customs duties collected, totalling around ISK 50 billion, while receiving only a fraction in return. The EU is said to have presented plans to raise these charges by more than half.
art.161.title: Shouldn’t Daði Már, Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs, be paying closer attention? Or does he not want to?
art.161.summary: The finance minister is said to be ignoring the Central Bank’s criticism of a currency report by four foreign experts prepared at his request. The Central Bank is said to have pointed out that monetary policy and a floating exchange rate have served Icelanders very well in recent decades.
art.162.title: Steingrímur J. Sigfússon does not want talks with the EU
art.162.summary: Attention is drawn to an article by Steingrímur J. Sigfússon on Vísir in which, in light of his experience from the accession talks after the crash, he says Iceland’s interests are best served outside the EU and states that he has very limited faith that a new round of talks would achieve anything.
art.163.title: The European Union is burning in the summer heatwaves that wipe out this year’s economic growth
art.163.summary: Reference is made to coverage by BBC, Reuters and EuroNews stating that heatwaves and wildfires are reducing economic growth in EU countries by up to one percent and wiping it out this year. Debt accumulation, low growth and sluggish business activity are said to characterize the Union.
art.164.title: Grandpa, I’m going to say yes
art.164.summary: The author’s conversation with his grandchild frames the case for YES: young people live with high interest rates and index-linked loans that European households do not know. The question is not what talks cost, but what it costs not to examine whether citizens’ welfare can be improved; yes means only completing the talks and then deciding on the basis of facts.
art.165.title: A thousand cod on the conveyor belt
art.165.summary: EU tariffs on processed seafood products prevent cod and salmon from being fully processed into consumer packaging here at home. Full domestic processing could generate ISK 35–55 billion annually, 1,100–2,300 jobs and increased municipal revenues; without tariff barriers, the added value would remain in the fishing communities.
art.166.title: What could the EU do for Austfirðir?
art.166.summary: Austfirðir faces population decline, unreliable transport links and reduced healthcare services. EU regional development funds (€392 billion over seven years), TEN-T transport funding, fibre-optic rollout and tariff-free market access for seafood products could reverse the trend, as happened in Lapland after Finland’s accession.
art.167.title: What could the EU do for Norðurland?
art.167.summary: Norðurland could draw on EU regional development funds, direct payments under the Common Agricultural Policy like Finnish and Swedish farmers, full participation by the University of Akureyri in Horizon Europe, and transport funding for difficult winter roads. Talks would be an exploration; if the terms proved unfavorable, the nation could reject the agreement in a later referendum.
art.168.title: What could the EU do for Vestfirðir?
art.168.summary: Vestfirðir faces depopulation, poor roads and reduced healthcare services, and young people are moving away. EU regional and infrastructure funds could finance development in the region, as in peripheral areas of the other Nordic countries.
art.169.title: Stand together
art.169.summary: An economics professor is surprised by the large regional gap in support (59% in Reykjavík, 24% in Austurland) even though the national interest is the same. Finnish farmers opposed membership, but many changed their minds after accession; the EU’s agricultural policy supports peripheral regions, and Iceland should stand with Europe with the euro in times of uncertainty.
art.170.title: Iceland’s negotiating objectives should guide the accession talks
art.170.summary: The chair of the Foreign Affairs Committee says in an interview that clear negotiating objectives on agriculture, fisheries and the import of live animals will guide the talks. Nothing will be accepted unless the outcome is considered satisfactory and the nation votes on the final agreement.
art.171.title: Information is still lacking
art.171.summary: An editorial in Bændablaðið criticizes the authorities for not presenting clear answers before the vote on control over resources and agricultural policy. History shows that permanent exemptions from the EU’s agricultural policy are rare, and it asks why Iceland should place resources it already controls under negotiation with a supranational authority.
art.172.title: The referendum is about giving the government a mandate to negotiate EU membership
art.172.summary: The chairman of Miðflokkurinn says in an interview that the vote is not about “taking a look inside the package” but about granting the government a mandate to negotiate membership; a yes vote would amount to a blank check on the nation’s sovereignty to the Minister for Foreign Affairs.
art.173.title: Guðlaugur: Extremely dangerous to vote yes in the referendum
art.173.summary: The former Minister for Foreign Affairs says it is extremely dangerous to begin new accession talks; in practice, this would mean applying for full membership on the basis of the 2009 application. The experience of the mackerel dispute, Icesave and vaccine distribution shows that the EU puts the interests of member states ahead of Iceland, and in negotiations Iceland’s position would be exposed to pressure.
art.174.title: Yrsa and Ólafur intend to vote no on membership of the European Union
art.174.summary: The writer Yrsa Sigurðardóttir and Ólafur Þór Þórhallsson say in an interview that they intend to vote no. Yrsa says her experience in publishing shows how extensive the EU’s regulatory framework is, and she fears increased bureaucracy; Ólafur believes Iceland does well independently and should retain its decision-making power.
art.175.title: “If I were Icelandic, I would vote no” — former President of the EFTA Court
art.175.summary: Carl Baudenbacher, former President of the EFTA Court, warns against viewing the referendum as an innocent poll: a yes vote would set the EU’s entire political and institutional machinery in motion, and “the first yes is the decisive vote”. It would be much harder to reject an accession treaty later, and the burden of proof rests on those who want to leave the EEA arrangement.
art.176.title: SFS: EU membership would fundamentally alter Iceland’s control over marine resources
art.176.summary: Analysis by Samtök fyrirtækja í sjávarútvegi: EU membership would entail a fundamental change in Iceland’s control over marine resources and fisheries management. Control over the resource would be transferred in part to the Union’s Common Fisheries Policy.
art.177.title: SFS warn against foreign control over fishing quotas upon accession to the EU
art.177.summary: SFS warn that the current 25% ceiling on foreign ownership in Icelandic fisheries would not comply with the rules of the EU internal market and that Iceland’s EEA exemption would lapse upon accession. The experience of other European countries, they say, shows that foreign companies can gain control over fishing rights through subsidiaries and that ownership, profits and decision-making can move out of the country.
art.178.title: Þorgerður demands control over fisheries in EU talks
art.178.summary: Sharing of an RÚV news item about the foreign minister’s non-negotiable demand for control over fisheries in the talks. The author says it is high time to determine once and for all whether control can be negotiated after twenty years of dispute over the issue; if the conclusion is that it cannot, then Iceland simply will not join.
art.179.title: Frjáls verslun 2. TBL. 2014: “Guðrún Hafsteinsdóttir is the new chair of Samtök Iðnaðarins. She wants to complete the EU talks but says joining the EU without exemptions in fisheries and agriculture is out of the question”
art.179.summary: An interview from Frjáls verslun in 2014 is recalled in which Guðrún Hafsteinsdóttir, then chair of Samtök Iðnaðarins, wanted to complete the EU talks. The thread contrasts that position with her current opposition to the talks as chair of Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn.
art.180.title: Why am I saying no at the end of August? - Vísir
art.180.summary: A user shares an article by Steingrímur J. Sigfússon, former chair of VG, on Vísir and echoes his doubts about Iceland’s room for manoeuvre in the talks. Iceland would seek “huge exemptions” in fisheries and agriculture that many mistakenly believe can be negotiated. Most comments in the thread disagree with the author.
art.181.title: Over 70 percent opposed to accession talks
art.181.summary: A user criticises an mbl.is report on a survey said to show that over 70% were opposed to the talks: the survey was sent only to 288 marketing and research contacts, and 80 responses were received (28% response rate). It therefore does not reflect a cross-section of the nation, and the presentation in Morgunblaðið is misleading; comments agree and discuss Mogginn’s propaganda mode in the run-up to the election.
detail.timagluggi.0: The YES side argues that Iceland currently has an exceptionally strong negotiating position and that this opportunity will not come again. Reference is made to a changed global landscape, increased EU interest in westward enlargement, and the possibility that the situation could change if the UK moves closer to the Union again or if Norway applies before Iceland.
detail.timagluggi.1: In an article on visir.is under the headline “An opportunity that will not come again”, economist Árni Gunnarsson says that the referendum provides the clearest picture of the national will, undistorted by the constituency system, and that current international circumstances make Iceland’s negotiating position unusually strong.
detail.skyrslan.0: The NO side questions whether the currency report, which the Ministry of Finance commissioned four foreign experts to prepare, can support the government’s core arguments for the euro. It is pointed out that the Central Bank of Iceland has criticised the report sharply and that, in the bank’s view, monetary policy and a floating exchange rate have served Iceland well.
detail.skyrslan.1: On Heimssýn’s website, it is also pointed out that one of the report’s authors, the Norwegian economist Hilde C. Bjørnland, believes that Norway itself should not adopt the euro because of the distinctive nature of its economy — and asks how her conclusions can then serve as a core argument for adopting the euro in Iceland.
motrok.timagluggi.0.title: The timing described as hard to understand — the EU itself in crisis
motrok.timagluggi.0.text: Kristinn Sv. Helgason, a public administration scholar, says the timing is simply wrong, not a unique opportunity: according to the Draghi report, the EU’s worsening competitiveness threatens its key objectives, and “significant political uncertainty prevails in key European Union states, such as Germany, France and Italy.” In light of the economic and political uncertainty surrounding the EU’s development, “the timing of the referendum is hard to understand.”
motrok.timagluggi.1.title: Negotiating position changes nothing — the framework has been fixed since 2010
motrok.timagluggi.1.text: Hreinn Loftsson, a Supreme Court lawyer, rejects the idea that a strong negotiating position matters: “The negotiating framework already defined in 2010 what was and was not on offer” and “the uncertainty therefore concerns only implementation within the system, not the fundamental issues themselves” — the EU’s requirements on the Common Fisheries Policy and internal market rules would remain unchanged whenever an application was submitted.
motrok.timagluggi.2.title: There is no rush — a costly process unlikely to deliver anything
motrok.timagluggi.2.text: Ingveldur Anna Sigurðardóttir, an MP for Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn, rejects the idea that this supposed opportunity must be seized now: the previous talks in 2009–2013 produced nothing, “we do not need the EU in order to get inflation and interest rates under control” and “we must not give up on governing ourselves” — a YES vote in August would commit the nation to a costly process that is unlikely to produce a result.
motrok.skyrslan.0.title: Minister of Finance: The criticism is neither justified nor fair
motrok.skyrslan.0.text: Daði Már Kristófersson responded in Alþingi to criticism of the interpretation of the report: the ministry’s discussion highlights five main conclusions, three supporting adoption of the euro and two supporting an independent monetary policy, and critics choose only what suits them. “I therefore find it difficult to agree that the criticism is justified and fair” — the króna is not useless and the euro is not flawless, and the conclusions should be discussed with the seriousness the matter deserves.
motrok.skyrslan.1.title: Minister advances the Central Bank’s own analysis
motrok.skyrslan.1.text: In response to the objection that a floating exchange rate has served Iceland well, Daði Már Kristófersson cites a 2012 special publication by the Central Bank itself — “the flexible exchange rate of the króna does not appear to be useful in protecting the domestic economy” from fluctuations — and points out that both new expert reports conclude that external factors drive inflation here: it was above 5% for 77 months in 1997–2020, but never above that threshold in the euro area during the same period.
motrok.skyrslan.2.title: "Currency depreciation does not increase the number of fish in the sea"
motrok.skyrslan.2.text: Minister Jóhann Páll Jóhannsson responds substantively to the shock-absorber arguments of krona supporters: Iceland’s main export industries cannot increase production even if the exchange rate falls — "currency depreciation does not increase the number of fish in the sea" — and he cites Indriði H. Þorláksson to the effect that devaluations "do not save the national economy from damage already done, but determine who bears it"; the ongoing cost of having the world’s smallest independent currency outweighs the benefits of the shock absorber.
arg.tollfrelsi.title: Tariff-free access and full processing at home
arg.tollfrelsi.text: Full membership would abolish EU tariffs on processed seafood products and make it possible to fully process the catch in Iceland instead of exporting it unprocessed; the added value and jobs would then remain in the country.
art.182.title: The nation called to the table
art.182.summary: A lawyer says membership is out of the question without the direct participation of the nation, and that the vote on 29 August is a democratic way to settle a dispute that has lasted for decades. The vote would not divide the nation; if the result is close, then it was already divided to begin with.
art.183.title: Let us join the EU
art.183.summary: A former provost supports joining the EU; he says people there know better how to deal with interest rates and indexation, and that the currency serves the public rather than only capital owners. The experience of the Southern Isles and Orkney with Brexit shows that the EU strengthens peripheral communities.
art.184.title: The marine resource in the EU
art.184.summary: A former Pirate Party MP rebuts claims that foreign vessels would seize Icelandic quotas and fishing communities would decline; vessels would need an Icelandic flag and fishing permits under Icelandic law. He cites EU Regulation 1380/2013 directly to argue that the interests of each member state determine the allocation of fishing opportunities.
art.185.title: “You know perfectly well what is in the package”
art.185.summary: Quotes Uffe Ellemann-Jensen saying that the contents of the “package” are already known. The application process is not a simple chat but adaptation to EU rules and administration alongside negotiations, as the Union’s documents and the words of Olli Rehn show.
art.186.title: What lies ahead?
art.186.summary: Responds to Björn Bjarnason’s criticism of the Foreign Ministry’s information page and reviews the supplementary material linked there, including all documents from the 2009–2013 negotiations. The vote is on continuing the negotiations, and an accession treaty would then be put to the nation.
art.187.title: To “look inside the package” that is already open
art.187.summary: The contents of the “package” were decided long ago; new states must adopt the entire EU acquis, and “Europe à la carte” belongs to the past. Cites Heather Grabbe of Bruegel saying that exemptions are no longer on offer, only transition periods, as Polish farmers experienced.
art.188.title: EU supporters — it is forbidden to deceive!
art.188.summary: Says the YES side uses misleading claims such as “let’s look inside the package” and “a seat at the table.” The euro does not automatically follow membership; strict Maastricht criteria on inflation and interest rates must first be met. It recalls the prime minister’s words that it is “forbidden to deceive.”
art.189.title: Prestigious posts on offer for EU states
art.189.summary: An MP from Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn points out that the most important chapters on fisheries and agriculture were never opened in 2009–2013. He recalls a bill stating that those who safeguard Iceland’s interests in negotiations may not accept posts with the EU immediately after leaving office, so that future appointments do not influence the negotiations.
art.190.title: Inga Sæland and independence
art.190.summary: The author does not want to “look inside the package” if that would mean surrendering the independence and self-determination that took the nation centuries to regain. Decisions about Icelanders’ welfare would be taken by others, and membership is likened to Siamese twins who cannot be separated; the Cod Wars and Icesave show that alliances do not protect Iceland.
art.191.title: The EU package is wide open
art.191.summary: An MP from Miðflokkurinn says there is nothing unexpected in the “package”; the EU rulebook is already known and no permanent opt-outs are on offer. Cites Heather Grabbe at Bruegel as saying that 95% of the EU’s rulebooks are non-negotiable and that only the implementation timeline can be negotiated.
art.192.title: People who do not trust the nation to have the sense to decide for itself
art.192.summary: The executive director of Samfylkingin’s parliamentary group says the opposition does not trust the nation to decide its own fate. The vote is on negotiations, not membership, in a two-step voting process of the same kind that Sjálfstæðisflokkur and Framsókn themselves wanted in the 2009–2013 term.
art.193.title: I have paid for many years, yet I owe more
art.193.summary: A nurse describes how loans keep rising despite regular repayments; the student loan went from 4 to 8 million and the housing loan from 53 to 61 million. She wants to examine other options, look at the package, and says yes to continuing the accession talks.
art.194.title: The group that would benefit the most
art.194.summary: Responds to an article by Magnús Árni Skjöld Magnússon and says the arguments do not hold up; Draghi’s report describes a regulatory burden that holds back investment, innovation and productivity in the EU. The euro area’s low interest rates are a manifestation of economic stagnation, and membership would bring Iceland inside the Union’s tariff walls.
art.195.title: The EU debate will not solve the economic problem
art.195.summary: An MP from Sjálfstæðisflokkur says the government has put accession talks on the agenda contrary to its pre-election promises and is using the debate to divert attention from the difficult economic situation. Broad consensus on membership, which the prime minister herself has said is a prerequisite, is not in place.
art.196.title: Yes or No – An attempt to frame the debate
art.196.summary: A lawyer and specialist in EEA law says opponents need to answer what advantages the EEA Agreement offers over full membership and why having a say in shaping the rules of the internal market is not desirable. Speculation about special arrangements will only be resolved by settling the matter in negotiations.
art.197.title: Why is the 2009 application to the European Union being hidden?
art.197.summary: A doctor recalls the 2009 parliamentary resolution and Iceland’s application letter to the EU and asks whether the vote is on continuing that application or on a new application. The question in the foreign minister’s parliamentary resolution proposal is deliberately incorrect and misleading; in reality, the vote will be on EU membership.
art.198.title: Quota hopping and the EU
art.198.summary: Responds to Björn Leví and says the right of establishment and the free movement of capital make quota hopping entirely legal in the EU; foreign fishing companies could buy Icelandic seafood companies and the profits could flow out of the country. The Factortame judgment shows that EU law trumps domestic laws on quota allocations.
art.199.title: The EU and fisheries: Who should control the waters off Iceland?
art.199.summary: Opening the fisheries chapter would mean transferring part of fisheries management from Icelandic jurisdiction into the EU’s Common Fisheries Policy, where quotas are a political compromise rather than a scientific outcome. The Icelandic system is an international model of sustainability, while the EU system struggles with discards and weak enforcement.
art.200.title: A real betrayal of the nation’s sovereignty
art.200.summary: Says claims that negotiations inevitably lead to membership are a snowball fallacy; Norway rejected membership twice in referendums after negotiations. Iceland already implements 70–80% of EU legislation through the EEA without voting rights, and the króna benefits quota kings and capital owners more than the general public.
art.201.title: "Can this be substantiated"
art.201.summary: Points out that the explanatory notes to the Minister for Foreign Affairs’ parliamentary resolution proposal acknowledge that accession negotiations are about new states adapting to EU rules. The process therefore entails adaptation alongside negotiations, in line with the Union’s own documents.
art.202.title: A non-political factoid about the EU
art.202.summary: A Centre Party MP criticises the University of Iceland Science Web for Eiríkur Rögnvaldsson’s biased response that the Icelandic language would be best protected within the EU. The Union’s guiding idea, he says, is the economic and political integration of states, which carries more weight than the distinctiveness of nation states.
art.203.title: The path of Sigmundur Davíð and Trump, or more options for Iceland?
art.203.summary: A board member of Ungir Evrópusinnar and Uppreisn links the Centre Party to the isolationism of the Trump movement. The vote, she says, is about gathering information and getting an agreement on the table, not about joining, and she rejects what she calls fearmongering by isolationists.
art.204.title: They want to lead the nation blindfolded to Brussels
art.204.summary: An assistant to the Independence Party parliamentary group says the date, 29 August, was chosen deliberately so that no parliamentary debate would take place before the vote. The Prime Minister and the Minister for Foreign Affairs have both said that people do not need all the information about the EU in the run-up to the vote.
art.205.title: The nurse who owes more, is making a fortune, and wants to peek inside the package
art.205.summary: The chair of Heimssýn responds to an article by Berglind Guðmundsdóttir and calculates that the nurse has grown richer by 18 million due to rising property prices. Real interest rates on mortgages vary between eurozone countries, and membership comes with hefty bills: membership fees, an expanded bureaucracy, militarisation and tariff wars.
art.206.title: In the European Union, workers’ rights are on the market’s terms
art.206.summary: Says EU labour legislation is based on market principles; the Union’s agreement with Moldova allows large corporations to exploit the poor conditions of workers on Europe’s periphery. Iceland, it says, has an independent labour-market model with statutory rights through the EEA and should not become part of such a system.
art.207.title: Þorgerður Katrín does not trust the nation
art.207.summary: Says the Minister for Foreign Affairs is fostering misunderstanding by talking about “peeking inside the package”; under the EU’s own definition, formal accession negotiations are preparation for implementing the Union’s laws and standards. The public is not being given accurate information about what a YES vote entails.
art.208.title: What happened to Ireland’s "special solution"?
art.208.summary: An economist explains that in 1973 Ireland negotiated only an adjustment within the Common Fisheries Policy, not a permanent exemption; power was transferred to the Union. The Hague criteria are not enshrined in the EU treaties, and disputes last winter show that they can be revised.
art.209.title: The lucky nurse who is supposed to make a fortune
art.209.summary: Responds to criticism from Haraldur Ólafsson; a paper increase in property values pays for neither food, heating nor electricity, and many people feel their debts are rising despite making repayments. Accession negotiations should be reopened so that Icelanders can have an informed debate and real choices.
art.210.title: Is the EU a "decline alliance"?
art.210.summary: Refutes the theory that EU cooperation causes economic stagnation; growth and unemployment differ widely among member states, and Poland is growing faster than Iceland. The stagnation since around 1975 stems from the 1973 oil crisis, not from the euro or the Union’s regulatory framework.
art.211.title: What happens if the majority says “yes” this summer?
art.211.summary: An MP for the Independence Party says Iceland’s alignment with the entire EU acquis would begin as early as September if the outcome is yes; this is stated in the explanatory notes to the proposal itself. No applicant country has received permanent exemptions, and Iceland is one of Europe’s richest nations, with a defence agreement with the United States and dozens of free-trade agreements.
art.212.title: Neither obtained permanent exemptions
art.212.summary: Malta and Norway both requested permanent exemptions from EU control over fisheries and were refused; the Norwegians received only a temporary adjustment period of just under four years. The only thing that can be negotiated is how and when power is transferred to the Union, not whether it is.
art.213.title: A national leader no one listens to anymore. What is she for, then?
art.213.summary: Says Kristrún Frostadóttir promised to avoid divisive issues, yet still put one of the most controversial issues in Icelandic politics on the agenda with a referendum on continuing the talks. The gap between the government’s promises and decisions raises questions about the prime minister’s credibility.
art.214.title: Can I also settle in euros?
art.214.summary: Points out that many of Iceland’s largest companies keep their accounts in euros, borrow in euros, and make contracts in euros for stability, while ordinary people are paid in krónur and bear the exchange-rate risk. Asks whether the euro could also create predictability for households.
art.215.title: Knowing more today than yesterday
art.215.summary: An MP for the People’s Party says it is never harmful to get more information; the nation will decide what happens next and will again have the final say on any agreement in a second vote. The Independence Party itself proposed in 2009 that the nation should first be asked whether talks should begin, and changes in world affairs call for a reassessment.
art.216.title: The homeowners’ association
art.216.summary: The deputy chair of the Independence Party compares the EU to a gigantic homeowners’ association in which the founders with the largest apartments decide almost everything and ten apartments out of 27 keep the building fund afloat. Iceland would be a net contributor, and the rules stipulate that the homeowners’ association controls the use of the “garden”, i.e. the resources.
art.217.title: Does it matter whether Jens Garðar is in parliament?
art.217.summary: Responds to Jens Garðar’s homeowners’ association analogy; since 1994, Iceland has been in “alignment” with EU rules without any representative at the table where the rules are made. The influence of small players depends on diligence, just as the MP from Eskifjörður has influence in Alþingi even though he is only 2% of its members.
art.218.title: Isn’t it time to stop demonising the Brussels bureaucracy?
art.218.summary: A young woman responds to criticism of the EU regulatory framework and says it is a defence against the harmful effects of unrestrained technological development, including digital gender-based violence that tech giants leave unchecked. The regulatory framework protects the public where American non-intervention does not.
art.219.title: Applauded the European empire
art.219.summary: Says the ultimate goal of the EU’s integration process is a single federal state and recalls that Guy Verhofstadt received a standing ovation at Viðreisn’s national convention for a speech about the EU as an empire. Iceland’s weight would be six MPs out of more than 700 and about 0.08% in the Council of Ministers, equivalent to a 5% share in one member of Alþingi.
art.220.title: I do not want an election this autumn on a possible EU application
art.220.summary: Says EU membership was only an election issue for one party with about 15% support, and it is therefore absurd to enter negotiations now; it would be more appropriate for parties to seek a mandate in parliamentary elections and then for the nation to vote on a completed agreement. He himself will vote no because he does not want to surrender the nation’s independence to EU institutions.
art.221.title: Special arrangements – not exemptions
art.221.summary: A European studies expert distinguishes between opt-out exemptions, which new states do not receive, and special arrangements within the regulatory framework that may be permanent; Danes, Malta, Sweden and Finland have all made use of them. The special nature of the Icelandic fisheries sector has no parallel within the EU, and Iceland could come to the negotiating table from a position of strength.
art.222.title: Unnecessary “search for truth”
art.222.summary: A cattle farmer says the EU’s interest in Iceland stems from the country’s strategically important location, not from a strong negotiating position. Living standards are good, the króna has been stable for six years, and negotiations are not a buffet of choices but submission to terms; none of the governing parties made much noise about the issue before the election.
art.223.title: …and I want the nation to have its say
art.223.summary: Responds to the argument that there should not be a vote because the EU was not a key issue in the parliamentary election; elections are never about a single issue but about an overall vision. A referendum is precisely the right tool to obtain the nation’s clear position, and nothing is more democratic than asking it directly.
art.224.title: Otherwise, the power would move to Brussels
art.224.summary: Permanent exemptions would be the only way to retain control over resources, but applicant states have never received them, as Andrés Pétursson himself acknowledges. Special arrangements such as the Finns’ Arctic agriculture and Malta’s 25-mile rule do not change the fact that ultimate authority over these policy areas would move to Brussels.
art.225.title: A peculiar harmony
art.225.summary: Says that two nations live in Iceland: companies that settle accounts in euros or dollars with access to lower interest rates, and the other one, stuck in the króna economy along with indebted individuals. Criticises the fact that members of SA are forbidden from discussing the pros and cons of EU membership and the euro at public meetings.
art.226.title: The codependent family
art.226.summary: Responds to Jens Garðar’s housing association analogy with another metaphor: Iceland is sometimes like a codependent family where one must not ask whether living standards could improve, interest rates fall, or food become cheaper. Accession talks are solely about exploring the possibilities.
art.227.title: A surrender of sovereignty – or not. Is that even a question?
art.227.summary: Reviews provisions of the EU treaties and says the member states unequivocally transfer part of their legislative and decision-making powers to the Union, including exclusive competence in the customs union and monetary policy. Such transfer is, by its nature, a surrender of part of sovereignty in defined areas.
art.228.title: Which eight billion, Þorgerður?
art.228.summary: Questions the foreign minister’s claim of an annual payment of eight billion due to the EEA; payments to the EEA Grants average about 1.7 billion per year. A direct payment to the EU would amount to about 38 billion annually, Iceland would be a net contributor, and imported goods from outside the Union would become more expensive because of its tariff walls.
art.229.title: What the foreign minister does not want to say
art.229.summary: A member of parliament from Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn says the foreign minister refused to answer questions at an open meeting of the parliamentary foreign affairs committee, including whether the government’s conditions would be “full and permanent control” over Iceland’s resources. The words appear only as a quotation referring to the objectives of the Jóhanna government, which are said to be “for guidance”.
art.230.title: Ireland vs. Iceland. Is there only one letter’s difference?
art.230.summary: Says the reduction in the Irish mackerel quota is based on ICES scientific advice due to overfishing and is not an example of the EU picking on a small nation. Fisheries account for less than 0.2% of Ireland’s GDP but around 6% in Iceland, and according to Eurobarometer, 91% of Irish people believe membership has benefited the country.
art.231.title: Monitoring the negotiations — banned for children!
art.231.summary: A pensioner compares opponents of the talks to the old Film Censorship Board that used to forbid people from seeing things; now, he says, they want to forbid the nation from seeing an unwritten agreement. The question is simple: the nation will itself vote on the accession treaty, and he says yes in order to know more.
art.232.title: A few words for the well of wisdom
