art.232.summary: A senior citizen mocks the NO side’s arguments about a “burning house” and lost sovereignty; there is hardly more sovereignty in sitting out in the corridor and receiving regulations than in sitting at the table where decisions are made. Welcomes the government for keeping its election promise on holding the referendum.
art.233.title: The EU customs union and the limits of “special arrangements”
art.233.summary: An economist says the customs union falls under the EU’s exclusive competence; tariffs between member states are abolished from day one, and it is not possible to negotiate a postponement of tariff-free treatment for agricultural products. The Finns tried that without success, and in Iceland’s 2009–2013 talks the Farmers Association’s demand for continued tariff protection was considered unrealistic.
art.234.title: What the MP wants to say
art.234.summary: A Viðreisn MP responds to Diljá Mist and says allegations of secrecy over ministers’ communications with the EU are insinuations; ministers’ schedules are public. Iceland has full and permanent control over its territory, and the Minister for Foreign Affairs has clearly said that Iceland’s control over its fishing jurisdiction must be ensured.
art.235.title: Agreed terms betrayed by the EU
art.235.summary: Responds to Andrés Pétursson and says the core of the Ireland issue is that the special arrangement the Irish believed they had, the Hague criteria, proved worthless when tested; the most populous states prevented it from being honoured by virtue of their population size. The Common Fisheries Policy falls under the EU’s exclusive competence, where the majority rules.
art.236.title: I very much hope this is not true
art.236.summary: An Independence Party MP cites people in the business community who ask whether the government is keeping the economy in disarray to increase the chances of a YES vote in the referendum. Refers to remarks by Kristrún Frostadóttir from 2024 that support for EU membership increases when inflation and interest rates are high.
art.237.title: He who has the power decides!
art.237.summary: Responds to Erna Bjarnadóttir and says the Irish did not define fisheries as economically important when joining in 1973, but instead relied on the Hague criteria, which are not part of the EU’s primary law. If Iceland’s authority is tied down in an accession treaty, it cannot be changed except with the approval of all member states, including Iceland.
art.238.title: To reject talks is to reject information
art.238.summary: The chair of Evrópuhreyfingin says the vote is about continuing the talks, not membership; talks are a way of obtaining information so the nation can make an informed decision later. Rejecting talks is a decision not to want to know more, while Iceland already adopts a large part of the EU acquis without a seat at the table.
art.239.title: Half-truths and falsehoods by Magnús Árni Skjaldar Magnússon
art.239.summary: Responds to an article by the chair of Evrópuhreyfingin and says he is repeating falsehoods that talks are a simple information exchange. According to the EU itself, accession talks involve adopting the Union’s existing laws and implementing reforms, not neutral information-gathering.
art.240.title: Iceland in the European Union
art.240.summary: Reviews the EU’s division of powers under the Treaty of Lisbon and says the member states are in charge; Iceland would get six Members of the European Parliament and representatives in the Union’s institutions. Says opponents of Europe rely on misrepresentations and conspiracy theories from social media.
art.241.title: Could Agree with Himself
art.241.summary: Points out that the chair of Evrópuhreyfingin himself said in January that willingness to join was a prerequisite for negotiations, but now claims it is possible to apply just to see what is on offer. The EU negotiating framework states that the common objective of an application is membership, and the process involves adapting to the Union’s regulatory framework.
art.242.title: Those Who Go to Sea Do the Fishing
art.242.summary: The Minister for Foreign Affairs says Icelandic fisheries are strong and that the negotiating objectives from the last round of talks still stand: control over the fishery resource and a share in shared stocks. The EU rule on relative stability means that other nations would not be permitted to fish within Icelandic jurisdiction; the fisheries and agriculture chapters would be opened as early as possible.
art.243.title: Should the National Electoral Commission Comment on the Question?
art.243.summary: Compares the wording of the question with the Venice Commission standards of the Council of Europe that referendum questions should be clear and not misleading. The words “continue” imply a process already under way, but according to the explanatory notes to the proposal, talks would have to be restarted under rules set by the EU.
art.244.title: Good to Get That Clarified, Þorgerður
art.244.summary: Responds to the Minister for Foreign Affairs and says the rule on relative stability in fishing provides no guarantee; it has no basis in the Treaty of Lisbon and could be abolished by a qualified majority in the Council of Ministers. Ireland’s experience of a comparable agreement shows that control over fisheries policy would pass to the EU.
art.245.title: Two Things Can Be True at the Same Time
art.245.summary: The Minister for Foreign Affairs says there is no contradiction in wanting to strengthen ties with Europe and see what is on offer by having a seat at the table, while at the same time defending sovereignty, culture and language. For a small nation, active participation in international cooperation is a prerequisite for defending its interests, values and standard of living.
art.246.title: Just as Well the Nation Doesn’t Know Too Much
art.246.summary: An MP from Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn says the government does not trust the public with accurate information; the explanatory notes to the parliamentary resolution itself state that negotiations are about applicant countries adapting to EU rules. The date of the vote was chosen to minimise debate.
art.247.title: Do States Become Poor by Joining the European Union?
art.247.summary: Rejects the argument that Iceland would lose out by being a net contributor: new member states have experienced rapid economic growth (Romania +558% since 2004), and contributions are based on a proportion of national output. Icelandic institutions and municipalities could apply for substantial infrastructure grants, and experience of the EEA shows that more comes back in return.
art.248.title: Six Reasons to Vote Yes to EU Talks
art.248.summary: Sets out six arguments for yes: the nation should decide, Iceland has taken major decisions before in difficult times, a customs union provides shelter in tariff wars, and the króna costs households and businesses 170–270 billion a year in higher interest rates. A yes in August is not membership but keeping the door open.
art.249.title: Special Interests or the Public Good
art.249.summary: Says politicians who once called for a referendum on the EU are now fighting against letting the nation take a position. There are strong links between politics and special interest groups — fisheries, banks and real-estate companies — that profit financially from high interest rates and indexation outside the EU.
art.250.title: Do You Want to Know?
art.250.summary: Reviews the history of the EEA Agreement and the freezing of the talks in 2013, and says that no member state has lost sovereignty, independence or resources. Croatia got much lower interest rates and greatly increased investment after accession and adopting the euro; Iceland has the highest policy interest rates in the Nordic countries.
art.251.title: Dividing the nation down the middle
art.251.summary: Says that feelings of inferiority about a small population and lack of influence were not appropriate in the Cod Wars and do not apply now either. The nation is divided: one half settles accounts in euros or dollars, while the other is locked inside the krona economy with high interest rates and the burden of inflation.
art.252.title: Is my sovereignty now to be taken from me?
art.252.summary: A short article in which the author says he wants to see an agreement on the table so that he can take an informed position as a sovereign voter. It is a serious encroachment on his sovereignty when others want to decide on his behalf that he should never get to see what the arrangement would look like.
art.253.title: The fear of no
art.253.summary: Says the government majority is talking down to the nation out of fear of a no vote. Cooperation among European nations is good through the EEA Agreement and independent agreements, but it would be unwise to join the EU and surrender the right to negotiate with nations outside the Union; the chair of Samfylkingin has gone back on her word.
art.254.title: Speaking against what the EU itself says
art.254.summary: Quotes EU documents stating that the adoption and implementation of the regulatory framework is the basis of the negotiations and that their speed depends on the applicant country's adaptation. The same appears in the explanatory note to the foreign minister’s parliamentary resolution proposal; a yes is therefore a commitment to a years-long adaptation process, not simple talks.
art.255.title: No negotiations anymore - only an application for membership
art.255.summary: Says the EU no longer offers negotiations like those Norway once had; now states apply for membership and gradually adapt to the regulatory framework. An EU booklet and the words of the enlargement commissioner make clear that no permanent exemptions are on offer, only temporary special arrangements.
art.256.title: Putting your fingers in your ears and calling it policy
art.256.summary: Points out that there is no legal obligation to vote on negotiations; the referendum is an extra step to make the process more democratic by involving the nation at both stages. Negotiations are not membership but a way to get the facts on the table, and a no would freeze the issue for many years or decades.
art.257.title: Take your sovereignty away, Eiríkur??
art.257.summary: Responds to an article by Eiríkur Hjálmarsson and says supporters of the European Union cannot explain what information would be obtained from an accession treaty that is not already available. The application process is years-long and costly and consists mainly of adapting to the EU’s regulatory framework and administration before any agreement would be on the table.
art.258.title: Europe for Icelanders
art.258.summary: Looks at the issue from the perspective of household finances: fluctuations in the krona, higher interest rates, and limited competition in a small market drive up everyday costs. European regulations have lowered consumer costs, for example by abolishing roaming charges and limiting banks’ card fees.
art.259.title: Misdirecting the debate on the EU
art.259.summary: Says opponents distort the term accession negotiations into “adaptation negotiations” and rely on 15–17-year-old quotations taken out of context. Reports prepared at the initiative of Guðlaugur Þór confirm that the accession negotiations were never formally terminated, only paused in 2013.
art.260.title: The National Electoral Commission comments on the question
art.260.summary: Points out that the opinion of the National Electoral Commission echoes its earlier criticism: the wording “continue negotiations” is based on a disputed premise and could affect voters’ understanding. If the question needs to be changed in substance, the nation is in reality being asked for a different mandate than was originally envisaged.
art.261.title: The light put out on the rubbish heap
art.261.summary: Reviews documents from the Ministry for Foreign Affairs from August 2025 confirming that the accession application from 2009 was never formally withdrawn; that the EU never regarded the letters from the Icelandic authorities as a withdrawal. Criticises Björn Bjarnason and Gunnar Bragi Sveinsson for claiming otherwise.
art.262.title: Don’t we have enough to do with our money?
art.262.summary: Asks what the vote is actually about when the Prime Minister says it is not a vote on joining; accession talks involve adapting all legislation to the EU, and no permanent exemptions are available in fisheries and agriculture. The cost of “taking a look in the package” would run to hundreds of millions that would be better used at home.
art.263.title: Sólveig Anna on the position of workers inside or outside the EU
art.263.summary: Responds to the chair of Efling and says the Icelandic labour market system would continue within the EU, as in Denmark and Sweden; the EU sets only minimum rules. Iceland already follows European labour market rules through the EEA without influence, and stability in the currency and interest rates would give workers job security and better conditions.
art.264.title: In the interests of households… outside the EU
art.264.summary: Points out that the EU warned Poland and Spain that lowering VAT on fuel would violate European legislation; a comparable anti-inflation measure by the Icelandic government would therefore have been blocked within the EU. The interests of the Union always take precedence over the interests of the inhabitants of individual states.
art.265.title: The interests of wage earners and the European Union
art.265.summary: Says persistent unemployment and stagnation characterise the EU, and that the euro’s fixed-exchange-rate policy shifts fluctuations into employment levels. The EU adopted a minimum wage directive in 2022 despite protests from the Danish and Swedish governments and labour movements, and the Court of Justice of the Union rejected the demand to annul it.
art.266.title: Iceland’s negotiating objectives must not be a secret
art.266.summary: Reviews Iceland’s negotiating objectives in 2010 and says they conflicted with EU rules: the Common Fisheries Policy gives the Union exclusive authority over the conservation of marine biological resources under Article 3 TFEU, and agricultural tariff protection is incompatible with the common market. The issue was therefore a systemic clash, not a minor adjustment.
art.267.title: Would Icelanders be conscripted into a European army?
art.267.summary: Refutes claims that Icelanders would be conscripted into a European army: Article 42 of the treaty respects the constitutional particularities of states, and NATO commitments take precedence; establishing an army would require unanimous approval. In the last negotiations, the defence chapter was opened and closed on the basis that Iceland would remain without an army.
art.268.title: Iceland’s adaptation to the EU: Three different channels
art.268.summary: Analyses Iceland’s relationship with the EU in three channels: EEA implementation without participation in decision-making, voluntary cooperation such as Schengen, and the accession process with IPA support. Iceland has adapted to the EU regulatory framework for more than three decades, and the referendum is about on what basis that cooperation should continue.
art.269.title: In brief: Misleading talk about adaptation talks
art.269.summary: A Samfylkingin MP says talk of adaptation is misleading: a report on the progress of the negotiations from April 2013 states that the negotiating parties agreed that Iceland would not undertake changes to institutions or legislation until after a referendum on an approved agreement had been concluded.
art.270.title: Sovereignty or the EU: Who pays the household bills?
art.270.summary: Says an informed nation has a duty to examine the terms of an accession treaty before taking a position; that is neither weakness nor a surrender of sovereignty. Opposition is rooted in broken trust in the political class and the gap between the capital area and rural Iceland rather than in the substance of the issue.
art.271.title: How does this claim hold up, Dagur?
art.271.summary: Responds to Dagur B. Eggertsson and says that claims that no adaptation would be required until after a referendum do not hold up: an EU press release from December 2012 states that Iceland would need to continue delivering results in adapting to and implementing the acquis, including in chapters outside the EEA.
art.272.title: 30 years of adaptation without influence
art.272.summary: Says Iceland has adapted to EU rules for 30 years without any involvement in shaping them, and that dire predictions about the EEA have proved exaggerated. The rule of relative stability ensures fishing track record, and the EU Director-General for Maritime Affairs and Fisheries has confirmed numerous examples of consideration being given to the particular characteristics of applicant countries.
art.273.title: This is what the EU minutes of 18 December 2012 say about adaptation
art.273.summary: Describes minutes of the EU Council from December 2012 stating that progress in Iceland’s accession talks depended on progress in adapting to the acquis; requirements for legislative changes and administrative capacity in taxation, monetary affairs and regional policy applied while the talks were under way, not after a final agreement.
art.274.title: The perfect (European) union
art.274.summary: Compares opposition to the EU to Seinfeld characters who end relationships over trivial details; rumours about bent cucumbers and power in Brussels must not come at the expense of security, stability and lower consumer prices. Brexit shows the regret that follows when a decision is driven by information disorder.
art.275.title: Adaptation is part of the accession process
art.275.summary: Says that an application under Article 49 of the Treaty entails joining the Union with its existing acquis, and that screening reports require legal adaptation while negotiations are under way. In the 2009–2013 talks, the agriculture and regional policy chapters were never opened, and IPA grants were directed at adapting the administration.
art.276.title: It may be old if it suits me
art.276.summary: Says the term adaptation talks describes the process better than accession talks, and cites the EU Commissioner for Enlargement as saying that the process largely concerns adapting the applicant country’s legislation. His critic himself refers to older sources than the ones he complains about.
art.277.title: A well-founded conclusion by the Venice Commission
art.277.summary: The chair of the Foreign Affairs Committee says the opinion of the Venice Commission confirms that the voting arrangements comply with European standards; the vote concerns the continuation of the negotiation process, not entry, and the final outcome would be put to the nation in a second vote.
art.278.title: “It is more blessed to give than to receive” – What can we contribute within the EU?
art.278.summary: Asks what Iceland can contribute within the EU: culture, a tradition of peace, equality, education and knowledge of the sustainable use of marine resources. Good agreements would ensure security, freedom of trade and comparable growth, and the voice of a small nation can carry considerable weight.
art.279.title: Fisheries, food security and global developments
art.279.summary: Says the EU has confirmed that only temporary special arrangements are available in fisheries, which does not change the fact that power would pass to the Union. Fisheries are the second-largest export pillar and the lifeblood of rural communities, and growing global emphasis on food security further increases their importance.
art.280.title: Deliberate deception and information disorder about sovereignty
art.280.summary: The chair of the Labour Council of Sjálfstæðisflokksins says claims that Iceland has implemented up to 80% of the EU acquis are deceptive; according to the report Gengið til góðs, the proportion is 13.4%. EU procedures have changed since the Norwegians’ time, and real adaptation now takes place continuously throughout the process.
art.281.title: Let us speak loudly and proudly about peace; say no to militarisation
art.281.summary: Says the EU has been on a path of militarisation and warns against a “military Schengen”, a regulatory proposal from November 2025 on the rapid movement of soldiers and military equipment within the Union. Iceland should keep its own voice for peace and not adopt the EU’s foreign policy.
art.282.title: Rattling around in an old Land Cruiser in a national referendum
art.282.summary: Compares voting no to refusing even to inspect a dream car for fear of possible defects and thus missing the opportunity. The vote is about talks, not membership; the nation would get the agreement in hand and say yes or no in a later referendum, while no is a lost opportunity that will not come again.
art.283.title: Impact assessment: What membership would mean for the average Icelander
art.283.summary: Authors with experience in advocacy in Brussels present an impact assessment for undecided voters: adopting the euro would lower housing interest rates by 200–300 points and could increase international trade by up to 60%, although the króna has historically served as a shock absorber in times of crisis.
art.284.title: When fear becomes an argument
art.284.summary: Accuses EU supporters of fearmongering: Iceland is said to be on the brink of ruin unless it votes yes. EU member states themselves are grappling with debt problems, slow economic growth and internal tensions, and ideas about turning the Union into a federation are being aired by influential figures within it.
art.285.title: Lower interest rates are the BIG ISSUE
art.285.summary: Compares debt-service costs: on a 60 million króna loan over 25 years, monthly payments are 509 thousand with króna interest rates but 293 thousand with euro interest rates, and total payments are 152 million versus 88 million. Contractors pay roughly four times the financing cost during the construction period compared with the euro area.
art.286.title: Why are interest rates low, Dagur?
art.286.summary: Says a shortage of building plots in Reykjavík under Dagur’s leadership is the main cause of inflation and interest rates, not the króna, and cites Gylfi Magnússon as saying that the overall framework matters more than the currency. To adopt the euro, inflation and interest rates would first have to be brought down, and the euro area’s low interest rates are explained by economic stagnation.
art.287.title: When the conclusion comes before the analysis
art.287.summary: Criticises the “impact assessment” by Matthías Ólafsson and Caileans Macleod and says the conclusion was predetermined: grain products are already duty-free to Iceland, and with membership tariffs would be imposed on goods from third countries such as the United States. Claims about lower food prices are made without numerical support.
art.288.title: Municipalities in Iceland and the European Union
art.288.summary: A Viðreisn MP says membership could strengthen municipalities: access to EU grant and development funds for infrastructure building, environmental projects and innovation, along with lower interest rates and a more stable currency. European regional development funds could create job opportunities in rural areas and reduce depopulation.
art.289.title: When continuation becomes a setback
art.289.summary: Compares the EU to the fall of the Roman Empire: a growing burden of regulation, economic fatigue in Germany and France, political division and costly militarisation. The referendum on “continuing talks” exposes weaknesses in the process itself.
art.290.title: It would come out of our own pockets
art.290.summary: Points out that the chair of the Foreign Affairs Committee has admitted that Iceland would be a net contributor to EU funds; the difference would amount to several billion krónur annually. Grants to municipalities would therefore in reality come out of the public’s own pockets, and it would make more sense to use the money for development at home.
art.291.title: Going behind Parliament and the people’s backs?
art.291.summary: Reviews materials submitted to the Foreign Affairs Committee that indicate the Minister for Foreign Affairs began talks with EU leaders about a new accession process as early as January 2025, long before the matter came before Alþingi in March 2026. Asks whether it is now government practice to prepare major issues in discussion with foreign actors before Parliament and the public get them for consideration.
art.292.title: Iceland should become part of a European federal state
art.292.summary: Reviews the Schuman Declaration and says the ultimate goal is a European federal state; the main EU institutions are federalist, and Evrópuhreyfingin is a member of European Movement International, whose main objective is a federal state. Guy Verhofstadt reportedly said at Viðreisn’s national congress that the EU needed to become an empire.
art.293.title: Was the wording of the question shaped in Brussels?
art.293.summary: Discusses a report by the European Parliament Research Service from January 2026 which specifically addresses the importance of how the referendum question is worded and treats Iceland’s application as a live process that was never withdrawn. Asks whether this amounts to interference in Iceland’s political debate.
art.294.title: International cooperation is vital for Icelanders
art.294.summary: The chair of Heimssýn rejects the idea that people skeptical of EU membership are opposed to international cooperation; free trade with the outside world is vital for Icelanders. On joining, Iceland’s negotiating power would be diminished because the EU would handle trade agreements with states outside the union on behalf of all member states.
art.295.title: The question changed — but not the underlying assumptions
art.295.summary: The wording of the question was changed to “resume talks” following criticism from the Venice Commission, the National Electoral Commission, and Carl Baudenbacher. However, the majority opinion of the Foreign Affairs Committee still rests on the premise that the 2009 application is “still valid” and that talks should continue. Iceland has nevertheless been removed from all official EU lists of applicant countries.
art.296.title: Who is in charge in the Barents Sea?
art.296.summary: The EU has pressured the Norwegians to scale back fisheries cooperation with the Russians in the Barents Sea, but Norway is holding on to its sovereign authority as a coastal state. The conservation of the biological resources of the sea falls under the EU’s exclusive competence, and academic literature confirms that no permanent exemptions have been granted in fisheries. This explains why Norway rejected membership in 1994.
art.297.title: Ólafur Ragnar and handball
art.297.summary: An MP from Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn refers to an interview with Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson in which he warns against a “reckless rush” in foreign affairs. The government is moving the EU issue with undue haste, and Alþingi is being given only four days for debate. Iceland has achieved unique economic success by virtue of its independence.
art.298.title: Yes, truly a magnificent defence
art.298.summary: Iceland would be a net contributor to EU funds and would receive less back than it paid in, including in regional and agricultural subsidies. The euro area’s low interest rates are said to be a manifestation of economic stagnation. In the tariff war, the EU obtained worse terms from the United States than Iceland did and had to make concessions.
art.299.title: Where is Iceland presented as an applicant country?
art.299.summary: In the conclusions of the Council of the EU from June 2024, Iceland is repeatedly referred to as an EEA and Schengen country, but nowhere presented as an applicant country or as part of the enlargement process. This is said to conflict with government claims that the 2009 application is still valid. The document also states that non-EU countries cannot enjoy the same rights as member states without the same obligations.
art.300.title: Icelandic soldiers?
art.300.summary: An MP points out that Europe’s security environment is changing dramatically: states are expanding their militaries, reinstating conscription, and Article 42.7 of the Treaty of Lisbon obliges member states to come to one another’s defence. Within the EU there are plans for its own armed forces, and the union’s foreign policy chief has called for a standing army of 100,000 troops. Nothing guarantees that Icelanders would not be called into a possible EU army, and Iceland’s position is strong with its defence agreement with the United States and NATO membership.
art.301.title: You can safely trust us
art.301.summary: Every voter can be fully trusted to answer a simple question on whether accession talks should be resumed. A changed world order and deteriorating rules of international relations for small states call for a reassessment of Iceland’s position. The EU’s values of human dignity, freedom, democracy and the rule of law are the same values on which Icelandic society is built.
art.302.title: The people will decide the course
art.302.summary: An MP for Flokkur fólksins says it is absurd for the nation to take a position on membership now, when the results of negotiations are not yet available; two referendums are envisaged, and the nation will have the final word on the agreement. She urges MPs not to muddy the debate with the false claim that negotiations amount to membership.
art.303.title: Dagur and Diljá – the verdict is in
art.303.summary: The editor of Verðbólguvaktin calculates that Dagur B. Eggertsson’s claim of 100 billion in annual interest costs for households because of the króna is more likely an underestimate than an overestimate; based on 2.896 trillion in housing debt and a 6.5–7 percentage point interest-rate gap, the cost could be 188 billion. Unemployment in Iceland is no longer lower than in the euro area, and housing costs are above the EU average.
art.304.title: Croatians and the benefits of EU membership
art.304.summary: A political scientist reviews Croatia’s experience since joining in 2013: the country has paid about 5.2 billion euros in membership fees but received about 30 billion in grants and foreign investment. GDP per capita has doubled, exports have increased by as much as 70%, and unemployment has fallen from 18% to 6%.
art.305.title: First information and stability, then a vote
art.305.summary: A Framsókn MP says it is only natural that the nation should get to vote, but the referendum must be based on neutral and transparent information and not be rushed through just before election day. Debate on the government’s fiscal plan is being drowned out by the EU noise while interest rates are rising and the position of households and businesses is growing heavier.
art.306.title: What would you do with an extra million a year?
art.306.summary: An MP points out that the króna’s interest-rate differential could mean one to two million krónur in lower annual interest payments for an average family with a 40 million housing loan. Large companies settle in foreign currency at lower interest rates while ordinary people are left stuck with the króna. The counterarguments resemble the fearmongering once used against the EEA, and reopening negotiations does not amount to joining.
art.307.title: Wind power – a new financial bubble in EU states?
art.307.summary: EU regulation, including the RED III directive, is driving rapid wind-power development that has proved financially inefficient; in Finland, the market value of wind power has halved since 2019 and pension funds have lost money on projects. Iceland already has sufficient clean energy from hydropower and geothermal power, and large-scale wind-power development would diminish the country’s wilderness.
art.308.title: Didn’t think we’d end up footing the bill
art.308.summary: Croatia has received about 20 billion euros more from the EU than it has paid into it, whereas Iceland would, by contrast, be among the net contributors financing such transfers. The states that pay more than they get back are in a small minority, and Icelanders would be paying for infrastructure development in Croatia and 16 other countries.
art.309.title: Voting for an opportunity, or rejecting it
art.309.summary: Once negotiations are concluded, there is an agreement that both Icelanders and the member states must approve; all 27 member states joined the Union through democratic processes because they saw it as serving their interests. The Icelandic economy is unusually vulnerable to shocks, as history shows, and the task is to reduce their number and their impact.
art.310.title: International cooperation on environmental issues: the EU as a driver of solutions
art.310.summary: A rebuttal to the chair of Heimssýn: the EU has been the continent’s most important instrument for turning international will into binding action, from acid rain and the ozone layer to the EU ETS emissions trading system since 2005. The Union implements international agreements faster and more strictly than international law requires, and uses the size of its internal market to drive technological change.
art.311.title: Does Iceland have to be the most expensive country in the world?
art.311.summary: According to an analysis by the economics department of Viska, prices in Iceland are 84% higher than the average in 27 European countries, and a grocery basket is 44% more expensive than in the other Nordic countries; a family of four could save up to a million a year on food purchases. The high cost of living is said to be a consequence of running an indexed krona with ever-rising policy interest rates.
art.312.title: The moneyed elite, populism, the horseshoe & the EU
art.312.summary: A lecturer at HR applies the elite theory of Mills and Domhoff to the Icelandic campaign: large employers and their interest groups defend the unchanged krona system and use their own media outlets against membership. The election campaign is marked by populist methods in the spirit of Müller — noise, accusations of betrayal and fear — and the far right and the farthest left use the same arguments against membership.
art.313.title: Taking an airplane apart in mid-flight
art.313.summary: The EU’s withdrawal clause is said to be more apparent than real, as the British found out in their exit process; the Union was above all concerned with deterring other states from taking the same path. Britain’s exit was nevertheless easier because it never adopted the euro — with the euro it would have been “comparable to a nuclear attack”. Leaving the EU and the euro is like taking an airplane apart in mid-flight.
art.314.title: The EU for the elite — or for the country’s ordinary people?
art.314.summary: A Samfylkingin MP says stability is the great equality issue: rising inequality, crushing interest costs and imbalances in the housing market make it harder for people to work their way up than before. Reduced currency risk would make it easier to maintain balance in public finances and give the children of future generations predictability and a stable interest-rate environment like that enjoyed by their Nordic peers.
art.315.title: Viðreisn’s soldiers
art.315.summary: A response to an article by Óðinn Freyr: Andrius Kubilius is not a Member of the European Parliament but the EU’s defence chief, the Union’s highest official in defence affairs. Numerous leaders, including von der Leyen, Juncker, Merkel, Macron and Sánchez, have expressed support for an EU army, as has the leader of the ALDE alliance to which Viðreisn belongs.
art.316.title: Not daring to talk to your neighbours
art.316.summary: A merchant compares talks with the EU to his own successful business dealings with foreign wholesalers, which began without all the answers being known in advance. Rejecting talks would rule out greater competition, more diverse banking services with lower interest rates, lower food prices, a real currency, and access to the Union’s funds for transport and fragile rural communities.
art.317.title: Whose interests are being protected?
art.317.summary: An MP from Flokkur fólksins asks whether the loudest objections to the referendum come from those who profit most from oligopoly and control over natural resources and fear EU competition rules. The vote on 29 August is about gathering information, not membership, and all parties have declared that membership will never be approved without full control over natural resources.
art.318.title: Czechs want to keep the krona, and the same arguments apply to Iceland
art.318.summary: The Czech government says the krona is key to economic sovereignty and intends neither to adopt the euro nor to take steps toward it, with even constitutional protection of the currency being discussed. With the euro, a state gives up an independent interest-rate and exchange-rate policy, and interest rates are determined by the circumstances of the largest countries. The same arguments are said to apply to Iceland as a small, open and volatile economy.
art.319.title: A tale of two kronas: The right to drown in the name of sovereignty
art.319.summary: Since 1970, the Danish consumer price index has gone from 100 to about 856, while the Icelandic one has risen to nearly 157,000. The difference lies in the institutional framework of monetary policy: Iceland used repeated devaluations as a hidden tax on households to rescue export companies, while the Danes pegged the krona to the euro through ERM II.
art.320.title: If Iceland applies for “the job”
art.320.summary: A response to Dóra Magnúsdóttir’s job-interview analogy: Iceland knows perfectly well what is in the package because 95% of EU law is non-negotiable, and the country would have to amend its constitution and recognize the primacy of EU law before a final decision is made. The process costs billions and would not be easily reversible.
art.321.title: Let us choose our future
art.321.summary: A woman in her early twenties says the vote is about her generation’s standard of living: high prices, limited competition, indexation, and interest rates. A yes to talks is not a decision on membership but on getting the facts on the table and putting any agreement to the nation. She points to Brexit, where older generations closed a door that young people have to live with.
art.322.title: We are all on the same team
art.322.summary: The author, who has lived in seven countries, says most people are aiming for the same goals — stability, lower interest rates, and a strong economy — and that the disagreement is about the route to get there. Iceland should calmly examine whether monetary cooperation or membership could help achieve those goals, and stop accusing those who want to explore the European path of being less Icelandic.
art.323.title: A burning house
art.323.summary: The phrase describing the EU as a “burning house” does not stand up to scrutiny: in the European Parliament’s survey from November 2025, 62% of residents of member states considered their country’s membership a good thing, including 86% in Ireland and 85% in Denmark and Sweden. Iceland has no more to fear than its Nordic neighbours.
art.324.title: Is there really nothing to negotiate?
art.324.summary: If there were nothing to negotiate, all member states would not have gone through years of accession talks. Talks are a way to find out what terms are on offer to Iceland, just as an employment contract is reviewed before it is signed. The cost of ignorance may prove greater than the cost of negotiations, and the nation can simply say no if the agreement is not in its interest.
art.325.title: What can be negotiated?
art.325.summary: EU information material itself says the term “negotiations” can be misleading; the talks concern the conditions and timing for adopting the Union’s regulatory framework, and Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos has emphasised this. Only special arrangements and temporary exemptions can be negotiated, not permanent opt-outs from the Union’s overarching authority.
art.326.title: What are you afraid of, Jón Pétur Zimsen?
art.326.summary: The author admits to having wrongly referred to Kubilius as an MP, but points out that a list of supporters of an idea is not the same as a binding decision — there is no resolution, decision, or treaty on an EU army. EU battlegroups from 2007 have never been deployed in a military operation because state sovereignty effectively prevents that. The core issue is economic security in a world of tariffs and trade sanctions.
art.327.title: Sustainable agriculture is a security issue
art.327.summary: A Framsókn MP says tariff protection is a prerequisite for Icelandic food production to remain viable under demanding conditions; if it were removed, family farms would be hit hardest, as they are the first to disappear when times get tough. It is irresponsible to promise consumers lower prices without answering what it would cost the Treasury — possibly 15 to 20 billion a year — to protect comparable production and settlement across the country.
art.328.title: Who won the Cod Wars?
art.328.summary: A response to articles by the managing director of SFS and the chair of Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn linking the Cod Wars to the EU referendum: the real winners of the wars were the fishing vessel owners, not the nation, because quotas were allocated for free in 1985 and transfers were permitted in 1991. The number of fishing companies has fallen from 350 to fewer than 50, and the five to eight largest control more than 60% of catch quotas.
art.329.title: When the debate and the facts do not match
art.329.summary: The claim that Iceland has fallen behind other European countries is completely false: Iceland ranks first on the United Nations Human Development Index (HDI), while the highest-ranked EU country, Denmark, is in 4th place. Iceland’s Gini coefficient (24,2) shows less income inequality than in Germany, France, and Italy, and the EU is not a single bloc when it comes to living standards.
art.330.title: The supposed festival of democracy
art.330.summary: A member of Til vinstri við ESB objects to the notion that people over 55 should not vote or ought to “vote correctly” for young people. The older generation remembers the Cod Wars and the pride of independence, and studies the issues for itself instead of letting algorithms or influencers form its views.
art.331.title: What is really being asked?
art.331.summary: A Progressive Party MP says it is wrong to frame the choice as cooperation or isolation; Iceland is already in the EEA, NATO and close Nordic cooperation. The question is whether decision-making power in important areas should be transferred to EU institutions and what permanent guarantees should be in place regarding control over natural resources before the nation takes a position.
art.332.title: I choose the hats myself
art.332.summary: The author rejects being a “hardline pro-European”, as Hjörtur J. Guðmundsson called her; she says she has not yet formed a final view on membership. Even so, she hopes the nation votes yes so it can see what is actually on offer to Iceland and make an informed decision on an agreement — which the nation could just as well reject, as the Norwegians did twice.
art.333.title: Snakes and ladders and the scam wheel
art.333.summary: Opponents of the vote make contradictory claims about the EU and discuss everything except the heart of the matter. The greatest benefit of membership and the euro would be tackling “usurious interest rates”: with the European Central Bank as a backer, interest rates could fall so that people’s loans become cheaper with every repayment, as has happened in other countries.
art.334.title: Iceland and the EU: negotiating objectives, accession talks and the euro
art.334.summary: The euro is not part of the accession talks but only comes into consideration after membership and after fixed conditions have been met for at least two years. The chances of the EU accepting Iceland’s demands for permanent exemptions as part of the union’s primary law cannot be considered high. The euro would have both advantages and disadvantages, and no objective yardstick determines what best serves Iceland’s interests.
art.335.title: Viðreisn’s soldiers and mannequins
art.335.summary: The MP’s third article in the exchange over an EU army: according to a poll for Politico in March, 69% of respondents in six EU countries support such an army, with the highest figure, 83%, in Belgium. The beginnings of an army are already in place, and it is to be expected that Iceland would be expected to contribute its share on an equal footing with other states.
art.336.title: Let’s get the agreement on the table
art.336.summary: The cost of the króna appears in higher interest rates, currency risk, more expensive financing and indexed loans that rise when households can least bear it. Indexation shifts inflation and exchange-rate risk from the financial system onto the public and reduces the effectiveness of monetary policy. The agreement should be put on the table.
art.337.title: Króna or euro? A debate that deserves more than slogans
art.337.summary: An MP from the Independence Party says the governing parties’ claims that households would gain hundreds of billions by adopting the euro are not supported by a recent currency report. The Central Bank Governor has pointed out that the path to lower interest rates is the same whether the currency is the króna or the euro: low inflation, responsible public finances and a stable labour market. Adopting the euro would mean surrendering independent monetary policy for a small, open economy with specifically Icelandic challenges.
art.338.title: Is the EU really this popular?
art.338.summary: A response to Pawel Bartoszek’s article on Eurobarometer: polls measure attitudes but do not prove that EU membership is more desirable than the EEA. Whole generations in member states have never lived under any other arrangement and have no personal basis for comparison; being content with a system one has always known is not the same as choosing it over a real alternative.
art.339.title: A “ram-style explanation” of Iceland’s fisheries mismanagement
art.339.summary: A response to the question “Who won the Cod Wars?”: the war over fishery resources is far from over. The author defends meetings of Til vinstri við ESB against accusations of supporting “oligarchs” and sets out the left-wing parties’ policy of taking the quota out of the hands of wealth and power and returning it to local communities.
art.340.title: A blank cheque with sovereignty at stake
art.340.summary: A former supporter of membership who changed his mind after looking into the issue: the acquis communautaire is not open to negotiation; the talks are about how and when the rules are implemented — adaptation is the accession process itself. Permanent exemptions are no longer part of the EU’s enlargement policy, and the currency debate is a false dichotomy between the króna and the euro.
art.341.title: What is the difference between Þorgerður Katrín and Donald Trump?
art.341.summary: Membership would mean legislative power shifting from Alþingi, judicial authority falling under the courts of the EU, and EU law taking precedence over national law. Foreign ministers have already undermined sovereignty through the Third Energy Package, Protocol 35, and ETS carbon charges, which have hurt Icelandic companies such as Play and Icelandair. Presenting the question as “innocent” is misleading.
art.342.title: Dear fellow citizens – Why should we say YES in August?
art.342.summary: A yes in August is a yes to information and negotiations, not to membership; we should look 20 to 100 years ahead. Young people live with higher interest rates and a more unstable environment than their peers in Europe, and start-up companies are moving their headquarters abroad. Small states such as Malta, Denmark, and Ireland show that sparsely populated nations can be influential within the EU.
art.343.title: Þorgerður seeks EU support from the most unlikely quarters
art.343.summary: The foreign minister is seeking support from foreign politicians who themselves are in a weak position at home; Beate Meinl-Reisinger, Austria’s foreign minister, has been heavily criticised for going against her own nation’s tradition of neutrality and for supporting European defence cooperation and armaments. Presenting such a politician as an ally is hardly a sign of a strong position for an unarmed republic.
art.344.title: Can we learn from Bjartur in Sumarhús?
art.344.summary: Bjartur in Sumarhús chose scarcity and hardship rather than relying on anyone; the desire to stand alone became so strong that he failed to see the value of cooperation. Talks with the EU are neither surrender nor a commitment, but a way to obtain information — an independent nation should dare to examine all options.
art.345.title: It would make no difference unless we join the EU
art.345.summary: A response to Berglind’s Bjartur analogy: Icelanders are among the peoples engaged in the greatest international cooperation, and cooperation on an equal footing is something entirely different from merging toward a federal state where influence depends on population size. Permanent opt-outs are not on offer, and alignment with the regulatory framework takes place in parallel with the negotiations, so the vote is about beginning entry into the Union.
art.346.title: The fish, the power, and the feeling of sovereignty
art.346.summary: Although transferring decision-making power over fisheries through membership is a real issue, the author asks what kind of power is actually being defended: quotas have accumulated in fewer hands, large companies settle accounts in foreign currency and mortgage fishing rights, while coastal communities experience declining influence. The nation’s legal ownership and the public’s real access to the value are two different things.
art.347.title: ETS, the EU and the EEA – Getting a seat at the table
art.347.summary: The CEOs’ call for a permanent solution for Iceland in the ETS system highlights the difference between the EEA and full membership: the EEA Agreement gives the EFTA states no formal role in shaping EU legislation, only adaptation texts after the legislation has been adopted. A permanent special solution in a system undergoing constant development will not be obtained through the EEA.
art.348.title: Yes, I support accession talks
art.348.summary: The economist stresses that opponents of negotiations have wrongly used his critical writings on the króna as arguments for their side; he wholeheartedly supports accession talks and will vote yes on 29 August. A no in August means it will not be possible to choose yes or no later, which is precisely why opponents of membership are urging people to vote that way.
art.349.title: From sovereignty to Brussels
art.349.summary: Reference is made to an article by the Irish scholar Patrick Murphy arguing that a series of decisions and the EU’s institutional development have gradually undermined Ireland’s neutrality, far beyond what was envisaged when it joined in 1973. Institutions evolve beyond their original role, including through the case law of the European Court of Justice, and states cannot know what they are signing up to for decades ahead.
art.350.title: Do as I say, not as I do!
art.350.summary: The same actors who defend the króna as an instrument of sovereignty — the large fishing companies and the biggest firms — themselves settle accounts in euros and borrow abroad on better terms, having effectively exited the króna economy while the public is left with volatility, inflation, high interest rates, and currency depreciation. The same hypocrisy as among car-city advocates who spend their summer holidays in Europe’s pedestrianised cities.
art.351.title: The world's most expensive country in the name of independence
art.351.summary: Debate in Iceland is said to be stuck in the past while Europe's leaders discuss security and the position of small states; Finland's President Stubb mentioned the referendum in Iceland specifically. The króna is said to be society's greatest source of instability, with high interest rates, indexation and exchange-rate fluctuations that affect households.
art.352.title: Should unread books be burned?
art.352.summary: Likens rejecting negotiations without seeing an agreement to burning unread books. Points out that 70–80% of EU residents want to remain in the Union and that a majority of Britons regret Brexit; says YES should be chosen for the sake of young people.
art.353.title: Was the negotiating committee working under Alþingi's mandate?
art.353.summary: The 2009 parliamentary resolution bound the negotiating committee to core interests concerning control over the fisheries resource. Cites a committee opinion from the German Bundestag stating that Iceland had not counted on exemptions in fisheries and asks whether the committee worked under Alþingi's mandate.
art.354.title: EU representatives on RÚV
art.354.summary: A former Minister of Fisheries and Agriculture describes the 2009–2013 application process as an adaptation process on the EU's terms; IPA grants were intended to facilitate institutional changes, and propaganda funding flowed into the country.
art.355.title: Dear fellow citizens – why should we say NO in August?
art.355.summary: Asks why people should say no to getting information and seeing what agreement Iceland could reach; the issue is bigger than party politics. Young people live with higher interest rates than their peers in Europe, and a changed security environment calls for examining what an agreement could bring.
art.356.title: Low unemployment? Let's look at the numbers
art.356.summary: The low unemployment figure is said to be misleading because disability in Iceland (9.4% of people of working age) is nearly double that in the EU and amounts to hidden unemployment; moreover, the misery index leaves out interest rates, which Icelandic households feel most strongly.
art.357.title: Stability or flexibility
art.357.summary: Reviews the findings of the Ministry of Finance's currency report: the euro could bring lower interest rates, lower transaction costs and greater stability, while the benefits of the króna have been overestimated. Responds to the reservations of the Central Bank Governor and says labour-market reforms are desirable regardless of currency.
art.358.title: Inflation or unemployment, which would you rather have?
art.358.summary: Inflation in Iceland is said to have been on average 0.8 percentage points higher than in the euro area in 2011–2025, while unemployment was 4.1 percentage points lower; having its own currency allows the economy to respond quickly to shocks and keep people in work.
art.359.title: Sorcerers of past centuries
art.359.summary: Criticises the currency report for being based on the assumptions of the crash years; with the euro, Iceland could not pursue an independent monetary policy and would become an "tiny crowberry" in an economy guided primarily by Germany and France.
art.360.title: Sovereignty is the foundation of flexibility: Why EEA cooperation is enough for us
art.360.summary: It is possible to support European cooperation while rejecting further transfers of power; the EEA and the four freedoms ensure market access without sacrificing the independent monetary policy, resource management and foreign policy on which the flexibility of the Icelandic economy is based.
art.361.title: The Faroe Islands are not in the EU, but…
art.361.summary: The Faroese króna is pegged to the euro via the Danish krone, and interest rates there are 1.6% compared with 7.75% in Iceland; the Faroe Islands are in practice part of the euro area and therefore not an example of a country doing well without cooperation with the EU.
art.362.title: Do Icelandic consumers have weaker rights than European consumers?
art.362.summary: Reviews rulings on compensation for air passengers and consumers’ choice of forum; the EU has responded to the globalization of consumer purchases with rules allowing consumers to pursue their rights before their own courts.
art.363.title: Let others pay
art.363.summary: Young people and smaller companies are stuck in the króna economy and bear the full burden of interest-rate hikes, while larger companies operate in euros or dollars; the opponents’ dire predictions about the EEA Agreement thirty years ago have proved groundless.
art.364.title: How wealthy are we really?
art.364.summary: GDP per capita overstates Iceland’s position because it is based on high labour-force participation and long working hours; productivity per hour worked is lower than in many EU countries, and lower capital costs would make it easier to invest in higher productivity.
art.365.title: A well-informed nation refuses to be played
art.365.summary: The government is said to have kept documents from voters in a locked room in Alþingi until the matter was decided; “looking inside the package” is said to be a deceptive tactic by supporters of accession, who have in reality never changed their view on membership.
art.366.title: When the EU bullies a small nation
art.366.summary: Reviews the territorial-waters disputes, the UK anti-terrorism laws of 2008, Icesave, and EU protective tariffs on ferrosilicon as examples of great powers and the EU system bullying a small state when interests clash; also mentions ETS charges and carbon taxes.
art.367.title: No one should push Iceland in through the back door
art.367.summary: Caution toward the EU is natural, but a yes to negotiations can only mean yes to putting the agreement on the table, not yes to membership; without an outcome, the nation chooses based on images and fear rather than Iceland’s actual interests.
art.368.title: Kos did not confirm the existence of an agreement
art.368.summary: RÚV is said to have wrongly claimed that Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos confirmed an agreement on there being no adaptation in earlier talks; the 2010 negotiating framework is still in force and provides for adaptation alongside the negotiations.
art.369.title: How do we safeguard Iceland’s independence for the future?
art.369.summary: Independence in the 21st century means choosing cooperation rationally; the vote is not about membership but about gathering information, and the nation itself will have the final say on approving or rejecting any agreement.
art.370.title: Freedom for young Icelanders in the future
art.370.summary: Describes the founding meeting of Ungir gegn ESB-aðild on National Day; the fight is for young people’s right to self-determination so that Icelandic politicians of the future will not be bound by the decisions of distant foreign officials.
art.371.title: EU membership is economically unwise
art.371.summary: Reviews the University of Iceland Institute of Economic Studies’ answers to nine questions from the Foreign Affairs Committee: GDP per capita is said to have grown nearly three times faster in Iceland than in the EU since 2010, the effects of the euro on prices and interest rates are uncertain, and monetary policy would be lost as an economic policy tool.
art.372.title: EEA for businesses, EU for people?
art.372.summary: The EEA is said to have benefited the business sector, but to have given the banks a European market with an Icelandic backstop and opened the labour market without a corresponding housing system; with the euro, inflation in Iceland’s small housing market would not alone determine the interest terms of all households.
art.373.title: Why not say No … why say maybe?
art.373.summary: The government itself chose to hold a vote on the process rather than the outcome; it could have finished an agreement and put it to a national referendum. No is presented as a legitimate position on timing, procedure and political mandate, not a “deprivation of rights” of other voters.
art.374.title: Who gets the seats at the table?
art.374.summary: Influence in the EU is determined by population size; Iceland would get 6 MEPs out of 726, about 0.08% voting weight, and its representative in the Commission would not be allowed to defend Icelandic interests. Politicians and civil servants are themselves said to have professional interests in the “seats at the table”.
art.375.title: I want to decide my own summer holiday
art.375.summary: Compares the talks to a package tour to Brussels where the small print must be read; there is said to be no need to look inside the package because the EU’s rules, powers and order of precedence are already known, and Iceland’s voting weight would be next to nothing.
art.376.title: A seat at the table – or a seat in the corridor?
art.376.summary: Responds to an article by Diljá Mist: Iceland currently adopts a large share of internal market rules from the corridor without voting rights, but under membership it would have representatives in the Council of Ministers, the Commission and committees; small states such as Malta, Luxembourg and Denmark are said to wield influence far beyond their population size.
art.377.title: Small nation, big opportunities
art.377.summary: Living standards are said to have improved greatly under self-government, and Iceland ranks highly in prosperity measures; the EU is said to struggle with slow growth and indebtedness, Iceland would pay more into the Union than it would get back, and the EEA already provides broad market access.
art.378.title: Do Icelanders vote with their feet?
art.378.summary: Nearly five times as many Icelanders live in eight Western European countries as citizens of those countries live in Iceland; migration flows toward those EU countries that offer the best living standards, and this is presented as a sign that Iceland has much to strive for.
art.379.title: You do not need the agreement to see what matters most
art.379.summary: The biggest issues are already set out in the EU treaties: about 0.09% voting weight in the Council of Ministers, six seats out of 720 in Parliament, the Union’s exclusive authority over the conservation of fish stocks, and no permanent exemption from the Common Fisheries Policy. Set up the website jatiladfela.com with sources.
art.380.title: The elephant in the room
art.380.summary: The currency debate is said to distract attention from surrendering sovereignty over resources and from effects on civil rights; the Common Fisheries Policy would shift power to Brussels, and EU instruments such as the “democracy shield” could constrain freedom of expression.
art.381.title: An agreement on the EU’s terms
art.381.summary: The negotiation framework from 2010, approved unanimously by all member states, provides for the adoption of the entire EU acquis and only temporary adjustment measures; ideas about permanent exemptions from the fisheries policy have no basis in official documents.
art.382.title: A momentous development
art.382.summary: Welcomes the fact that the nation will get to say yes or no on negotiations and points out that it still holds all the trump cards, since any accession treaty would go back to a referendum; criticises opponents’ „garbage claims“ about the EU as a „burning house“, recalling the doom-laden predictions made about the EEA.
art.383.title: Is a 25% reduction in food prices realistic with the euro?
art.383.summary: The 25% claim based on a single fast-food item is an oversimplification, but food prices would still fall over the longer term with the euro: the interest-rate differential affects every stage of the value chain, the exchange-rate premium would disappear, and tariffs weigh heavily in households’ grocery spending.
art.384.title: Brexit and Iceland - What can we learn, and where should we be heading?
art.384.summary: Ten years after Brexit, the British economy is said to be 6–8% smaller than it otherwise would have been, and 16.400 companies have stopped exporting to the EU; half of the blow is attributed to the uncertainty itself. Access to the single market is described as the lifeline of a small export-dependent economy like Iceland’s.
art.385.title: Would EU accession expand bureaucracy? The numbers say otherwise
art.385.summary: Claims that membership would bloat Icelandic bureaucracy do not stand up to scrutiny: Iceland ranks 15th on the World Bank’s government effectiveness indicator, there is no correlation between EU membership and inefficiency, and efficiency increased in Finland, Malta and Croatia after accession.
art.386.title: Food prices, tariffs and source work
art.386.summary: Viðreisn’s claims of a 25% reduction in food prices are based on weak source work; the drop in Finland after accession was closer to 10–11%, and developments in Sweden are largely explained by exchange-rate changes. The authorities could abolish tariffs immediately without EU membership.
art.387.title: Left waiting out in the corridor in hopes of news
art.387.summary: In negotiations on shared stocks in the North Atlantic, EU states such as Ireland and Denmark wait out in the corridor while Iceland, Norway and the Faroe Islands sit at the table; within the Union, Iceland’s weight would be only about 0,08% in the Council of Ministers.
art.388.title: Would Iceland become a fragile settlement?
art.388.summary: Iceland’s negotiating position is said to be greatly overestimated, given that Icelanders make up only 0,08% of the EU’s population; upon accession, foreign food chains could buy up the largest fisheries companies and ship fish abroad unprocessed, as there are already examples of.
art.389.title: Informed debate and the transfer of state powers
art.389.summary: Iceland has already transferred part of its state powers through participation in the ECHR, NATO, the defence agreement with the United States and the EEA; the country adopts extensive legislation through the EEA with very limited opportunities to influence it, while EU member states shape that legislation themselves.
art.390.title: Who owns this cottage? Yes or no?
art.390.summary: The vote is only on whether to seek negotiations, not on membership; many of the most important advances in consumer protection in Iceland have come through the EEA. It asks what vested interests fighting against negotiations fear might come to light.
art.391.title: The nation stuck in the Groundhog Day of the króna
art.391.summary: Inflation, high interest rates and exchange-rate volatility keep repeating as a systemic problem of a micro-currency; the same conditions as in 2005–2008 and 2016–2019 have re-emerged in 2024–2026, and the system amplifies fluctuations instead of spreading risk.
art.392.title: Negotiating with oneself
art.392.summary: Responds to the managing director of SFS: the right of states to bind themselves by treaties is an inseparable part of sovereignty and an exercise of it, not a surrender of it; cites Bjarni Már Magnússon and Einar Arnórsson to the effect that limiting freedom of action does not deprive a state of sovereignty.
art.393.title: Dear fellow citizens – Should we reject an agreement we have not seen?
art.393.summary: The vote concerns only obtaining an agreement so it can be assessed in an informed way; if it proves bad, the nation will reject it. Quotes Davíð Þór Björgvinsson saying that small nations within the EU receive support to preserve their language and culture.
art.394.title: Will Flokkur fólksins’s lust for power be its downfall?
art.394.summary: Flokkur fólksins is said to have betrayed its sovereignty policy for ministerial posts: backing Protocol 35 on the primacy of EEA rules contrary to earlier statements by Inga Sæland, and dropping the demand to withdraw the EU application.
art.395.title: Who has a fairer fatherland?
art.395.summary: Freedom and sovereignty are the cornerstones of society, and Icelanders have always wanted to govern themselves; the nation can itself change the banking system and society without interference from the EU or burdensome regulations from it.
art.396.title: The housing package
art.396.summary: Pro-EU advocates are selling the belief that membership will solve the housing problem, but an EU report shows that housing prices there have outpaced incomes and around 30% of people aged 25–34 still live with their parents; no “European average interest rates” await Icelanders.
art.397.title: Is the EU undermining its own interests?
art.397.summary: Describes criticism by Carl Baudenbacher, former President of the EFTA Court, that the EU is trying to move Iceland from the EEA into the EU; on the contrary, the Union should preserve the EEA as an important model of cooperation for the future.
art.398.title: Who owns the Icelandic flag?
art.398.summary: The managing director of SJÁ criticises the Icelandic flag having become a symbol of a particular political stance; no one has a monopoly on patriotism, and democracy is based on people being able to disagree and discuss the country’s future respectfully.
art.399.title: Speaking with two tongues
art.399.summary: Points to the hypocrisy of NO supporters, who say information is lacking yet themselves pretend to know everything about an agreement no one has seen; the Cod Wars show what a small nation can do instead of belittling itself into “5% weight” and standing silently out in the corridor.
art.400.title: “Get your own damn jack!”
art.400.summary: Tells the joke about a man who imagines the farmer’s hostile reception before asking to borrow a jack; the arguments of opponents of negotiations rest on the same kind of preconceived resentment instead of examining what is actually on offer.
art.401.title: Adopting the euro is risky for small economies
art.401.summary: A study by a Central Bank economist shows that a single monetary policy suits peripheral states poorly and that the opportunity cost is highest for them; Finland is struggling with 9.6% unemployment, and the currency report did not consider itself able to recommend adopting the euro.
art.402.title: Tried to prevent Iceland from getting justice
art.402.summary: Replies to Ingólfur Sverrisson: the EU backed the British and Dutch against Iceland in the Icesave case and entered the case before the EFTA Court; Iceland won through the strength of its sovereignty, as in the Cod Wars.
art.403.title: Thanks, but NO thanks
art.403.summary: Lists reasons for no: Iceland would pay more to the indebted EU than it would get back, alignment would begin immediately alongside the talks under the parliamentary resolution, there would be an EU army and upheaval in defence cooperation and free trade agreements, and neither the nation nor parliament supports the journey.
art.404.title: Yes, onward Iceland!
art.404.summary: Describes how generational shocks have taught Icelanders to accept conditions that could be changed; persistent inflation and interest rates that would be considered a state of emergency elsewhere are a storm the nation creates for itself, and yes would break the vicious cycle.
art.405.title: The professor, the economist and sovereignty
art.405.summary: Reviews the exchange of views between Margrét Einarsdóttir and Erna Bjarnadóttir and says the key is to distinguish between obligations under international law and the formal transfer of state power; according to the Supreme Court, the EEA did not entail a transfer of legislative power, but EU membership would go further.
art.406.title: The elite’s fear alliance in the ivory tower
art.406.summary: Replies to an article by Jón Pétur Zimsen and says it is a textbook example of fearmongering: the EU does not have an army and defence cooperation with the United States is bilateral. An elite that profits from monopoly, tariff walls and fluctuations in the króna does not want the public to be allowed to see the agreement.
art.407.title: The man who trusted the nation, but no longer does
art.407.summary: Points out that Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson, who referred Icesave to the nation twice in the name of democracy, now leads a movement against letting the nation vote; on Áfram Íslands’s speakers’ list, the CEO elite and labour leadership unite to shut the door before people see the agreement.
art.408.title: The illusion of lower housing costs with the euro
art.408.summary: Lower interest rates in euros do not lead to lower capital commitment when buying housing because property prices rise in response; adopting the euro caused housing bubbles in Spain, Ireland and Portugal, and residents of eurozone countries are on average older than Icelanders when they buy their first home.
art.409.title: Will we lose our sovereignty if we join the EU?
art.409.summary: Replies to Bjarni Már Magnússon: the question is not whether a state may join the EU, but what constitutional consequences membership has while it lasts; it would be more apt to compare membership to a broad power of attorney under which others are given real decision-making authority.
art.410.title: The agreement that everyone has read
art.410.summary: A satire of those who pretend to know exactly what will be in an agreement that no one has seen; the vote is about whether the nation gets to see the agreement before taking a position, and conviction is not the same as knowledge.
art.411.title: What do we know in August? Facts and possibilities for Iceland
art.411.summary: The vote would be on completing an agreement for the nation to assess afterward, not on membership; no one knows today how fisheries or resource issues would be resolved. Compares Iceland with Malta, where new mortgages carry interest of about 2% compared with about 10% in Iceland.
art.412.title: Can we do even better? Yes in August
art.412.summary: Iceland’s top place on the UN quality-of-life index is not an argument against membership, since seven EU states are among the top fifteen; the index measures neither interest burdens, indexation nor exchange-rate fluctuations. Iceland already adopts most internal market legislation without a seat at the table, and a yes vote commits no one to membership.
art.413.title: Military adventurism
art.413.summary: Rejects claims that the EU is moving toward conscription and a European army; defence matters remain under the authority of sovereign member states. Europe’s increased defence spending is explained by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and deterrence, while Icelandic households are fighting their own defensive war against the interest-rate system.
art.414.title: Efficient now, but not if we join the EU
art.414.summary: Cites an EU Commission MIPD document from 2011 stating that the Icelandic administration is too small to handle the obligations of membership and that major institutional expansion would be required. A response article to Halldór Jörgen Olesen; operations would be financed at the expense of the Treasury.
art.415.title: The individual and sovereignty
art.415.summary: A personal account of the 2008 crash in which the author’s 9 million housing loan became 34 million before it was ruled illegal. Sovereignty did not protect individuals when 10,000 families lost their homes, and the elite is now fighting against a different kind of economic system.
art.416.title: Information is not a threat; it is a prerequisite
art.416.summary: The vote is about getting an agreement on the table, not about membership, and no one makes a major decision without information. Quotes Churchill, Kofi Annan, Jón Sigurðsson and Mandela to argue that information and negotiations are prerequisites for a democratic decision.
art.417.title: What’s in the package?
art.417.summary: An applicant country must adopt all EU laws under the Copenhagen criteria, and the adaptation process would begin immediately after a yes vote. Iceland has implemented only 13.4% of EU acts through the EEA, and 13 policy areas that Iceland now controls itself would come under the EU; the euro is no magic solution.
art.418.title: New analysis: How much would mortgage interest rates fall with the EU and the euro?
art.418.summary: Presents an analysis by Professor Gauti B. Eggertsson of Brown University: repayments on a new mortgage would fall by a third with the euro, and asset accumulation would be much faster. The total annual cost of the króna to households is estimated at over 100 billion krónur a year.
art.419.title: On life and death, sovereignty and the EU
art.419.summary: Sets out the understanding of Bjarni Jónsson frá Vogi and Einar Arnórsson, architects of sovereignty in 1918, that international obligations are an expression of sovereignty rather than a limitation of it. A sovereign state itself decides which obligations it undertakes.
art.420.title: Brexit not the cause of Britain’s economic challenges
art.420.summary: Criticises the media for blaming Brexit for Britain’s economic difficulties; post-Brexit economic growth has been higher in Britain (1.4%) than in Germany, France and Italy. The Draghi report describes an economic existential crisis in the EU due to declining competitiveness.
art.421.title: The króna economy and household costs
art.421.summary: Prices in Iceland are 70–80% above the EU average, and devaluations of the króna amount to a transfer of wealth from households to export companies. It drives a cycle of the indexed króna in which inflation raises the principal of loans and erodes purchasing power.
art.422.title: On life and death, sovereignty and the EU II
art.422.summary: A follow-up article citing a 1962 lecture by Ólafur Jóhannesson arguing that membership in powerful international institutions does not generally deprive a state of its sovereignty. The concept of sovereignty is said to be relative and to adapt to the changing views of each era.
art.423.title: Carved in stone, or perhaps, possibly, maybe
art.423.summary: The obligations of membership are legally binding, but the promised benefits are only forecasts: the acquis regulatory framework is carved in stone, while lower interest rates and prices are uncertain. The European Central Bank sets interest rates with the largest economies in mind, and Finland received no exemption from the agricultural policy.
art.424.title: Quoting correctly
art.424.summary: A response article to Hjört J. Guðmundsson, whom the author says has misquoted him; Icelanders have often sought justice in foreign courts. There is nothing to lose by voting yes in August and seeing what agreement is on offer — knowledge is better than guesswork.
art.425.title: Why vote “No” on 29 August?
art.425.summary: Those who do well in the oligopolistic króna economy do not want to see the agreement, while the public pays many times over for their homes and the most expensive food in Europe. There is nothing to lose from negotiations, and the nation will have the chance to approve or reject the draft agreement.
art.426.title: Why I changed my mind about Iceland joining the European Union
art.426.summary: A lawyer and former supporter of membership changed his mind after reading the Treaty of Lisbon. The stated goal of an ever closer union among the peoples of Europe is said to point to political integration that runs counter to Iceland’s constitutional status.
art.427.title: Ask yourselves: Who does the Icelandic króna work for?
art.427.summary: Interest rates would fall sharply with the euro, according to an analysis by Gauti B. Eggertsson, and the thousand-billion foreign exchange reserve could be cut in half. Iceland is the most expensive country in the world, and the króna protects oligopoly; it works for capital owners, not wage earners.
art.428.title: Don’t regret your vote!
