art.428.summary: A young voter urges people to vote yes in order to see the agreement; the decision concerns the next 50–100 years. The opportunity may never come again, and the agreement can always be rejected later if it turns out to be bad.
art.429.title: In the voting booth, we are alone
art.429.summary: It outlines the process of a two-stage referendum: first on negotiations and later on a completed accession agreement; if the nation says no, nothing changes. The process is described as being as open, transparent and democratic as possible, and in the voting booth each person decides for themselves.
art.430.title: Yes or no? The vote on 29 August 2026
art.430.summary: It asks whether Iceland shares a common path with the diverse nations of the EU and points out that the EEA Agreement has served Iceland and Norway exceptionally well for 32 years. Membership would involve costly contributions to EU funds, and joining is not even under discussion in Norway.
art.431.title: The wrong question in the right debate
art.431.summary: Warns against conflating dissatisfaction with Iceland’s economic situation with the question of the EU; membership is not an economic measure and would not automatically solve problems that can be traced to the nation’s own decisions. Membership also concerns fisheries, agriculture, regional communities, and the scope for setting our own rules.
art.432.title: Who is running Kristrún Frostadóttir’s government?
art.432.summary: Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir is said to have taken the leading role in the EU issue while the Prime Minister remains silent; the National Electoral Commission made strongly worded comments about the leading wording of the question. It is not possible to enter into negotiations without a formal application for membership.
art.433.title: Wait! Aren’t we voting on the same thing?
art.433.summary: The vote is only about starting negotiations and obtaining an agreement that the nation would then assess for itself, but the debate is full of misinformation about the euro, fishing grounds, and a European army. The same fearmongering was heard about the EEA at the time, but the agreement turned out to be a major step forward.
art.434.title: RÚV’s bias in the EU debate
art.434.summary: Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten is said to have confirmed in the Dutch parliament that the EU’s fisheries policy is non-negotiable and that Iceland would have to surrender control over its resources. This is said to conflict with the Foreign Minister’s statements, and RÚV’s news desk remains silent on the matter.
art.435.title: The European Union and fisheries
art.435.summary: Iceland sells about 70% of its catch to the EU, and within the Union tariffs on processed fish would be abolished, so revenues could rise significantly. The rule of relative stability from 1983 ensures that no EU states can fish in Icelandic waters, and Iceland would become a leader in the Union’s fisheries management.
art.436.title: What do young people see that I don’t?
art.436.summary: An internationalist reflects on why young, well-educated people are leaning to the right and intend to vote NO. He himself wants to thoroughly examine what kind of accession agreement Iceland could obtain before taking a final position.
art.437.title: It pays to consider the options
art.437.summary: Echoes the Justice Minister’s call to consider the options, but asks why the nation is being given only a few weeks in the height of summer to discuss a matter that the Speaker of Parliament compares to NATO membership in 1949. The nation is not only being asked for information, but to approve an extensive accession process.
art.438.title: Maybe we are asking the wrong questions
art.438.summary: The question should be whether the króna system has lived up to expectations: households face one of the highest interest-rate levels in the developed world, and the króna’s flexibility comes at the cost of higher interest rates and uncertainty. Those who reject the EU owe the nation a credible plan for what should come instead.
art.439.title: The króna tax on the generations: the biggest tax in Icelandic history
art.439.summary: The small size of the króna creates a risk premium and higher interest rates that fall on households: the difference between 10% and 3% interest on a 50 million króna loan is about 250 thousand krónur per month and 115–120 million over the life of the loan. The króna tax delays young people’s financial independence and asset building.
art.440.title: Goodbye duty-free Temu, Shein and Alibaba
art.440.summary: Responds to Sveinn Atli Gunnarsson’s criticism and reiterates that EU membership would disrupt defence cooperation with the United States, citing former NATO ambassador Gunnar Pálsson. The EU already has military command structures and rapid reaction forces, and its leaders, including von der Leyen, support the creation of a European army.
art.441.title: JP Zimsen’s small-parcel talking points or Iceland’s real interests
art.441.summary: A reply to Jón Pétur Zimsen: abolishing the duty-free exemption on small parcels protects consumers and domestic retail against the undercutting of state-subsidised giants. The EU is an economic and political union, not a military alliance, and it is unwise to rely solely on the United States under Trump’s leadership for the country’s defence.
art.442.title: When the great powers do as they please, the EU is our best option
art.442.summary: Statistical comparisons with the past look at a world that no longer exists; now Russia attacks its neighbours, China exports unemployment, and the United States threatens Denmark over Greenland. EU membership would reduce the risk faced by a small, wealthy, undefended island — Europe is more likely to come to Iceland’s aid if super-trawlers, subsea cable cutting, or the ambitions of great powers threaten the country.
art.443.title: Overfishing in the EU 500 years ago
art.443.summary: Dissatisfaction with the EU’s fisheries policy was a major factor in Brexit, and the fishing industry has contracted in most of the union’s coastal states. Without notice, fishing quotas in Icelandic waters would be allocated from Brussels on the basis of advice from the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea, which is built on seriously flawed calculation models; the Norwegian-Icelandic herring stock measured 16% larger despite alleged overfishing for 13 years.
art.444.title: Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson and cherry-picking
art.444.summary: Accuses Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson of cherry-picking data at an Áfram Íslands meeting, where he cited 25% youth unemployment in Finland. According to the national statistical offices, youth unemployment is 23,8% in Iceland and 23,2% in Finland on the ILO measure, while registered unemployment is much lower; the high figures are explained by the fact that students seeking work are counted as unemployed.
art.445.title: Limited power is not necessarily small power
art.445.summary: A reply to Davíð Þór Björgvinsson: in assessing a transfer of sovereignty, what matters is not only how many areas fall under supranational authority but how important they are. Most policy areas that matter to member states fall under shared competences, and the integration process from Maastricht to Lisbon has moved more and more policy fields under expanded majority rule.
art.446.title: A story from Sweden — living standards are not measured in percentage growth
art.446.summary: The author lived in Sweden, where ordinary people had no chance of buying property and securing a long-term rental contract was the big goal; the EU itself acknowledges a severe housing crisis in Europe. A lower interest rate does not tell the whole story, because higher fixed expenses and lower wages eat up the difference.
art.447.title: Privileged people who say no
art.447.summary: Privileged groups have throughout history defended their vested interests against change, and now a former president and a stock exchange CEO are using power and wealth to persuade people to reject a democratic vote. The vote is only on accession talks, and the nation would then get to vote on the agreement itself.
art.448.title: Can an idealistic pro-European convince a fearful nation?
art.448.summary: Describes how opposition and fear of foreign influence accompanied NATO membership in 1949, EFTA in 1970, the EEA in 1994, and even beer in 1989 — yet the opponents were wrong in every case. The EU was founded on an ideal of peace and is Iceland’s anchor in turbulent times when fascist forces are advancing and the United States cannot be relied on.
art.449.title: No or yes?
art.449.summary: A former sceptic about membership says claims about loss of sovereignty are nonsense; the Danes, Finns, and Swedes manage their own affairs through democratic elections. Icelanders have not done well at managing public finances and interest rates on their own, and it is impossible to take a position before an agreement is on the table — she intends to vote yes in order to know more.
art.450.title: Why not choose something cheaper than the euro?
art.450.summary: Examines restaurant annual accounts: wages are 40–45% of revenue, ingredients 25–35%, and profits rarely above 10%, so the promised 25% price reduction with the euro does not add up unless purchase prices fall several times more. Wages do not fall upon entry, and lower financing costs would rather push asset and rental prices higher.
art.451.title: Does Iceland have a national football team?
art.451.summary: Recalls that a small nation won all three Cod Wars against Britain and secured a 200-mile fishing limit on the international stage — but would never have won them without NATO. Expresses confidence that the same spirit of strong negotiators will prevail at the negotiating table if talks with the EU continue.
art.452.title: We could do without misleading households
art.452.summary: A response to Berglind Guðmundsdóttir of SJÁ: by its very nature, an accession treaty will say nothing about future interest rates or inflation, and nothing of the sort will be written into any agreement. People's hardships are being exploited for political purposes; the problem stems mainly from sharply rising housing prices caused by an insufficient supply of building plots.
art.453.title: The limits of the rule of law and the privacy of private communications
art.453.summary: Explains how the Chat Control 1.0 regulation on scanning private communications remained in force in the European Parliament even though 314 members voted against it and 276 in favor, because an absolute majority of all 720 members was required to reject the Council's position. The procedure just before the summer recess sits poorly with democratic fundamentals and the EU's constant references to its values.
art.454.title: Heimssýn’s military syndrome
art.454.summary: Refutes claims by Heimssýn chairman Haraldur Ólafsson that the EU has an army and is moving toward a European army: there are no plans for such a force, and the 5,000-strong RDC rapid reaction force from 2007 has never been used. The emphasis within the EU is on strengthening NATO, and support for a common army is low in many places, for example only about 35% in Ireland.
art.455.title: Saying “YES” is about fairness and progress
art.455.summary: An immigrant who has lived in Iceland for two decades describes how EU funding built up infrastructure in member states: Ireland got motorways, six billion euros for schools, and 1,500 social housing units; Poland got hospitals; and Finland sent 130,000 students abroad through Erasmus+. Iceland faces an underfunded education system, overcrowded hospitals, and insufficient social housing, and should not reject similar support.
art.456.title: A currency that was never meant to exist and that the nation is still stuck with
art.456.summary: The króna was not an objective of the independence struggle but an emergency solution when the First World War broke up the Scandinavian Monetary Union, which Iceland belonged to in 1874–1916 and which was explicitly referenced in the Act of Union in 1918. The monetary union was the euro of its time and ensured low interest rates and stability; households have since been left to pay the bill for the króna in the form of inflation, currency depreciation, and high interest rates.
art.457.title: Are the arguments of SJÁ meaningful?
art.457.summary: In a video, SJÁ claimed that a carton of milk costs 380 krónur in Iceland, but the correct price is 235 krónur, as media outlets have pointed out. Whether this was a deliberate falsehood or simply sloppy work, it renders the organisation’s arguments about more complex economic indicators unreliable.
art.458.title: When a staunch opponent of EU membership in Norway changed his mind
art.458.summary: Kjell Magne Bondevik, who campaigned against Norway joining the EU in 1972 and 1994, now believes Norway would be better off inside the Union because of an aggressive Russia and growing isolationism in the United States; fears of a centrally controlled superstate have proved unfounded. Iceland adopts most EU legislation through the EEA without a seat at the table, and the referendum is only about completing the negotiations — the nation will have the final say.
art.459.title: Ideals and interests go hand in hand
art.459.summary: The EU transformed a continent of wars into a community of states that resolve disputes through law and democracy; the question is where Iceland belongs in a world where great powers exert pressure and large corporations have more influence than individual states. Small states have limited influence on their own, but the EU can set rules that even the world’s largest tech companies must respect.
art.460.title: Permanent exemptions?
art.460.summary: The argument that no permanent exemptions are available is not an argument against negotiations: no one backs out of buying an apartment in a multi-unit building because they cannot get a permanent exemption from the house rules; instead, they assess the agreement as a whole. The only way to find out whether exemptions are possible is to test it in negotiations and then reject the agreement if it proves unacceptable.
art.461.title: A study trip to Brussels or an application for membership?
art.461.summary: An X next to yes is a declaration of a desire to join, because the EU does not launch an accession process unless there is a clear will to accede, in accordance with Article 49 of the Treaty of Lisbon. Every step of the process requires the unanimous approval of all 27 member states, and the process is aimed at aligning the applicant country with the acquis, not at “exploring what is on offer”.
art.462.title: What is the government aiming for?
art.462.summary: Voters have the right to know the government’s negotiating objectives, because the vote is not about gathering information but about a formal accession process under Article 49 of the EU Treaty. The negotiating framework from 2010 provided for the adoption of the entire acquis, and the German Bundestag stipulated in 2010 that Icelandic fisheries would be opened to investment from the EU.
art.463.title: The small-boat fisherman and the EU
art.463.summary: Upon accession, the nation would relinquish control over fishing beyond 12 miles and would be unable in any way to depart from Brussels’ decision on the total quota within its jurisdiction; EU and UK fishing grounds now deliver about one tenth of the cod and haddock catch they once did. EU concessions for small boats could be implemented without membership, and a permanent exemption would require the approval of all member states.
art.464.title: Let’s make Iceland better
art.464.summary: Expresses surprise at labour leaders’ opposition to negotiations when fish processing has disappeared from their areas; with EU membership, all tariffs would be abolished and processing could move back home, with product sale prices up to 50% higher and new jobs created. The interest-rate difference versus Denmark on a 50 million loan is about ISK 250,000 per month, and inflation has averaged over 14% since 1944.
art.465.title: Resource control, offshore capital and the asymmetric war over 29 August
art.465.summary: Claims that the fishing-industry elite is waging an asymmetric war ahead of 29 August with unlimited offshore capital, lawyers, public relations firms and psychological warfare techniques to ensure that the nation votes no. The vote is about whether the nation retains constitutional control over its shared natural resources.
art.466.title: Need teaches a naked Icelander to spin
art.466.summary: Recounts the 2008 crash, when the krona’s enormous interest-rate differential drew in foreign capital, fuelled debt accumulation and multiplied the problem when the krona collapsed. Alþingi approved the membership application in 2009 without asking the nation, unlike what is now proposed, and Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson praised the útrásarvíkingar in the run-up to the crash.
art.467.title: Enormous welfare gains from adopting the euro
art.467.summary: Cites a 2014 report by Alþjóðamálastofnun HÍ, prepared at the request of ASÍ, SA, FA and Viðskiptaráð, stating that adopting the euro would bring enormous welfare gains and that Iceland had already secured special solutions, exemptions and transition periods in many areas. Ásgeir Jónsson, the current central bank governor, wrote most of the currency chapter; the krona is said to have led to higher interest rates, inflation and exchange-rate volatility.
art.468.title: Dagur, no cheating!
art.468.summary: A response article to Dag B. Eggertsson: he omits the conclusion of the same report that the sacrifice of an independent monetary policy is accompanied by greater variability in unemployment and that higher nominal wage increases would lead to a weaker competitive position and crisis. The report is based on an outdated monetary policy from the era of capital controls, and Iceland is today among the highest-income nations with some of the greatest income equality in the world without EU membership.
art.469.title: Are Icelanders inept at negotiating?
art.469.summary: Criticises no supporters for declaring in advance that Icelanders are incapable in negotiations; with that attitude, no success would have been achieved in the cod wars. The country’s wealthy want to prevent people on ordinary incomes from escaping the vicious circle of the Icelandic krona.
art.470.title: Stability in a death grip
art.470.summary: The exchange rate of a country’s own currency is above all an adjustment tool when shocks hit, especially in Iceland where fisheries and aluminium production cannot be increased at will. If that tool is thrown away by adopting a foreign currency, the adjustment shifts to employment levels, wages and investment, as Finland’s experience shows.
art.471.title: Króna or euro?
art.471.summary: The chair of the Central Bank’s supervisory board explains how the króna has lost value since 1922 and is now worth less than a Danish five-øre coin. The króna has never been adequate as a store of value, and indexation is a consequence of that.
art.472.title: What can be negotiated?
art.472.summary: Says it is undisputed that inflation and interest rates would fall upon accession and criticises the NO side’s “hysteria”. Iceland shares neither borders nor fishing grounds with EU states and therefore has strong arguments for special arrangements in fisheries.
art.473.title: The big correction affair, some Dutch people and colleagues
art.473.summary: A former minister refers to clear answers from the Dutch prime minister and Danish ministers that Iceland would have to submit to the EU’s common fisheries policy. Criticises the Minister for Foreign Affairs for not correcting a misleading news report until 11 days later and demands answers from her.
art.474.title: Why ordinary working people should say YES
art.474.summary: Working people bear all the risk of the króna and indexation while banks and large fishing companies settle in euros. The euro would provide predictable repayments, EU rules would not curtail the right to strike, and abolishing tariffs would lower food prices; the nation should be allowed to see the agreement.
art.475.title: What demands should we make?
art.475.summary: The Minister for Foreign Affairs reviews the status of the agriculture chapter, which was never opened in 2009–2013, and what demands Iceland should make in the talks. Domestic production covers 90% of meat consumption and 99% of dairy products, and the special arrangements of the Finns and Swedes should be the minimum benchmark.
art.476.title: Why “no” is the only logical answer on 29 August
art.476.summary: The EU’s basic position is non-negotiable: new states must adopt the entire acquis, and permanent exemptions are not on offer, only temporary derogations. The fisheries and agriculture chapters were never opened in 2009–2013 because the gap was unbridgeable, and therefore new talks would serve no purpose.
art.477.title: This is about membership
art.477.summary: A former Minister for Foreign Affairs points out that the process launched in 2009 was a formal application for membership under Article 49 of the EU Treaty. The vote on 29 August is therefore about continuing an application for membership, not about “seeing what is on offer”.
art.478.title: Informed democracy - The lesson of one correction
art.478.summary: Describes Vísir’s correction of a report about the Minister for Foreign Affairs’ alleged discussions with the Dutch authorities on fisheries policy; the minister had never spoken to Jetten himself. The Dutch parliament confirmed by 146 votes to 4 that full membership entails full participation in the fisheries policy.
art.479.title: Let us not accept unemployment
art.479.summary: Members of the leadership of Ungir vinstri grænir say the conditions of euro cooperation call for labour-market “flexibility”, moderate wage demands and higher unemployment. Strong trade unions explain equality in Iceland, and decisions should be taken here rather than in Brussels.
art.480.title: Who enters such “negotiations”?
art.480.summary: Cites the EU Commissioner for Enlargement, the Union’s brochure and the negotiating framework to argue that the talks are about adapting an applicant state to the acquis, not genuine negotiations. Even the explanatory notes to the Minister for Foreign Affairs’ parliamentary resolution acknowledge this.
art.481.title: The bankruptcy history of airlines is a serious reminder of the damage caused by the króna
art.481.summary: Traces the bankruptcies of Arnarflug, WOW air, PLAY and other airlines to periods when the microcurrency króna was overvalued. Air Atlanta and Cargolux show that Icelandic aviation operations fare better within larger currencies such as the euro.
art.482.title: Permanent exemptions are possible
art.482.summary: A former head of department in the Åland Islands self-government administration describes her own experience of Finland’s accession in 1995, when the Åland Islands received a permanent protocol (Ålandsprotokollet) on special rules that conflict with core EU rules. Permanent exemptions are therefore a realistic possibility.
art.483.title: Feeling out the “package”
art.483.summary: The author says he has “felt out the EU package well enough” to know that the answer is no. New EU directives to deny residence permits to Ukrainian men who refuse military service undermine freedom of conscience and Iceland’s peace tradition; outside the EU, Iceland still has a choice.
art.484.title: Is Iceland Manchester City and the EU Sheffield United
art.484.summary: A professor of economics recalculated the figures in Áfram Ísland’s 40-page analysis and found more than ten misleading or incorrect points. Iceland is more expensive than all 27 EU countries, has the worst household borrowing terms, and 13 EU countries have a lower debt ratio than claimed.
art.485.title: The foreign minister’s claims about Iceland’s room for negotiation
art.485.summary: The agriculture and food chapters (11 and 12) were never opened in 2009–2013, no negotiating position was submitted, and no conclusions were reached. The foreign minister’s claims about what special solutions Iceland can secure therefore are not supported by primary sources.
art.486.title: Foreign rule is trouble
art.486.summary: Recounts the history of the trade monopoly and Danish rule: when power moves farther from the people, a small nation’s interests are sacrificed for the larger whole and bureaucracy grows. Icelandic companies only truly flourished when decision-making power moved back home, in the spirit of Jón Sigurðsson.
art.487.title: A little standard, please
art.487.summary: A member of parliament from Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn lists fourteen reasons for no: bureaucracy in Brussels, weak energy policy, regulations that kill innovation, pension system debts, upheaval to 70 free trade agreements and the defense agreement with the United States. No is yes to the best living standards in the world according to the United Nations.
art.488.title: One small and innocent step at a time toward Brussels
art.488.summary: Only 11% of voters named European issues among the most important issues in the last election, and Viðreisn received 15,8% of the vote. The party is said to have advanced the membership issue in small steps without ever having to seek support for the final goal itself.
art.489.title: That is why yes
art.489.summary: The international order Iceland has relied on has begun to fracture; the United States is using tariffs to coerce former allied states and is no longer the ally it once was. Membership is about shared fundamental values, national security and the social contract among nations, not only accounting examples.
art.490.title: The time for permanent exemptions has passed
art.490.summary: Denmark’s and Britain’s opt-out exemptions arose from political necessity during treaty changes in 1992–2009, when those states could exercise a veto from within. Applicant states today must adopt the entire acquis communautaire, and no state since 2004 has received a permanent exemption.
art.491.title: Response to Per Ekström’s article regarding permanent opt-outs
art.491.summary: The Åland Islands’ opt-out on tax-free ferry sales is minor and 32 years old, and in no way comparable to keeping an entire fishing industry outside EU control. Greenland, Norway and Ireland show that an opt-out from the fisheries policy has not been obtained.
art.492.title: The agreement that quietly keeps expanding
art.492.summary: Over 32 years, the EEA Agreement has expanded into climate issues, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence and financial supervision without being rewritten. Iceland is adapting its economy and public administration to an ever broader regulatory framework but has no vote when the rules are adopted.
art.493.title: A look inside the package
art.493.summary: Compares the “take a look inside the package” message to the travelling salesmen of earlier times: the one who only meant to look ended up as a buyer. States apply for membership, the process is about adapting legislation chapter by chapter, and no one in Brussels recognizes the opt-outs the minister is promising.
art.494.title: Sigmar Guðmundsson, the United States, and Iceland’s security
art.494.summary: The security of demilitarized Iceland rests on the United States within NATO, but EU membership would oblige Iceland to stand with the Union in foreign and security affairs. Criticizes the government for not examining what consequences membership would have for defense cooperation with the United States.
art.495.title: Responding to Gauti’s distractions and misrepresentations
art.495.summary: The author of a report by Áfram Íslands and RSE responds to criticism from Gauti Eggertsson. Per capita economic growth is said to be a limited measure because of shorter working hours, purchasing power is among the highest in Iceland, and GDP per capita shows the country’s very strong position.
art.496.title: Does ideological intimidation belong in an election campaign?
art.496.summary: Criticizes the framing of “Já til að sjá” for portraying a no vote as anti-democratic and ignorant. The movement’s promise that negotiations will reveal growth and food prices does not hold up, because such information does not appear in an accession treaty.
art.497.title: The EU and your fellow thinkers
art.497.summary: A satirical checklist of who fills the ranks of the no side: owners of capital, beneficiaries of oligopoly and high interest rates, and others. The author says they will vote yes to see, and then make an informed decision on the treaty.
art.498.title: Tosca shoots up from the tower in Brussels
art.498.summary: The vote is on negotiations, not membership; approving negotiations is like being allowed to see the menu. Iceland is already a small nation in NATO, the UN and the EEA, and already adopts many EU rules without having any say over the agenda.
art.499.title: Armed with nothing but fear
art.499.summary: Corrects claims from the no side: the rule of relative stability ensures that fishing quotas in Icelandic waters would remain unchanged, there is no common European army, and Iceland’s pension system is among the three most reliable in the world according to Mercer.
art.500.title: The nation should get the benefit of the doubt
art.500.summary: A Centre Party MP says it is generally recognized that accession brings higher unemployment and that free movement of people has developed in an unsustainable way. Full membership would further reduce a small nation’s freedom to live independently and narrow Iceland’s options for responding.
art.501.title: Why yes?
art.501.summary: The EU is said to be among the world’s leading regions in consumer protection, data protection, environmental and climate matters, and its rules have become international benchmarks. The United States is said to have taken a different path, where corporate interests often carry more weight than consumer interests.
art.502.title: Kristrún finally explained what the vote will be about
art.502.summary: In an interview with The Rest Is Politics, the Prime Minister confirmed that a yes vote gives the government a mandate to begin the formal accession process and complete it. That is a completely different question from “taking a look in the package” or gathering information.
art.503.title: Sovereignty for whom?
art.503.summary: Iceland has already shared decision-making power through the EEA without a vote, yet the experience is said to have been good overall: data protection, air passenger rights, consumer protection, and competition rules came through the EEA. State sovereignty and citizens’ freedom do not always go hand in hand.
art.504.title: The EU debate and artificial intelligence
art.504.summary: Describes a conversation with artificial intelligence which, after being corrected, acknowledged that candidate countries are now required to align with the regulatory framework in parallel with negotiations and that no country has received permanent exemptions since the EU’s policy shift around the turn of the century.
art.505.title: Refusing to seek
art.505.summary: Voting no to negotiations means passing judgment before the facts are on the table; voting yes preserves both a future yes and a future no. A sovereign nation need not fear negotiations, but should instead put forward demands, as Iceland has done before on territorial waters, the EEA, and free trade.
art.506.title: Slogans instead of data: Snorri Másson’s article on EU membership
art.506.summary: Refutes Snorri Másson’s claim about unemployment: Estonia went from 10,3% unemployment to 4,6% after joining in 2004, and Croatia from 17% to 6,5%. Free movement of people is already in place through the EEA and would not change with membership.
art.507.title: “No” is not the end of the matter — it is a postponement of it
art.507.summary: More than 14.000 EU legal acts have already been adopted into the EEA and a large share of the regulatory framework is already in place. Negotiations are about reaching an outcome on the issues that remain unresolved — fisheries, agriculture, currency, and regional funds — so that the nation can judge it.
art.508.title: RKV injustice or EU injustice?
art.508.summary: People in East Iceland are said to have suffered from remote rule from Reykjavík, and the EU is portrayed as an even larger version of the same system, with longer chains of command. The EU’s ETS emissions tax system, implemented since 2007, raises the cost of all inputs to the country and harms the purchasing power of the population.
art.509.title: Is the old always good?
art.509.summary: An obstetrician compares an old radio alarm clock, now starting to fail after 44 years, to what the nation faces in the referendum. He asks whether Icelanders know how to bid farewell to the old and dare to choose the new in a dangerous world.
art.510.title: Big capital is better off in Brussels — not the nation
art.510.summary: A former minister points to positive remarks by the CEO of Brim and the chairman of the board of Ísfélagið about EU membership: the large fishing companies would thrive within the Union, but smaller businesses, the general public, the regions, and the national economy would fare worse.
art.511.title: Euro or króna?
art.511.summary: An MP says he supports membership primarily because of currency issues, although he would not accept just any agreement. It is undisputed that interest rates would be lower with the euro; the inflation of the króna system erodes real wages and automatically raises indexed loans.
art.512.title: A failure of humanity - the EU and refugees
art.512.summary: Criticises the development of EU refugee policy: Frontex operates like an army without a legitimate mandate or oversight, and the Union has laid the groundwork for the mass deportation of people to camps outside the EU area, probably in North Africa.
art.513.title: Kristrún Frostadóttir agrees with the no side
art.513.summary: The prime minister’s remark that an accession process would “suck oxygen out of the administrative system” confirms the argument of the no side: the process is a wide-ranging, time-consuming and costly adaptation of legislation and public administration across 35 policy areas, not simple feelers.
art.514.title: Claims and reality
art.514.summary: The claims of EU opponents are fiction, never supported by examples. Icelandic farmers would gain access to a better subsidy system and free exports, and the fishing industry’s predictions of doom about the end of it all are not grounded in reason.
art.515.title: Iceland in a new world order
art.515.summary: Discussion among US policymakers about control over Greenland shows that the old world order can no longer be taken for granted and that US politics has become unpredictable. It is natural for Iceland to reassess its position and examine whether political ties with Europe should be strengthened; the vote is on talks, not membership.
art.516.title: Six reasons to vote YES in August
art.516.summary: Six questions for voters: whether to keep the door open for young people, explore a more competitive interest-rate environment, and ask whether the EEA will suffice in the coming decades when tariffs on processed products move jobs out of the country and Iceland has no representative at the table.
art.517.title: Haraldur’s conscription scare stories distort a realistic view of defence matters
art.517.summary: Responds to the chair of Heimssýn: the EU’s increased defence emphasis is a response to Russia’s invasion, not an independent drive toward militarisation. Haraldur mixes up facts, proposals and his own forecasts of the future, and the document he cites on conscription is only an educational report.
art.518.title: Every lie creates a debt to the truth
art.518.summary: Recalls the fearmongering against the EEA Agreement that proved false, and how lies before the crash and in the Panama Papers ultimately led to a reckoning. Opponents of talks now make claims about the contents of an agreement that does not exist.
art.519.title: The misrepresentations still stand, and nothing has been retracted
art.519.summary: Reiterates that Gauti Eggertsson’s criticism did not answer six specified misrepresentations about the report by Áfram Ísland and RSE. The report is also based on productivity and GDP per capita, and shows Iceland in a very strong position compared with peer countries.
art.520.title: Interest rates gone astray
art.520.summary: Interest-rate comparisons in the debate are misleading because they do not distinguish between nominal and real rates; the real rates on Icelandic government bonds are 1.2–2.4 percentage points above the euro area, not 4.5–5.5%. Negative real rates in the euro area are, among other things, evidence of the EU’s poor growth outlook.
art.521.title: Correction regarding an article about Kristrún on a British podcast
art.521.summary: Corrects a quotation attributed to the Prime Minister but stands by the conclusion: that her words about the process "draining oxygen from the administrative system" and being an "enormously large task" can scarcely refer to exploratory talks to look over the package.
art.522.title: The world is not waiting for Iceland
art.522.summary: The international system that protected small states is weakening, and when the rules break down, countries like Iceland lose out, not the great powers. Membership would secure a seat at the table where rules affecting Iceland are shaped; a yes in August would only be a yes to talks and to putting the facts on the table.
art.523.title: Iceland and the EU: Seen from the bridge
art.523.summary: An economics professor says Russia’s war of aggression and the waning commitment of the United States to NATO have fundamentally changed Iceland’s security environment. The EEA amounts to "light" membership, with obligations but no voting rights, and membership may be necessary for security and economic reasons.
art.524.title: What Mom and Dad taught me
art.524.summary: A board member of SJÁ says the vote is about obtaining a negotiated outcome that the nation can assess, not about membership. He acknowledges that talks are part of the accession process and cost time and money, but do not automatically bind Iceland; if the outcome is unacceptable, the nation should reject it.
art.525.title: Voting yes to see is an illusion
art.525.summary: Compares a yes vote to Hotel California: according to the EU’s enlargement guide, an extensive adaptation process begins in which Icelandic legislation is aligned with the acquis chapter by chapter. A yes is in practice approval of an accession process aimed at full membership and cannot be reversed without consequences.
art.526.title: A table gone astray
art.526.summary: Responds to Agnar Tómas Möller: figures of 4.5–5.5% real interest rates apply to household mortgages according to Central Bank data, not government bonds. A family with a 60 million króna loan pays about 113 thousand krónur more per month with the króna than at euro area interest rates.
art.527.title: What exactly are we sacrificing for "lower unemployment"?
art.527.summary: A devaluation of the króna is an automatic wage cut for the entire nation. According to Eurostat, eight EU countries had both lower unemployment and lower inflation than Iceland in 2025; the choice between inflation and unemployment is a myth.
art.528.title: Finns love the EU
art.528.summary: Despite unemployment above 10%, 79% of Finns in Eurobarometer say the EU provides shelter and 76% say Finland has benefited from membership. The economic difficulties stem from the collapse of trade with Russia, the decline of Nokia, and an aging population, not from the EU or the euro.
art.529.title: Icelandic voters or European officials?
art.529.summary: Power should rest with Icelandic voters, not the bureaucracy in Brussels, which is said to be out of touch with the realities of different member states. Within the EU, Iceland’s voice would be drowned out as one country out of 28, but outside it the country stands as a free island with a single voice.
art.530.title: Warning lights in European business
art.530.summary: Cites reports by Draghi and Letta on the EU’s declining competitiveness relative to the United States, and surveys by BusinessEurope and BDI on a worsening business environment and the flight of research and development from Europe. Letta emphasizes that the benefits of the single market are not tied to membership and describes the EEA Agreement as a cornerstone of cooperation.
art.531.title: Within the EU, “Iceland will manage fisheries in the North Atlantic”
art.531.summary: Restates Heimildin’s interview with Indriði Benediktsson, who worked for the European Commission for 30 years: Iceland would not need to change anything in its fisheries management unless it wanted to and could lead negotiations on migratory stocks on behalf of the EU. He says there is an extraordinarily good opportunity now that will never come again — if the UK or Norway joins first, Iceland will have no chance, and EEA cooperation will not be long-lived.
art.532.title: Summer festivals, exorbitant interest rates, and an unopened envelope
art.532.summary: A city councillor urges people to approach the vote with respect for differing views; the EU is no magic solution, but the agreement must be put on the table so that the debate is based on facts rather than speculation. A yes to talks is neither a decision to join nor a declaration that everything will be perfect, but a decision to gather the facts.
art.533.title: What matters most?
art.533.summary: A Maskína poll shows that 77% of the public do not make important decisions without all the information, and the EU issue should be approached in the same way: first, it is necessary to know what agreement is on offer. Red lines should strengthen Iceland’s negotiating position, not prevent negotiations from taking place; accession talks are not surrender, but a way to examine whether a better outcome can be achieved.
art.534.title: Accusations of treason and farce
art.534.summary: The writer says pitch-black negativity and insinuations have flooded the debate even though the vote is only on whether to enter talks. Ólafur Ragnar is now repeating the same dire predictions he made during the EEA period about disintegration, poverty, and the collapse of industries, all of which proved false.
art.535.title: More than the Copenhagen criteria
art.535.summary: Responds to an article by Ásta Guðrún Helgadóttir: the acquis communautaire covers far more than regulations and directives — the founding treaties, case law, and administrative practice — and the screening process assesses what changes an applicant country must make before chapters are closed. The Copenhagen criteria are the beginning of the accession process, not its endpoint.
art.536.title: EEA or EU — that is the question
art.536.summary: Explains the nature of the EEA Agreement: the EFTA states commit to adopting all EU legislation on the internal market without cherry-picking, and the EFTA Surveillance Authority and the EFTA Court enforce those obligations. Voters should assess whether the EEA is sufficient for the future or whether it should be explored whether full membership is the better option.
art.537.title: Mortgage loans in the real world: A response to Gauti B. Eggertsson’s comments
art.537.summary: Responds to Gauti B. Eggertsson’s criticism of his interest-rate comparison: the present-value difference in mortgage payments based on real interest rates is about 22%, while public debate has implied a many-times greater difference. Claims that Icelanders pay for housing three times over or 72% more do not take inflation and real variables into account.
art.538.title: What does the current situation cost retail trade and Icelandic consumers?
art.538.summary: Icelandic retail operates with higher financing costs, exchange-rate risk, and outside the EU customs union, resulting in higher prices, less product variety, and poorer service for consumers. The EU sets the rules for e-commerce and digital markets; the EEA Agreement is probably not enough for much longer, and Iceland has no seat at the table when the rules of business are being shaped.
art.539.title: Down into the trenches
art.539.summary: The offensive is self-inflicted: no one is attacking Iceland; rather, the government itself intends to sit down at the negotiating table, where it says it must “defend” fisheries, agriculture, and sovereignty. Applicant countries adopt the Union’s rules chapter by chapter, permanent exemptions in fisheries have never been obtained, and Iceland’s position outside the EU is strong.
art.540.title: My generation failed!
art.540.summary: After nearly 40 years in business, she says the system is designed for some: small companies and households cannot thrive with financing at 14% interest while large corporations operate outside the króna economy. The króna is unfair and discriminates against businesses and households; she says an unequivocal yes for her children and grandchildren.
art.541.title: Why I’m voting YES on 29 August
art.541.summary: Compares his 2.32% mortgage interest rate in Denmark with Icelandic conditions: the policy rate is 7.75% versus 2.25% at the European Central Bank, and indexation, unknown in Europe, increases the principal in line with inflation. Three banks all but dominate Iceland’s lending market because the króna keeps European banks from competing.
art.542.title: Ghost stories of the modern age
art.542.summary: Compares the NO side’s arguments to the ghost beliefs of earlier centuries; the EU has never seized resources from a member nation, and the doomsday predictions recall the „man-made hardships of the Laki haze“ that were predicted when the EEA Agreement was made thirty years ago. The rule of relative stability is based on fish stocks being caught by the nations with the fishing track record.
art.543.title: The European army and Icelanders’ share
art.543.summary: The chair of Heimssýn says there is a strong will within the EU for militarisation, from the public up to the highest levels of power, and that the European Parliament has adopted a resolution on the matter by a large majority. The latest four-year weapons plan would cost Iceland around 50 billion krónur a year, and it is odd to join in the belief that militarisation will never come to pass.
art.544.title: Was this the election promise?
art.544.summary: The government was elected to lower interest rates and achieve stability but is instead heading into a referendum on the EU, where the problems are even greater: youth unemployment, rising debt and heavy regulation. Iceland should retain all the tools of a sovereign state and make use of the strengths that come with being small.
art.545.title: The great know-it-alls
art.545.summary: Criticises the „know-it-alls“ who pretend to know exactly what an agreement will look like and what will happen after the vote. It is a pure lie that a yes vote to start negotiations means a yes vote to the European Union or that sovereignty will be lost — all states within the EU are sovereign.
art.546.title: On love of truth and workers’ rights
art.546.summary: Half-truths dominate the debate, and love of truth is less evident on the NO side; talk of surrendering sovereignty and judicial power is nonsense. Reviews the labour and consumer rights secured by the EEA regulatory framework and wants the nation to see the agreement and make an informed decision in a second vote.
art.547.title: Icelandic, Swedish, or no króna
art.547.summary: Corrects the claim that the Swedish krona is pegged to the euro, but notes that the Swedes joined the EU because of the customs union and a seat at the decision-making table, and negotiated special arrangements such as the snus exemption. The key interest rate is 7.75% in Iceland, compared with 2.4% in the euro area and 1.75% in Sweden; Icelanders see one of the main benefits of membership as getting rid of the króna.
art.548.title: Breathe into a paper bag! Iceland will be fine
art.548.summary: Calls for calm in a debate that quickly descends into trench warfare; there are valid arguments on both sides, and nothing terrible will happen whatever the result. Votes yes because of a changed international order in which the United States is unpicking the old system, the opportunities for households and businesses in a larger currency area, and the experience that increased international cooperation has greatly improved quality of life.
art.549.title: What if ...?
art.549.summary: There has been more fearmongering from the NO side; one might just as well ask, „what if we get a more stable currency and more favourable mortgage loans?“ and in the worst case it would be possible to back out of the process, as the British showed with Brexit. Fear of change must not prevent the possibility of a better future.
art.550.title: Did they laugh at Switzerland too, Ólafur Ragnar?
art.550.summary: Responds to Ólafur Ragnar, who cites the laughter of two unnamed men in Paris at the idea that a two-stage referendum is „absurd“. Sets out documented examples — Switzerland in 2001, Romania in 2003, Moldova in 2024 and North Macedonia in 2018 — where people voted on talks or an accession process, and the European Commission respected or welcomed the result instead of laughing.
art.551.title: What Would the Euro Deliver? - a response to Ásdís Kristjánsdóttir
art.551.summary: Responds to Ásdís Kristjánsdóttir: a 2014 report by ASÍ, SA, FA and Viðskiptaráð on the “enormous welfare gains” from adopting the euro is not outdated, and the committee on which Ásdís served was not allowed to examine any options other than the króna. The cost to households of housing loans amounts to over one hundred billion a year, inflation is twice above target, and the policy rate is 7.75% compared with 2.25% in the euro area.
art.552.title: A YES-minded film producer
art.552.summary: The producer of Hrútar and Héraðið finances about 60% of his projects in euros and describes millions in foreign-exchange losses caused by the instability of the króna, losses that small companies cannot hedge against. European banks lend at reasonable interest rates against euro payments, while no one wants anything to do with the króna, and an Icelandic commercial bank offers 13.5% interest.
art.553.title: We Would Pay for Montenegro’s Accession
art.553.summary: Cites unnamed European Commission officials in Politico saying that Iceland could join alongside Montenegro and would, because of its wealth, in effect pay for Montenegro’s accession. Iceland would be the first net contributor in over 30 years, 17 of the 27 member states receive more from EU funds than they pay in, and a 48% increase in contributions has been proposed.
art.554.title: The First Yes Is the Crucial Vote
art.554.summary: The former President of the EFTA Court responds to Gauti B. Eggertsson: the examples of Switzerland, Romania, Moldova and North Macedonia are not comparable to the Icelandic case, because in those cases the initiative came from the authorities themselves rather than from the nation. The first yes is the truly fateful vote.
art.555.title: Negotiating Against Oneself
art.555.summary: Compares Morgunblaðið’s coverage and the leadership of Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn on the “impossibility” of negotiating with the EU to the overblown ambitions and inferiority complex of Icelandic youth national teams in earlier times. The national team achieved the impossible in 2016 and 2018; he does not believe it is not worth stepping onto the pitch and saying yes to see what happens.
art.556.title: Political Weathercocks Who Now Want to Take the Decision Away from the Nation
art.556.summary: Recalls Bjarni Benediktsson’s words from 2009 that the euro with EU membership was the only strong alternative to the króna, that democracy should be activated, and that the nation should get to vote on whether to enter into talks. The same parties that demanded a double referendum in 2009 now want to take that decision away from the nation.
art.557.title: How Do We Secure a Future for Our Children in Iceland?
art.557.summary: The big question is whether young people in Iceland have the same opportunities as their peers in the Nordic countries to buy their first home, start a business and build international companies without high capital costs standing in the way. Tariff-free access could increase the full processing of seafood products, and investment does not go where there is uncertainty about market access.
art.558.title: Iceland, Yes Please
art.558.summary: A Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn MP says that about 95% of the EU acquis is non-negotiable according to the Union itself, and that Iceland would be a net contributor, in effect financing Montenegro’s accession. Iceland already has the best living standards, the greatest equality, security and social equality in the world, and EU supporters talk the country down.
art.559.title: Speculation
art.559.summary: A former MP and member of the Central Bank’s supervisory board criticises bank board chairman Bolli Héðinsson for talking down the króna in a radio interview and advocating the euro and EU membership. Such conduct is unprofessional and irresponsible and undermines confidence in the currency, monetary policy and the Central Bank itself.
art.560.title: A Yes-to-See Path to Yes-Yes
art.560.summary: A yes in August would mean a formal application for accession, followed by adaptation of the administrative system and legislation to the EU’s 170-thousand-page body of rules, which would be difficult to unwind. Cites Baudenbacher as saying that the process would gain its own momentum, and Ólafur Ragnar as saying that the EU would drag out the talks until a yes was likely in the second referendum.
art.561.title: A Shock Absorber for Whom?
art.561.summary: The minister responds to the “shock absorber argument” for the króna: the largest export sectors cannot increase production when the exchange rate weakens, because a weaker króna neither adds more fish to the sea nor conjures up aluminium smelters. A depreciation primarily increases the profits of export companies while shifting the cost onto the public through reduced purchasing power and a transfer of wealth from wage earners to capital owners.
art.562.title: The Nation Is Bleeding Out – and This Is Supposed to Somehow Work Itself Out
art.562.summary: For nearly half a century, Icelanders have been struggling with the same economic illness — inflation, high interest rates and exchange-rate volatility — while the explanations are always sought abroad instead of at home. Indexation introduced in 1979 is still in place, inflation remains far above target, and policy rates are many times higher than in the euro area; the bill is paid by families with mortgages and by young people.
art.563.title: The Dire Housing Situation of Young People in the EU
art.563.summary: Responding to Þorvaldur Ingi Jónsson: of the Nordic countries, only Finland has adopted the euro, while Denmark and Sweden rejected it in referendums. A new EU report paints a bleak picture of the housing situation of young people in the Union, where prices have tripled in some places, low interest rates have offered little relief, and many young people are forced to live with their parents well into adulthood.
art.564.title: I Intend to Trust Future Generations
art.564.summary: A teacher and visual artist intends to vote no and trust future generations to govern the country themselves instead of transferring an important part of power to the EU, as described in a legal opinion by the Institute of Law at the University of Iceland. The EU is no benevolent Santa Claus, and corruption and inequality there are certainly no less than at home.
art.565.title: What It Means to Have a Seat at the Table
art.565.summary: Responding to doubts about having a seat at the table: under the EEA, Iceland has no voice in the EU legislative process. Iceland’s weight would not be only six parliamentary seats out of 720, but also one commissioner out of 28 with equal voting weight, as well as membership in alliances of like-minded states, especially since the system contains built-in safeguards to protect the interests of smaller states.
art.566.title: Why I Am Voting NO on 29 August
art.566.summary: The author believes the EEA Agreement provides sufficient access to the internal market and that it is unrealistic wishful thinking to expect Iceland to obtain special arrangements and permanent exemptions in fisheries and agriculture. The main trade and industry associations and labour leaders have opposed reopening talks, and the government bears responsibility for the nation’s division.
art.567.title: Yes Is Surrender and No Is Not Enough
art.567.summary: The author says yes is surrender to authorities and a system she believes is built on deception; the banks profit by hundreds of billions a year while the public’s disposable income goes to interest payments. She does not trust the “valkyries” who, she says, have divided the nation with the vote.
art.568.title: Business Should Want to See the Agreement
art.568.summary: A former CEO is astonished that 66% of SA member companies oppose membership before any agreement is even on the table; in her long executive career, she cannot remember a board rejecting important negotiations without knowing what was on offer. Concerns about sovereignty and natural resources are legitimate, but they do not automatically mean that Iceland should not talk to the EU.
art.569.title: The First Yes Matters
art.569.summary: A yes is not a neutral search for information but a mandate to begin a formal accession process with a clear objective; sunk costs, expectations and interests that form around the process may make a no harder in the later vote. It cites Baudenbacher as saying that it can prove difficult to withdraw from a process once it has been set in motion.
art.570.title: 29 August ‒ Sovereignty Reclaimed?
art.570.summary: It compares the story of the “freedom” of American slaves after 1863 — free on paper but trapped in debt bondage — with the idea of sovereignty: formal sovereignty without real influence can be hollow. The sovereignty of nations in an interconnected world is more like coexistence in an apartment building than life in an isolated detached house.
art.571.title: An anchor and a safeguard for Iceland
art.571.summary: Iceland is effectively on a “subscription” to EEA rules without taking part in shaping them; his committee work on the EU Water Framework Directive showed rules being set with no involvement from Iceland whatsoever and poorly tailored to Icelandic conditions. Membership would make Iceland a full participant in shaping the regulatory framework, and it would be folly not to put negotiations to the test.
art.572.title: The disastrous housing situation for young people in Iceland
art.572.summary: The chair of the Tenants’ Association responds to Hjörtur J. Guðmundsson: he selectively chooses truthful information about housing problems in the EU while omitting the comparison with Iceland, which fares worse on most issues that matter to tenants and young people. Housing prices have risen by 103% in real terms since 2015, while high interest rates, indexation, a weak social housing sector, and limited housing security go hand in hand.
art.573.title: Where do we belong?
art.573.summary: The biggest question is not about krónur and euros but where Icelanders want to belong: the EU is a political partnership of democratic states built around human rights, the rule of law, and peace after two world wars. Iceland is inside the house through the EEA and Schengen but sitting out in the hallway — and one may ask who really owns Iceland when so few control the resources, the capital, and the rules of the game.
art.574.title: Should Iceland withdraw from UEFA?
art.574.summary: It places the sovereignty argument in an absurd context: under a strict sovereignty doctrine, KSÍ should withdraw from UEFA and FIFA because Icelandic football controls neither pitch size nor the offside rule. Icelanders accept common rules of the game because without them there is no common game — and little Iceland sometimes stands on equal footing with great nations there.
art.575.title: Who should have the final say on Iceland’s affairs?
art.575.summary: Supporters of membership have moved away from talk of a permanent exemption from the fisheries policy and now refer instead to relative stability; the Dutch parliament has approved the view that the policy is to be regarded as an inseparable part of the acquis in negotiations with Iceland. Upon accession, the four freedoms would extend to the fisheries sector, including investment and the right of establishment, and such a transfer of powers would require constitutional amendments.
art.576.title: There is much I do not understand
art.576.summary: It asks why a self-sufficient and sovereign nation would apply to join the EU after a centuries-long struggle for independence; self-government would pass to rulers in Brussels. No permanent exemptions are on offer — the same rules apply to all member states and only the adjustment period is negotiable — and the cost of the application process would be better spent at home. Interest rates and price levels are home-grown problems that politicians can fix themselves.
art.577.title: A U-turn or a trip to the trough?
art.577.summary: The founder of Evrópustraumar explains that tariff protection would fall away upon accession and the support system would be adapted to the EU’s Common Agricultural Policy; the OECD PSE support rate is about 47% in Iceland compared with 16.4% in the EU. Dairy products and eggs are about 76% more expensive in Iceland than in the six most expensive EU countries, and meat about 62% more expensive; increased tariff-free imports would lower prices. The effects would differ significantly across farming sectors, and accession negotiations would shed light on the underlying conditions.
art.578.title: “Take your medication”
art.578.summary: It says the NO side’s case is full of fallacies: no one can know in advance what the final agreement will look like, and the “snowball fallacy” that negotiations are equivalent to accession does not hold up — Norway rejected membership after accession negotiations. The nation can reject the final agreement in a second referendum, and claims to the contrary are misconceptions rooted in fear.
art.579.title: Iceland’s sword and shield
art.579.summary: The Minister of Finance quotes the words of Hans G. Andersen that law is the sword and shield of a small country, but says consensus on international rules of the game has broken down; trade disputes are intensifying and even fundamental rules on the inviolability of borders and sovereignty are coming under pressure. The question is where Iceland wants its political and economic anchor, and adopting the euro could significantly reduce the public sector’s interest burden.
art.580.title: The sovereignty of the nation and the sovereignty of the state
art.580.summary: It distinguishes between the state’s external sovereignty and the nation’s internal sovereignty: a nation can itself decide to bind state authority through supranational cooperation without surrendering its internal sovereignty. Opponents of negotiations first tried to block the referendum and then declared that the result might be disregarded if they gain power — they invoke sovereignty while at the same time rejecting its core, the nation’s ultimate power of decision.
art.581.title: Europe's Second Soul
art.581.summary: The former President of the EFTA Court says the EU should stop luring Iceland in with dubious promises and recognize the EEA as Europe's “second institutional framework.” The EEA/EFTA model shows that participation in the internal market does not require political integration and preserves state sovereignty; that framework could also serve the UK after Brexit, Switzerland, and even Turkey.
art.582.title: The Sovereignty of the Nation and the Sovereignty of the State
art.582.summary: Responding to Þorsteinn Siglaugsson: a referendum on negotiations carries political weight but does not alter the constitutional position of Alþingi — a new parliament is not bound by the decisions of a previous parliament and can halt the process. The comparison to the hierarchy of courts does not capture the constitutional order, because that involves a legal hierarchy established by law, which the referendum does not create.
art.583.title: EEA vs. EU - How Many Jobs Are We Losing Because of Tariffs?
art.583.summary: Iceland is outside the EU customs union, and fisheries and agriculture do not enjoy full free movement of goods; tariffs and uncertainty about future trade terms deter billion-krona investments in full processing in Iceland. We should ask how many valuable jobs in food technology, biotechnology, research, and product development will never be created in Iceland because of the current competitive position.
art.584.title: Do We Need Yet Another Authority?
art.584.summary: A substitute MP for Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn says the experience of local government representatives shows how decisions taken far from the field are less likely to reflect local circumstances; with membership, decisions on energy issues and resource utilization would increasingly be shaped in Brussels. The focus should be on favorable international agreements on our own terms, not on transferring decision-making power.
art.585.title: Is It Too Expensive to Apply for EU Membership?
art.585.summary: Responds to the cost argument with figures from the foreign minister's 2012 report: the application process from 2009–2012 cost the state about 400 million krónur, while Iceland received in return close to 30 million euros in IPA assistance, about 5 billion krónur at the time. The grants went, among other things, to statistics production, food safety, vocational education, and translations, and the term “adaptation grants” gives a misleading picture of what they actually involved.
art.586.title: Death or Resurrection
art.586.summary: Says Icelandic agriculture is in deep trouble regardless of the EU: the foundation of sheep farming has collapsed according to a 2022 report by Byggðastofnun, and it is absurd to blame the EU for developments in Finnish agriculture, which are explained by technological advances. The EU support system frees farmers from production quotas, greatly increases their freedom, and reflects the environmental demands of our time; therefore we should take a look at the package and vote yes on 29 August.
art.587.title: The Minister's Sweeping Judgments
art.587.summary: Points out that the key interest rate stands at 7,75% and inflation has risen despite Samfylkingin's promise to “hammer down interest rates,” and says Jóhann Pál Jóhannsson cites the currency report selectively: it also says that without the króna, adjustment to shocks would take place through direct wage cuts and unemployment. The Central Bank also noted in a letter that claims in a draft report about the króna's exchange-rate fluctuations being many times greater were based on flawed statistics.
art.588.title: “A Thousand Cod on the Conveyor Belt...”
art.588.summary: The author, who worked in fish processing when young, says EU tariffs on processed seafood products prevent whitefish and farmed salmon from being fully processed into consumer packaging in Iceland. Full processing of seafood products could become the next major industrial revolution in rural Iceland if the EU tariff wall were broken through membership. He says the vote is not about surrendering sovereignty, since all EU states are sovereign.
art.589.title: Is the EEA a Waiting Room or a Final Destination?
art.589.summary: A discussion of a new book by Carl and Laura Melusine Baudenbacher ahead of the referendum. The authors believe Iceland should strengthen its position within the EEA rather than begin accession talks; the EEA is not a waiting room but an independent and lasting model of European cooperation. The Icesave case shows that the EEA system gave a small state genuine room to defend its interests.
art.590.title: Opportunities in Full Processing - Why EU Membership Could Open New Doors
art.590.summary: Welcomes the fact that SFS is not taking a stand against accession talks if there are clear negotiating objectives on Icelandic ownership of the resource. The EU imposes higher tariffs on fully processed consumer goods than on unprocessed raw materials, thereby encouraging final processing to take place abroad; with membership, all tariffs would be abolished. At present, only 1,4% of the export value of seafood products consists of ready-to-consume consumer goods.
art.591.title: Negotiating Objectives
art.591.summary: An engineer says that demands to publish Iceland’s negotiating objectives in advance would weaken the country’s bargaining position; the other side should not know where the red lines lie. The EU is keen to get Iceland on board, and that should be used to Iceland’s advantage. The nation can judge the agreement in the later referendum.
art.592.title: What the IMF stated but Dagur does not highlight
art.592.summary: Responds to an article by Dagur B. Eggertsson on the IMF’s assessment of adopting the euro and says he omits the document’s caveats. The IMF points out that the euro removed the króna as a shock absorber and that major asymmetric shocks called for internal devaluation with unemployment, as in Spain and Greece. “Enormous welfare gains” is Dagur’s own conclusion, not the IMF’s, which takes no position.
art.593.title: No Defences Against Animal Diseases – An Irreversible Accident
art.593.summary: Warns that membership could disrupt Iceland’s decades-long defences against animal diseases and demands that the ban on importing live animals and other protective measures be made red lines in the negotiations. Cites examples of how import bans have kept the country safe from anthrax and mad cow disease. Regrets that the government has not declared these demands to be red lines.
art.594.title: On Sovereignty and Its Transfer
art.594.summary: A historian distinguishes between transferring and surrendering sovereignty and says that transfer is a precondition for human society to exist. Cooperation strengthens sovereignty because an isolated household or state is at the mercy of its surroundings and dangers over which it has no control. What matters most is having influence over the institutions that set the rules.
art.595.title: Why Fishermen Might Possibly Say “Yes”
art.595.summary: Says EU rules on equality and transparency would likely require the separation of fishing and processing so that catches would always be sold at market prices. That would improve fishermen’s terms, as they have received up to three times lower prices for capelin and mackerel than are obtained in the Faroe Islands, and it would increase the state’s fishing fees. Mentions Norway’s special arrangement for control over the northern part of its jurisdiction as a precedent.
art.596.title: What Is the Real Risk to Icelandic Fishing Quotas from EU Membership?
art.596.summary: Asks what will happen to ownership of Icelandic fishing quotas 10–30 years after accession, given that the European Commission has previously considered Iceland’s restrictions on foreign investment in the fisheries sector incompatible with the regulatory framework. An expanded pool of buyers could raise quota prices and tempt family-run fishing companies to sell their quotas. The EU’s Common Fisheries Policy is currently specifically excluded from the EEA Agreement.
art.597.title: What Has Never Happened Could Easily Happen Again!
art.597.summary: Rejects claims by Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson and Carl Baudenbacher that negotiations are an irreversible accession process and that the EU will seize the country’s resources. No EU state has lost its resources, and the principle based on fishing history ensures that local stocks would remain Icelandic. Recalls that dire predictions about the EEA Agreement never came true.
art.598.title: Joke of the Day
art.598.summary: A satirical article recalling that the predecessor of the EU was founded nearly eighty years ago to prevent another world war after tens of millions were killed. It mocks the idea that Icelanders assess European cooperation solely in terms of their own profit, given that the nation profited from both world wars.
art.599.title: The Performance of Icelandic Politicians
art.599.summary: Lists what Icelandic politicians are said to have neglected: the health, education and road systems, the 99.99% depreciation of the króna since 1922, indexation, and one of the most expensive grocery baskets in the world. Argues for voting yes to explore what the EU has to offer, because a different arrangement is needed.
art.600.title: Yes, for Everyone
art.600.summary: Intends to vote yes despite doubts about membership because he wants to know what agreement Iceland can get; it is possible to say no later. Refers to Brexit, where older generations decided the outcome of a decision that young people now live with, and says that 52% of Britons now want to rejoin the EU. Also mentions the negotiating strength of the customs union and the mutual defence obligation in the EU treaties.
art.601.title: On Debt — and Debts of Gratitude
art.601.summary: The former foreign minister defends his right to listen to Carl Baudenbacher and recounts how the EFTA Court resolved the Icesave dispute. He says accusations of treason and betrayal accompanied NATO membership in 1949, the defence agreement, EFTA membership and the EEA agreements — and that the same ugly story now seems set to repeat itself.
art.602.title: Let Us Think and Ask Together — What Best Serves Iceland in the Future?
art.602.summary: Asks whether sovereignty lies in standing outside or in having influence where decisions are made; NATO membership and the EEA have not taken away independence. Iceland already adopts a large share of the internal market acquis without a seat at the table. Iceland’s negotiating position could weaken if it waits while the positions of the Norwegians and the British change.
art.603.title: Norwegians Have Started Looking at Us
art.603.summary: At Arendalsuka, Norwegian policymakers discussed the future of the EEA, and Norway’s foreign minister says the authorities must allow for the possibility that Iceland could become an EU member state as early as 2030. Ine Eriksen Søreide, chair of Høyre, believes the EEA Agreement will not survive in the longer term, almost regardless of what Iceland does. The outcome of the Icelandic referendum would therefore have a direct impact on Norway’s position and the EFTA pillar.
art.604.title: Cheap Tricks in the Run-Up to 29 August
art.604.summary: The editor of evropumalin.is says the government has broken its election pledge not to put either accession talks or a referendum on the agenda. The Ministry for Foreign Affairs underestimates the cost of membership: an independent review by Samtök skattgreiðenda puts the net cost at ISK 23–44 billion per year, while the ministry mentions ISK 2–7 billion. The association sent a formal submission to the OSCE regarding the presentation.
art.605.title: The Struggle for Independence Never Ends
art.605.summary: Traces the struggle for independence from the abolition of the trade monopoly in 1787 to the founding of the republic in 1944, and says real independence is reflected in where decision-making power lies: who makes the laws, judges, and controls the resources. EU membership would affect the very foundation of the Icelandic state and the legacy of a long struggle. Iceland already has the EEA Agreement.
art.606.title: When Authority Replaces Reason
art.606.summary: Criticises Carl Baudenbacher for presenting academic assessments, political conclusions and predictions with the same authority as facts. It cannot be asserted that the EEA is a better option than an accession treaty that does not yet exist; any such comparison must acknowledge the uncertainty involved. The Icesave judgment proves the value of the EFTA pillar in one specific case, but says nothing about the future.
art.607.title: The Red Bus Has Arrived! Beware the Red Bus
art.607.summary: Likens the NO campaign’s messaging to the red Brexit bus, where the misleading £350 million figure led the way; ten years later, the British economy is unmistakably weaker. The referendum is about making use of Iceland’s strong negotiating position, and the nation could reject membership in a later vote. The vested interests of the króna economy and oligopolies are fighting against Icelanders being allowed to know more.
art.608.title: The Farmers’ Association Seminar from a Farmer’s Perspective
art.608.summary: A farmer says the agricultural assembly adopted, by a clear majority of votes, a resolution that farmers’ interests are best safeguarded outside the EU. Nordic farmer representatives at a Bændasamtökin seminar reportedly said that success within the EU requires lobbying in Brussels, and that the benefits Swedes gain from membership are aspects Icelanders already have through the EEA. A Norwegian representative pointed out that all lines of communication from citizens to the authorities become longer with membership.
art.609.title: We Do Not Want to Join the EU
art.609.summary: Says that “taking a look at the package” is a misleading framing because accession talks are an extensive political process with full membership as the ultimate goal. A Gallup poll shows 54% opposed to membership among those with a view, and only 26 of 63 MPs come from parties with membership in their party platform. Talks would take time and resources away from other tasks, and membership would mean giving up independent trade agreements such as free trade with China.
art.610.title: What Is the Difference for the Left Between the EEA and the EU?
art.610.summary: A left-wing perspective: the króna is a shock absorber that accelerated the recovery after the crash, while Ireland, Spain and Greece struggled with 15–27% unemployment. With the euro, both exchange-rate flexibility and fiscal room for manoeuvre would disappear because of the EU’s 3% deficit rule, as the Finns are now experiencing. Inflation and indexation are matters for Icelandic politics, not inevitable side effects of the króna.
art.611.title: Do you want Iceland to guarantee ISK 250 billion of EU debt?
art.611.summary: Explains the EU’s debt accumulation as an independent legal entity since 2009: the NextGenerationEU package amounts to about 807 billion euros, in addition to extensive loan financing for assistance to Ukraine. Repayments are to continue until 2058. If it joined, Iceland would guarantee a share of these debts amounting to about ISK 250 billion.
art.612.title: Farmers on the brakes
art.612.summary: Describes farmers’ poor financial position, their average age of 66, and the difficulty of bringing in new entrants; dizzyingly high interest rates and expensive inputs weigh on operations in Iceland’s economic environment. Recalls that the accession talks after the crash were terminated by a letter from the foreign minister without the nation’s involvement.
art.613.title: The resources are ours, whether we are in the EEA or the EU
