art.613.summary: A lawyer outlines the core principles of international law on states’ permanent sovereignty over their natural resources, and Article 194 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, which guarantees member states control over energy resources and their energy mix. The Court of Justice of the European Union is said to have confirmed this leeway in the Hinkley Point case. Claims that EEA or EU membership threatens Icelanders’ control over resources are misconceptions.
art.614.title: The nation is always divided
art.614.summary: Responds to remarks by Guðrún Hafsteinsdóttir that the nation is „split right down the middle“ over the EU issue, and says differences of opinion are not a symptom of illness but a sign of healthy democratic debate. The nation disagrees on countless issues without being considered divided. Quotes Sigmar Guðmundsson as saying that referendums are precisely for controversial issues.
art.615.title: Why I will vote no on 29 August
art.615.summary: Says Icelanders enjoy genuinely very good living standards in every international comparison, and that the EU path stems from political horse-trading within the government, in which Viðreisn gets its issue. There is probably no parliamentary majority for talks, and all opposition parties are against them. Representatives of the fishing industry and agriculture are opposed, and Iceland would pay more to the EU than it would get back.
art.616.title: Iceland’s special circumstances likely rule out EU membership
art.616.summary: A foreign affairs expert explains that talks on fisheries ran aground in 2011 when the EU demanded a time-bound plan for adaptation to the Common Fisheries Policy and the removal of restrictions on foreign investment in fishing companies. The EU is basically not designed for exceptions to special circumstances, and there is built-in resistance to exemptions that create precedents. Iceland’s special position in fisheries and energy therefore likely rules out membership; the requirement would have to be permanent exemptions.
art.617.title: Is Iceland really that much richer than the rest of the world?
art.617.summary: Uses the Big Mac Index to show that prices in Iceland are now 151% higher than in the United States and that the real exchange rate of the króna is at a historical high, at the same level as just before the crash. A persistent interest-rate gap with other countries keeps the exchange rate elevated despite higher inflation than in neighboring countries. In 2007, the same index predicted a 50% depreciation of the króna.
art.618.title: YES to see, or NO to save independence?
art.618.summary: Intends to vote yes in order to obtain an agreement as a basis for decision-making, while reserving the right to vote no to joining if the agreement does not protect farmers and food security. Says the fear over sovereignty implies the claim that the EU’s 27 nations are not sovereign. Resource tycoons in oligopolies and in the fishing industry are fighting against talks out of fear that the agreement will be too good and that competition will increase.
art.619.title: Let’s see what is on offer for rural regions
art.619.summary: A substitute MP for Samfylkingin in the Northeast constituency points to Þóroddur Bjarnason’s analysis that total regional development funding could increase fivefold to ISK 9–10 billion per year with EU matching contributions. The vote is only about restarting talks, and the only way to know what is on offer for fisheries and agriculture is to negotiate and see the agreement.
art.620.title: An opportunity for better transport links
art.620.summary: Explains how the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) supports transport infrastructure projects within the TEN-T network, in which Iceland is already mapped through the EEA. Membership could open access to funding for roads, ports, and airports; in negotiations, emphasis would need to be placed on the special circumstances of a sparsely populated country with harsh conditions. Lower interest rates and inflation, however, are the biggest issue of concern for households.
art.621.title: The Nation and Power
art.621.summary: An MP says it is right to trust the nation and give the public and civil society room to lead the debate; meetings and new organisations around the country show the strength of democracy. Membership would open a path to lower interest rates through the euro and a seat at the table, but no one knows what a finalised agreement would look like until negotiations are concluded. The NO side does not want to put its own claims to the test by allowing the nation to see the agreement.
art.622.title: Who Is the Man?
art.622.summary: Criticises the real-estate and package analogies in the “YES to see” advertisements: Iceland has been a party to the EEA since 1994 and knows full well what EU membership entails, including that Iceland would become a net contributor. What is missing is information about Iceland’s own negotiating objectives and red lines in fisheries, agriculture and energy policy. The unopened package is the government’s negotiating position, not the European Union.
art.623.title: An Ideological Reversal by xD
art.623.summary: Praises Kristrún Frostadóttir’s performance on a foreign podcast and contrasts her with the founding meeting of Áfram Ísland. Says Ólaf Ragnar Grímsson previously made the same arguments against integration, including against the EEA Agreement, and wonders that he has become the ideological leader of Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn.
art.624.title: “Norway is in accession talks with the European Union”
art.624.summary: The author, who lives in Brussels, imagines a scenario in which Norway joins the EU before Iceland and compares it with the COVID scenario “what if people stop flying to Iceland”, which was considered far-fetched. Short-sightedness could come back to haunt Icelanders if the foundations of EEA cooperation change without preparation.
art.625.title: Now It Is the Nation’s Turn – YES to See on 29 August
art.625.summary: Emphasises that the vote is only on accession talks and that the final agreement would be put to the nation in a second vote. Rejects Ólaf Ragnar Grímsson’s claims that there is no guarantee of a second vote; no state has joined the EU without a referendum, and Norwegians have twice rejected an agreement. A YES vote is the way to get all the facts on the table.
art.626.title: Finally United!
art.626.summary: Says the NO camp is united around a common enemy — Brussels — rather than a shared vision for the future; some see the EU as a socialist regulatory regime while others see it as a free-market alliance, and both cannot be true. Voting no now is not a rejection of a bad agreement but a rejection of gathering information. Power that is not in Brussels is not automatically in the hands of the public, but may instead rest with wealthy domestic groups.
art.627.title: Firsthand
art.627.summary: Describes personal experience with indexed student loans and mortgages that ballooned in the financial crash; 17 years later, the family is still paying hundreds of thousands a month under the króna’s “usurious interest-rate terms”. It recalls that the EU’s main objective has been to preserve peace in Europe for 70 years. NO supporters do not even want to allow the nation to see what agreement is on offer.
art.628.title: A Vision of Justice and Stability
art.628.summary: A Viðreisn MP says inflation and high interest rates act like an invisible tax that transfers capital from households to capital owners; a billionaire earns 75–85 million in interest in Iceland but 20–30 in the euro area. Full participation in the internal market would increase competition in banking and insurance services and lower consumer prices. A YES vote is a step towards seeing what an agreement could deliver.
detail.tollfrelsi.0: The YES side points out that EU tariffs on processed seafood make it unprofitable to fully process the catch in Iceland; the raw material is therefore exported unprocessed and the added value is created abroad. Full membership would abolish these tariffs and make it possible to process the catch at home.
detail.tollfrelsi.1: Authors such as Finn Torfa Magnússon argue that tariff-free access to the internal market could bring processing jobs and value creation back to Icelandic fishing communities.
arg.varnarsamningur.title: The Defence Agreement with the United States
arg.varnarsamningur.text: Iceland’s defence is secured through the bilateral defence agreement with the United States and membership of NATO; EU membership would add nothing in that regard and could complicate, or even jeopardise, that relationship.
art.629.title: Birgir Hermannsson writes: Framsókn and the EU
art.629.summary: The political scientist traces the history of Framsóknarflokkurinn on European issues and points out that the party congress in 2009 approved, by a large majority, the opening of accession talks. Halldór Ásgrímsson did not regard membership as a threat to fisheries and natural resources and put EU membership on the agenda of Icelandic politics. The party’s opposition now is historical amnesia.
art.630.title: Halldór Jörgen Olesen: Claims by the no side do not hold up – nearly 80% of EU residents are satisfied with membership
art.630.summary: The editor of Verðbólguvaktin says on Eyjan’s podcast that claims that all power would be transferred to Brussels do not withstand scrutiny; member states retain their sovereignty. The no side’s figures on unemployment in the EU are wrong and misleading, and nearly 80% of EU residents are satisfied with their country’s membership. He wants to see what is on offer for future generations.
art.631.title: Hrund Rudolfsdóttir: It is laughable to focus on the cost of accession talks – the interests at stake are far greater than that
art.631.summary: The entrepreneur says on Eyjan’s podcast that Iceland always ends up caught in the middle of great-power military manoeuvring and that Trump’s aggression toward Greenland should serve as a warning. Tariff wars and a radically changed geopolitical landscape call for a reassessment of Iceland’s position outside customs unions. Focusing on the cost of accession talks is laughable given the interests at stake.
art.632.title: Kristrún says the nation is not divided over the vote
art.632.summary: Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir said at Hólahátíð that the nation is approaching the vote with responsibility and deliberation, while certain leaders and commentators are trying to inflame division. People in Iceland are fully capable of making their own decision without being misled. She pledges to respect the outcome whatever it may be.
art.633.title: Davíð Þór Björgvinsson writes: The EU and member states’ debts
art.633.summary: The former judge explains the “no-bailout” rule in Article 125 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union: neither the Union nor member states are liable for the obligations of individual states. Claims that Iceland would assume the debts of other states or their pension funds are therefore false; see the Pringle judgment of the Court of Justice of the European Union from 2012.
art.634.title: Says the fishing industry’s opposition to the EU is about something entirely different from Icelanders’ control over marine resources
art.634.summary: Óskar Steinn Ómarsson, deputy municipal councillor for Samfylkingin, says the fishing companies’ opposition is about their financial interest in transfer pricing of seafood products, not control over the resource. He refers to the Samherjaskjölin and says that within the EU such profit shifting would be impossible.
art.635.title: Carl Bildt: Room for compromise on fisheries and agriculture – accession talks would proceed quickly
art.635.summary: Carl Bildt, the former Prime Minister and Foreign Minister of Sweden who received Iceland’s membership application in 2009, believes the talks would take less than two years and that there is room for compromise on fisheries and agriculture. Full membership would in fact strengthen Iceland’s sovereignty because the country would gain a say in decisions that it already implements through the EEA.
art.636.title: Jóhann Páll Jóhannsson: It costs substantial sums to remain outside the EU and engage in lobbying
art.636.summary: The Minister for the Environment, Energy and Climate says on Eyjan’s podcast that Iceland negotiated a three-year extension of its exemption from ETS charges on aviation and that the aim in accession talks would be to secure a permanent exemption. It costs substantial sums to remain outside the EU and conduct advocacy regarding regulations that Iceland implements anyway.
art.637.title: Jóhann Páll Jóhannsson: We must complete the negotiations in order to assess the situation
art.637.summary: The minister says that now is the right time, in light of the radically changed international situation, to complete accession talks so that the situation can be assessed. The price tag of sovereignty has become higher than before because it is no longer possible to trust that great powers will respect international law; that was the reason the vote was brought forward.
art.638.title: Gauti B. Eggertsson: You protect sovereignty among strong states with shared values
art.638.summary: Gauti B. Eggertsson, Professor of Economics at Brown, says the environment for free trade has collapsed with Trump’s tariff war and that the 1951 defence agreement has no value if NATO falls apart. Iceland best protects its sovereignty among states that respect the sovereignty of others, and there are major interests at stake in joining the EU customs union.
art.639.title: Sigmundur Ernir writes: Sovereignty increases with membership
art.639.summary: The columnist says there is a contradiction in wanting to remain within the EU regulatory framework through the EEA while fighting against membership. With the EEA without the EU, Icelanders live under “photocopy democracy” and accept rules from others without voting rights; sovereignty therefore increases with membership.
art.640.title: Sigvaldi Einarsson writes: The United States sold euros to save the yen – has the euro become the world’s new safe haven?
art.640.summary: The author recounts that in July 2026 the United States sold euros from its foreign exchange reserves to support the Japanese yen and believes this shows that the euro has become a genuine safe haven in the global financial system. This strengthens the case for the euro as Iceland’s future currency.
art.641.title: Davíð Þór Björgvinsson writes: The EU and natural resources
art.641.summary: The author explains that EU member states themselves retain authority over their natural resources and systems of ownership, cf. Article 345 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and the rule of international law on the permanent sovereignty of states over resources. Iceland already participates in the internal market through the EEA, so the rules on utilisation would change little with membership.
art.642.title: Sveinn Atli Gunnarsson writes: Salesmen of EU scepticism
art.642.summary: The author compares the arguments of opponents of the talks to the methods of the tobacco and oil industries: selling doubt instead of facts. NO supporters do not need to defend the current system with 10% mortgage interest rates, indexation, and a tiny currency in a feverish state – they just sow uncertainty ahead of the vote.
art.643.title: Davíð Þór Björgvinsson writes: The EU, legislative power, executive power and judicial power
art.643.summary: The author explains that the EU exercises only the powers conferred on it by the member states, and that the states retain full legislative, executive and judicial authority in other areas. Membership would eliminate the two-stage implementation of EEA acts, and Alþingi would no longer have to confirm regulations it cannot alter in any way. Membership would require a constitutional amendment, but would not amount to surrendering sovereignty.
art.644.title: Says the European Union must change and explains what helped Davíð stay in power for so long
art.644.summary: In an interview with The Rest is Politics, Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir says that under current global circumstances it would suit Iceland to join the EU and that it is therefore timely to resume talks. The vote was brought forward because of greater uncertainty in international affairs and Trump’s designs on Greenland. A YES at the end of August is not, however, the same as a yes to joining.
art.645.title: Svarthöfði writes: So sovereignty came to very little
art.645.summary: Svarthöfði points to a contradiction in Miðflokkurinn: the party claims to defend sovereignty against the EU while at the same time criticising the government for not having submitted the membership application to the US authorities. The NO campaign is therefore not about sovereignty but about maintaining Iceland’s role as a dependency of the United States.
art.646.title: Sveinn Andri Sveinsson: Public satisfaction the only measure of membership – people in the EU are the most satisfied
art.646.summary: The Supreme Court attorney says in Eyjan’s podcast that residents’ satisfaction is the only measure of whether membership works well, and in some places it measures above 90%. The cleanest approach is to get an agreement on the table and let the nation reject or approve it; Norway has twice voted down an accession treaty without joining. Voters do not let elites tell them what to do.
art.647.title: Þórdís Kolbrún: Of course EU membership must be an option for Iceland
art.647.summary: Þórdís Kolbrún Reykfjörð Gylfadóttir, vice-chair of Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn and former foreign minister, said in a keynote address at Skálholtshátíð that Icelanders must not pretend to be too grand to consider whether EU membership is an option – of course it must be. The international system that emerged after the Second World War stands on shakier ground than ever, and Icelanders must respond to the radically changed situation.
art.648.title: Criticizes Ólaf Ragnar’s involvement in the referendum – “A former president is dividing the nation”
art.648.summary: Writer Guðjón Jensson criticizes Ólaf Ragnar Grímsson for dividing the nation on behalf of a wealthy special-interest group opposed to negotiations. No nation has had to give up its sovereignty through cooperation with the EU, and the Union is ahead of Iceland in human rights, consumer affairs, social rights and environmental matters. He urges people to vote yes on 29 August.
art.649.title: Davíð Þór Björgvinsson writes: The EU and wage earners
art.649.summary: The author rejects the claim that membership would weaken the position of wage earners and outlines the EU’s protection of rights: workplace safety, working hours, equality, collective agreements and the right to strike, all of which are protected under the Union’s Charter of Fundamental Rights. The EEA has already brought Icelandic wage earners a large part of this protection, and states may go beyond the EU’s minimum requirements.
art.650.title: Pawel says Icelanders could adopt the euro in five years
art.650.summary: Pawel Bartoszek, a Viðreisn MP, says Icelanders could adopt the euro in no less than five years and asks whether it is right to reject a permanent solution to households’ interest-rate problems simply because it is not an immediate fix. He points to Croatia, where key interest rates fell rapidly during the accession process and are now 2-3%, compared with over 7% in Iceland.
art.651.title: Davíð Þór Björgvinsson writes: The EU’s limited supranational authority in the interest of the internal market
art.651.summary: The author responds to speeches at the founding meeting of Áfram Ísland and says they are based on the misunderstanding that the powers of member states are shared with the EU to a far greater extent than is actually the case. The Union exercises only those powers conferred upon it, and only about 10% of Swedes want to leave the EU.
art.652.title: Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir: The European Union provides particular support to rural areas – especially vulnerable communities
art.652.summary: The Minister for Foreign Affairs says on Eyjan’s podcast that the EU is a major supporter of rural and vulnerable communities, and that membership could support infrastructure development in Iceland, for example national roads in the countryside. Membership would also open large markets for Icelandic agricultural products, and she wants a welfare society in the European model.
art.653.title: Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir: EU membership can strengthen the position of Icelandic farmers and encourage new entrants to the sector
art.653.summary: The Minister for Foreign Affairs says on Eyjan’s podcast that Iceland will secure a strong outcome on fisheries and agriculture in accession negotiations. Lower financing costs through a link to the euro are a major interest for farmers who have invested or want to enter the sector, and strong demands should be made for continued targeted support for Icelandic agriculture.
art.654.title: Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir: The European Union’s unity and support were a source of strength for the Danes and the Greenlanders
art.654.summary: The Minister for Foreign Affairs says that when the United States set its sights on Greenland, the EU’s full support was a source of strength for the Danes and the Greenlanders; Europe stands guard over democracy, the inviolability of borders and the right of nations to self-determination. An application for membership is a real negotiating process, and the nation needs to say yes in order to see and know more before a final decision is taken.
art.655.title: Norway’s former negotiator with the EU: It is clear that Iceland will receive permanent exemptions from the EU’s Common Fisheries Policy
art.655.summary: Torben Foss, former permanent secretary at Norway’s Ministry of Fisheries and adviser to Iceland in the negotiations until 2013, says EU negotiators went a long way toward confirming that the total catch from Icelandic stocks would be decided in Reykjavík, since the Icelandic continental shelf is a distinct ecosystem; the Canary Islands and Madeira received a similar solution. He also believes that strategic military considerations should strongly encourage defenceless Iceland to join.
art.656.title: Davíð Þór Björgvinsson writes: The EU and Iceland’s rural communities
art.656.summary: The author outlines the EU’s cohesion and regional development policy (Articles 174–178 of the Treaty), which gives special attention to sparsely populated areas and islands, along with the Regional Development Fund, the Social Fund and the Connecting Europe Facility. Membership could provide the countryside with funding for transport infrastructure, for example by defining Keflavík Airport and ports within the TEN-T network.
art.657.title: Major believes Britain could return to the European Union: “This has harmed the nation”
art.657.summary: John Major, former Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, says Brexit costs the British economy £100 billion a year and that the promise of taking power back from Brussels was an empty slogan. North Korea is the only country that is sovereign in every respect; other nations share sovereignty in international cooperation.
art.658.title: Sigmundur Ernir writes: Satisfaction with EU membership has risen rapidly among EU nations
art.658.summary: The columnist points out that satisfaction with EU membership measures above 50% in 24 of the 27 member states, 76–85% in the Nordic countries, and highest at 86% in Ireland. These nations were given the chance to see an agreement and vote on it; none has lost resources, sovereignty or culture, since the member states govern the EU and not the other way around.
art.659.title: Davíð Þór Björgvinsson writes: The EU, the Icelandic language and culture
art.659.summary: The author corrects the misunderstanding that the EU aims to standardize culture; Article 167 of the treaty provides for respect for national diversity. Icelandic parties have received grants totaling ISK 3–4 billion from Creative Europe since 2014, and full membership could strengthen the Icelandic language and culture even further.
art.660.title: Þorsteinn Pálsson writes: Does Iceland belong in a customs union during a tariff war?
art.660.summary: The former prime minister says the United States' tariff war has upended security in global trade and that a small nation needs to assess whether it belongs in the EU customs union. He praises an independent Evrópustraumar report on the effects of membership on business competitiveness and criticizes SA and SI for remaining silent about the changed reality, unlike their Norwegian sister organizations.
art.661.title: Word on the Street: Þorsteinn Már plans to pay 25 million krónur for a phone bank in August
art.661.summary: The column says that Þorsteinn Már Baldvinsson, founder of Samherji, plans to pay 25 million krónur out of his own pocket for a phone bank campaigning against YES. Large companies that finance themselves at euro or dollar interest rates want to maintain their competitive advantage while the general public and smaller businesses pay Icelandic usury-level interest rates because of the króna. The vote is about special interests versus the public interest.
art.662.title: Davíð Þór Björgvinsson writes: The EU is democratic
art.662.summary: The author responds to talk of the EU’s democratic deficit and explains that the Union’s powers are based on the democratic mandate of the member states, the European Parliament is elected directly by citizens, and the Council of Ministers derives its mandate from national parliaments. The EU meets all fundamental conditions of a democratic constitutional order, even though it is a multinational institution rather than a state.
art.663.title: Hilmar Þór writes: The European Union, Greece and "raundæmi"
art.663.summary: The author responds to Þorsteinn Pálsson with figures from the AGS database: Greece has never met the EU’s 60% debt criterion, whereas Iceland does, and unlike the Greeks, Icelanders worked their way out of the debt problem without EU membership or the euro. In practice, the EU’s fiscal rules have been blown to the winds, as shown by the debt positions of France and Italy.
art.664.title: Halldór Jörgen Olesen writes: No conscription in the EU — and no legal route to impose it on Icelanders
art.664.summary: The author responds to an MP from the Centre Party: there is no conscription in the EU, there is no legal basis in the treaties to impose it on member states, and national security is solely the responsibility of each state. Only nine of the 27 EU countries have conscription, and each state decides that for itself; Germany abolished it in 2011 as a full EU member state.
art.665.title: Davíð Þór Björgvinsson writes: Cooperation between the United States and EU states in security and defence
art.665.summary: The author rejects the claim that EU membership would damage Iceland’s defence ties with the United States: 23 of the 27 EU states are in NATO, the EU treaty provides that the Union’s policy shall respect NATO obligations, and the United States has bilateral defence agreements with individual EU states such as Spain, Greece and Pólland.
art.666.title: Þorsteinn Pálsson tears apart Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson’s fearmongering about Iceland and the EU
art.666.summary: Þorsteinn Pálsson rebuts, point by point, seven "raundæmi" from Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson: Ireland, which is closer to Reykjavík than Oslo and London, is in the EU with the euro and has the strongest economic growth among neighboring countries; the currencies of Greenland and the Faroe Islands are pegged to the euro through the Danish krone. Taken as a whole, the examples are a strong argument for full membership.
art.667.title: Davíð Þór Björgvinsson writes: Protection of human rights within the EU
art.667.summary: The author traces the development of human rights protection within the EU: since the Lisbon Treaty in 2009, the Union’s Charter of Fundamental Rights has had the same status as the founding treaties and binds the institutions and member states when implementing EU law. Individuals can invoke it before the courts of the member states.
art.668.title: Kristrún Frostadóttir: The European Union gives more ground than we do – fisheries are not a major issue within the Union
art.668.summary: In Eyjan’s podcast, the Prime Minister says the EU is a flexible political partnership that has repeatedly changed its rules and accession conditions; fisheries management is not a major issue within the Union, leaving room for Iceland in resource matters. Accession talks would not change Iceland’s relations with the United States in any way.
art.669.title: Kristrún Frostadóttir: We are in constant alignment with EU rules through the EEA
art.669.summary: The Prime Minister says it would be momentous if the nation votes no, because a long time would pass before the decision would be reconsidered. It is completely wrong to say that Iceland’s negotiating objectives are undefined; they are set out in the explanatory statement to the parliamentary resolution and in the Foreign Affairs Committee’s report. Iceland is already in constant alignment with EU rules through the EEA Agreement.
art.670.title: University professor on Iceland’s EU membership: “It is not substantive to promise lower interest rates, more investment and higher living standards without showing the assumptions”
art.670.summary: History professor Sigurður Gylfi Magnússon criticizes Haraldur Ólafsson, chairman of Heimssýn, for cost calculations of 118 billion that forget the benefits of membership – both debit and credit must be counted. He calls on both sides to show the assumptions behind their figures and himself reviews the economic benefits based on adopting the euro.
art.671.title: University professor: Opponents of membership fixate on absolute minutiae – killing substantive debate in the process
art.671.summary: History professor Sigurður Gylfi Magnússon says opponents of membership fixate on minutiae, including attacking the wording of the referendum question, which he believes could hardly be otherwise, and criticizes the statement by the National Electoral Commission as political interference. He has not made up his mind on membership but intends to vote yes to continuing the talks.
art.672.title: Halla Hrund Logadóttir: EU membership increases the likelihood of interest rate cuts
art.672.summary: In Eyjan’s podcast, Framsókn MP Halla Hrund Logadóttir says interest costs weigh most heavily on young people and that interest rate cuts are more likely if Iceland joins the EU. Circumstances such as Norway joining could call for a review of Iceland’s position, although the EEA Agreement has served the country well.
art.673.title: Davíð Þór Björgvinsson writes: The EU’s supranational authority
art.673.summary: The author explains that the EU’s supranational authority is limited to certain areas, especially the internal market, where harmonized rules must apply equally everywhere. In other areas, the states retain self-determination and make decisions unanimously; the debate becomes confused when these two are conflated.
art.674.title: Halla Hrund Logadóttir: I support the referendum – I want clear red lines in the sand
art.674.summary: Framsókn MP Halla Hrund Logadóttir supports letting the nation decide on the continuation of accession talks, as matters affecting the long-term future are ideal for a referendum. She wants a more detailed parliamentary resolution with negotiating objectives and clear red lines on natural resources in the talks.
art.675.title: Eyjólfur Ármannsson: Voting on continuing the talks does not harm the EEA Agreement – the EEA is a Norwegian setup
art.675.summary: Infrastructure Minister Eyjólfur Ármannsson says the position of Flokkur fólksins is clear: the party is not in favor of EU membership, although it supports letting the nation decide on the continuation of the talks. He is very much in favor of the EEA Agreement, says Iceland has associate membership and is “80% inside” the Union.
art.676.title: Everyone knows what will be asked in the referendum
art.676.summary: Davíð Þór Björgvinsson, former judge at the European Court of Human Rights, objects to the National Electoral Commission’s conclusion that the referendum question is unclear. There are solid grounds for concluding that the 2009 membership application is still valid, cf. a memorandum from the Ministry for Foreign Affairs and statements from the EU, and everyone understands what is being asked.
art.677.title: Davíð Þór Björgvinsson: Baudenbacher is on the wrong track – If the EU and Iceland consider the membership application valid, then it is valid
art.677.summary: Davíð Þór Björgvinsson says Carl Baudenbacher’s argument that Iceland’s membership application was withdrawn does not hold up; the European Commission and the Commissioner for Enlargement have stated that the application remains fully valid. The dispute is much ado about nothing.
art.678.title: Davíð Þór Björgvinsson: Need for better explanations – can the talks end in any way other than with an agreement that would be put to the nation?
art.678.summary: Davíð Þór Björgvinsson, who describes himself as rather pro-European, believes it would be more honest toward voters if the main outlines of the negotiation objectives were clear before the vote. Ministers have already made full control over the fishing grounds a condition, and the talks would end with an agreement that would be put to the nation.
art.679.title: Davíð Þór Björgvinsson: Special arrangements are indeed on the table – accession treaties are real treaties – the terms need to be negotiated
art.679.summary: Davíð Þór Björgvinsson explains that, according to Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union, the terms of accession are based on an agreement between the member states and the applicant state. Applicant states have countless times received permanent special arrangements on the basis of their fundamental interests, and each accession treaty becomes an integral part of the founding treaties.
art.680.title: Davíð Þór Björgvinsson writes: The accession of new states to the EU
art.680.summary: The author summarizes his lecture on the EU’s accession rules: the accession treaties of individual states are part of the Union’s primary law because all member states must approve them, and the EU has no powers other than those that sovereign states have agreed to share with it.
art.681.title: Yngvi Ómar Sigrúnarson writes: Buying the nation’s vote
art.681.summary: The author points out that, according to Meta’s ad library, Áfram Ísland spent about ten times more on Facebook and Instagram advertising than Já til að sjá. The movement is said to have entered the campaign fully formed with a powerful advertising agency despite claiming to be unfunded, and the lack of transparency makes it impossible to see who is paying. The nation is being frightened with inflated nationalism.
art.682.title: Hrund Rudolfsdóttir: A NO now puts us in an extremely difficult position
art.682.summary: Hrund Rudolfsdóttir, a businesswoman and board member of Já til að sjá, says that a no on 29 August would only postpone an issue that needs to be resolved and leave the nation divided. It would be better to vote yes, complete the negotiations, and then take a position on the agreement; if it is bad, the nation says no, if it is good, it says yes.
art.683.title: Guðmundur Einarsson writes: Ólafur Ragnar has come home
art.683.summary: The author traces the political wanderings of Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson through the party system and says he has now become the leading spokesman for Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn as the main speaker at Áfram Ísland meetings in Sjálfstæðishúsið, attended by the leadership of the party and Framsókn. The article portrays the no movement as an alliance of old power blocs.
art.684.title: Word on the Street: A foreign know-it-all brought in to tell Icelanders their judgment cannot be trusted
art.684.summary: The column says Áfram Ísland brought in Carl Baudenbacher, who now does lobbying work including for Russian interests, to tell Icelanders that their judgment cannot be trusted and that Europe is not an attractive option. The meeting was moved from the ceremonial hall of HÍ after the hall was found to have been booked under false pretences.
art.685.title: Margrét Guðmundsdóttir: No good manager rejects important negotiations in advance
art.685.summary: Margrét Guðmundsdóttir, former CEO and chair of the Employers’ Association, says that in a 40-year management career she has never seen a board reject important negotiations before knowing what is on offer. Fundamental interests such as control over natural resources should be clearly stated at the negotiating table and the outcome rejected if it is unacceptable; Danish and Norwegian employers’ organizations view the internal market as the foundation of trade.
art.686.title: Word on the Street: The plot failed – Baudenbacher, a friend of Russia, works with the no side
art.686.summary: The column says Hannes Hólmstein Gissurarson and Ragnar Árnason booked the ceremonial hall of HÍ for a meeting that was in fact on behalf of Áfram Ísland, and that the rector stopped the use of the hall. Carl Baudenbacher, who is said to have done lobbying work for Russian interests, was brought in to cast the EU in a suspicious light.
art.687.title: Inga Dóra Ingvadóttir writes: The farmer, the fish, and the agreement that does not yet exist
art.687.summary: The author takes farmers’ fears seriously but points out that the Farmers’ Association report on EU membership was produced by an interest group, not as an independent review, and that many of the biggest questions remain unanswered. She warns against turning potential risk into a foregone conclusion before any agreement is on the table.
art.688.title: Word on the street: “If people want isolation, then they must bear its consequences”
art.688.summary: The column says opponents of the talks are using fearmongering in direct contradiction to statements by EU leaders that permanent special arrangements are on offer. It says Heimssýn advocates isolation and is largely funded by fishing companies and the Farmers’ Association, while the public pays mortgage interest rates three times higher than in eurozone countries.
art.689.title: Þorvaldur Ingi Jónsson writes: Does the interest-rate environment cost a young family three months of the working year in 2026?
art.689.summary: The author calculates that a 5.9% interest-rate gap with Denmark costs a young family with a 50 million króna home loan about 2.25 million krónur a year — equivalent to more than three months of full-time work. Over a 30-year loan term, even a more cautious 4% interest-rate gap would amount to more than four working years.
art.690.title: Svarthöfði writes: The YES side is advancing
art.690.summary: Svarthöfði mocks Framsókn for fighting against letting the nation take a position on an accession agreement and for wanting future generations to continue grappling with the same interest rates and indexation. Polls show support for yes is growing; among other things, 60% of the oldest voters have shifted in favor of membership since Áfram Ísland began its campaign.
art.691.title: Pawel Bartoszek: We do not need to change anything on our side during the negotiation period — completely beyond doubt
art.691.summary: Pawel Bartoszek, chair of Alþingi’s Foreign Affairs Committee, says the EU’s position has changed since 2009: Donald Tusk and other leaders now speak of flexibility toward countries like Iceland, a word that was once taboo. He says talk of adaptation applies to former Eastern Bloc states, whereas Iceland is already 75% inside the Union through the EEA and would not need to change anything during the negotiation period.
art.692.title: Sigmundur Ernir writes: YES is for the public, while NO is for the elite
art.692.summary: The columnist says employers’ opposition to the referendum is revealing: the króna shields an oligopolistic market from foreign competition and capital owners enjoy nine percent deposit interest while the public pays mortgage rates three times higher. The fishing industry takes out euro loans at three percent interest and buys up apartments in Iceland.
art.693.title: Pawel Bartoszek: There are good people among both the no side and the yes side — I would very much like to have many no supporters on my team
art.693.summary: Pawel Bartoszek, chair of the Foreign Affairs Committee, welcomes polls continuing to show a majority for YES and says support for continuing the talks has measured steady for years. He calls for a moderate and thoughtful debate and says there are good people in both camps.
art.694.title: Haraldur Ólafsson writes: X-NO for the children
art.694.summary: The chair of Heimssýn says being in the EU costs a great deal of money — membership fees, tariffs, expansion of the administrative system, and armament projects — money that could otherwise benefit children. Icelandic teenagers need not fear EU militarization plans if Iceland remains outside the Union, and an Icelandic passport already opens every door.
art.695.title: Thomas Möller writes: “It’s strange to say no”
art.695.summary: The author recounts a young man in the hot tub at Eskifjörður who pointed out that this autumn the vote is only on authorizing talks, not on joining; saying no is like refusing to look at a purchase offer before signing. Membership could later mean lower interest on a home loan.
art.696.title: Arnór Sighvatsson: To sit at the table or be on the menu
art.696.summary: Arnór Sighvatsson, former Deputy Governor of the Central Bank, says the United States no longer shares Iceland’s and Europe’s core values and that Iceland, one of the most trade-dependent states in the world, belongs among nations that respect sovereignty, borders, and human rights. The EU is built on these core values.
art.697.title: Kolbrún Bergþórsdóttir writes: The message of Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn
art.697.summary: The columnist praises Þórdís Kolbrún for saying membership is an obvious option but criticizes Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn for shutting down such voices and hammering home that there is nothing to negotiate. The nation is voting on continued talks, not membership, and should be given space to assess the options.
art.698.title: Sveinn Andri Sveinsson: Ólafur Ragnar has never had a prophetic stature
art.698.summary: The Supreme Court attorney says the YES camp’s message is simple — that the nation should grant a mandate to sit down at the negotiating table — while the NO camp has to spend its energy on fearmongering. He says adaptation talk applies to former Eastern Bloc states; Iceland has already adapted through the EEA and would receive support from the European Central Bank when adopting the euro.
art.699.title: Word on the Street: Let’s not allow an elderly flock to choose the future for young people
art.699.summary: The column says the vote is about the future of young people and criticizes well-known elder statesmen such as Hjörleifur Guttormsson, Jón Bjarnason and Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson for paternalism and propaganda against voters deciding their own future.
art.700.title: Erna Bjarnadóttir writes: Limited use of antibiotics in livestock farming is a social value
art.700.summary: The author points out that antibiotic use in Icelandic livestock farming is among the very lowest in Europe according to ESVAC, but much higher in the countries from which most agricultural products are imported. She argues that this distinctive position should be protected as a public health and social value in light of growing antimicrobial resistance.
art.701.title: Sveinn Andri Sveinsson: Desperation in the NO camp — vested interests betting on inflation against the public
art.701.summary: The Supreme Court attorney says Áfram Ísland is built on companies that profit from inflation: the real estate company Heimar would earn an extra 4,5 billion if inflation rose from five to ten percent, and the commercial banks two to three billion each for every percentage point. The powers that be, he says, fear above all that a negotiating committee might succeed in securing a favorable agreement with the EU.
art.702.title: Sigmundur Ernir writes: Independence Party members know what it means to sit at the table
art.702.summary: The columnist recalls that ministers from the Independence Party praised the opportunity to sit at the table in the EU Council of Ministers through Schengen, where Iceland and Norway in 2001 made it a condition that participation be institutional and political, not merely technical. Experience shows that small states have influence when they are inside the process.
art.703.title: Sigvaldi Einarsson writes: We are already tenants, just without voting rights
art.703.summary: The author says Iceland has already adopted about two thirds of EU legislation through the EEA without voting rights — the position of a tenant who lives in the house and follows the landlord’s rules but has no say. A NO vote would entrench that system; a YES vote is the way to the table. Loud opposition, he argues, protects oligopoly and special interests, not the interests of households.
art.704.title: Thomas Möller writes: Let’s say YES for young people
art.704.summary: The author says most analyses show that full membership would improve living standards, lower interest rates and food prices, and strengthen Iceland’s position in an uncertain world. 74% of residents in EU member states believe their country has benefited from membership, a historic high, and no member state considers itself to have lost sovereignty. Iceland would retain full control over its fishing grounds, as it shares fish stocks with EU countries only to a limited extent.
art.705.title: Sigurður Gylfi Magnússon: The substance of Ólafur Ragnar’s message is the same as when he praised the Outvasion Vikings before the crash
art.705.summary: Historian and professor Sigurður Gylfi Magnússon recalls a 2006 speech by Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson in which he praised the Outvasion Vikings and says the substance at the founding meeting of Áfram Ísland was the same: that Icelanders are better and superior to everyone else. He says that nationalist ideology proved very costly for the nation before the crash.
art.706.title: Word on the Street: Fishing magnates and representatives of special interests want to tell voters what to do
art.706.summary: The column criticizes Kristján Loftsson, CEO of Hvalur, for saying he does not believe the nation is „so foolish“ as to say yes, and says fishing magnates are putting up large sums of money for propaganda against negotiations. Such paternalism toward voters, it says, does not sit well with the public.
art.707.title: Haraldur Ólafsson writes: No thanks rests on the firm foundations of reason and weighty arguments
art.707.summary: The chairman of Heimssýn sets out the reasons of NO supporters: surrendering legislative power would lead to laws that could not be got rid of, European nations with centuries of fishing experience would want back into Icelandic waters, the EU is heading toward becoming a military power, Icelandic agriculture could collapse, and the direct and indirect costs of membership keep rising, among other things because of the debts of large member states.
art.708.title: Kolbrún Bergþórsdóttir writes: The clairvoyance of the NO side
art.708.summary: The columnist asks how Guðrún Hafsteinsdóttir and other NO supporters can claim in advance what kind of agreement will be offered to the nation – that would have to count as clairvoyance. People want to look inside the package and not let Ólaf Ragnar, Björn Bjarnason and others make the decision for them.
art.709.title: Svarthöfði writes: The only thing that can save Morgunblaðið is a YES on 29 August
art.709.summary: Svarthöfði asks why NO supporters fear the vote if they are certain the agreement will be impossible to accept – the nation would then simply reject it. Their eagerness suggests they expect a favorable agreement. The owners of Morgunblaðið have income and financing in euros at one-third of Icelandic interest rates and want to protect that advantage.
art.710.title: Brexit a model for the NO side – using the same propaganda tactics – the British now regret leaving
art.710.summary: A news analysis reporting that Haraldur Ólafsson, chairman of Heimssýn, says in The Sunday Telegraph that Brexit is a model for the NO movement and that the slogan “Take Back Control” is an inspiration. The article recounts that the promises made by Brexit supporters did not hold up, that the UK economy has been harmed, and that the arguments of the NO side suggest their ultimate goal is withdrawal from the EEA.
art.711.title: Thomas Möller writes: Don’t say NO ... say maybe
art.711.summary: The author points out that the vote is not about membership but about getting to see an agreement that would later be put to a vote; yes in reality means “maybe” and carries no commitment. No permanently closes off the option and is therefore a bigger decision than yes. He criticizes the one-sided coverage of Morgunblaðið, with 18 warning articles in a single weekend edition.
art.712.title: Sigmundur Ernir writes: Heimssýn is an alliance of fear
art.712.summary: The columnist says Heimssýn exposed itself by threatening RÚV for bringing academics into the TV studio, where one absurd claim after another was debunked, including the claim that no alignment process begins until negotiations have been approved. The organization feeds on fear and isolationism.
art.713.title: Word on the Street: Negativity and distortion characterize the NO side – arrogance is added when the arguments run out
art.713.summary: The column compares the conduct of Þorgerður Katrín and Sigríður Andersen on Kastljós after parliament approved the referendum by 34 votes to eight. Miðflokkurinn voted against allowing the nation to express its view, and the arguments of the NO side are marked by fearmongering and distortions such as calling the vote a “sham opinion poll”.
art.714.title: Halldór Jörgen writes: When a conditional no becomes “simply yes”
art.714.summary: The author replies to Hildur Sverrisdóttir, who interpreted the foreign minister’s conditional no to alignment as “simply yes”. The agreement from the 2009-2013 accession process, which Hildur says no one has seen, is a public parliamentary document from 2013, and the safeguard about independent domestic objectives refers to Icelandic legislation, not alignment; Croatia made 14 such changes without difficulty.
art.715.title: Says Dagur is right but Diljá Mist wrong - “Do we also need to take the numbers seriously”
art.715.summary: Halldór Jörgen Olesen, editor of Verðbólguvaktin, calculates that the interest-rate gap between Iceland and the euro area costs households 101-188 billion krónur a year based on 2.897 trillion krónur in housing debt; the 100 billion figure cited by Dagur B. Eggertsson is closer to the lower bound than the upper one. The Baltic states, Slovakia and Croatia show that interest rates fall permanently after accession.
art.716.title: Kristrún Frostadóttir: Who does not want to let the nation see an agreement? – Whose interests are they protecting?
art.716.summary: The prime minister says that joining the EU would immediately reduce the cost of the small and unstable króna and increase competition in groceries, fuel, insurance and the lending market. The public should ask who profits from the lack of competition and does not even want to let the nation see the agreement.
art.717.title: Kristrún Frostadóttir: Say yes if you are uncertain – you will always have the chance later to say no
art.717.summary: The prime minister says this is a good opportunity to secure an agreement that takes account of Iceland’s special circumstances and reminds people that Iceland has historically obtained special arrangements, from Marshall aid to NATO membership without contributions. Uncertain voters should say yes because the opportunity to reject an agreement will come later.
art.718.title: Sigmundur Ernir writes: Europe's most popular cooperative movement
art.718.summary: The columnist says the opposition fears that the negotiations will produce such a good outcome that the nation will like it; first it is claimed that there is nothing to negotiate and then that exemptions will not be permanent, even though both claims have been refuted. Public satisfaction with EU membership has increased everywhere after accession.
art.719.title: Thomas Möller writes: NO is bigger than yes
art.719.summary: The author says NO is a far more consequential decision than yes: it would shut off the possibility of membership for decades, entrench the EEA arrangement under which Iceland adopts rules without influence, and keep the nation in a krona economy with higher interest rates. Yes would only authorize negotiations and examination of an agreement, without any commitment whatsoever.
art.720.title: Kolbrún Bergþórsdóttir writes: The fear of yes
art.720.summary: The columnist says the opposition is consumed by fear that the nation will vote yes; it claims there is nothing to negotiate and no exemptions on offer, but the nation itself wants to learn what is on offer. Cooperation among the nations of Europe is a good thing and well worth exploring the advantages of membership.
art.721.title: Davíð Þór Björgvinsson: If NATO is wound up, the defence agreement with the United States is broken
art.721.summary: Davíð Þór Björgvinsson points out that the 1951 defence agreement means that the United States defends Iceland on behalf of NATO; if NATO comes to an end, all the legal foundations of the agreement collapse. The unpredictable conduct of the United States makes it necessary to reassess the pillars of Icelandic security.
art.722.title: Thomas Möller writes: The election of young people
art.722.summary: The author says the vote will shape the development of society for the next 40 years and is therefore the election of young people. Yes creates opportunities for freedom of movement, education and work in 27 countries, and for stability instead of economic swings with 20% interest rates, 50% devaluations and 100% inflation that older generations have had to endure; the vote is only about continuing the negotiations.
art.723.title: Word on the Street: The desperation is obvious – they have even dusted off Heiðrún Lind
art.723.summary: The column says the EU's fisheries chief has confirmed that accession talks are genuine negotiations in which account is taken of the specific circumstances of applicant countries, and points to precedents such as the Danes' permanent special arrangement on summer houses. Heiðrún Lind Marteinsdóttir of SFS is said to have claimed, without evidence, that there are no precedents for a permanent exemption.
art.724.title: Word on the Street: Elders of various ages against the future – typical writing by anti-Europeans in Morgunblaðið
art.724.summary: The column responds to an article in Morgunblaðið claiming that the krona proved a "saviour from collapse" and points out that the collapse in fact exposed the krona's greatest weaknesses when foreign nations wanted nothing to do with it. Isolationists are trying to scare the public away from fully examining the pros and cons of membership.
art.725.title: The National Electoral Commission must resign – it has stepped onto the political stage
art.725.summary: Professor of history Sigurður Gylfi Magnússon says the National Electoral Commission's opinion on the referendum question is a political statement and refers to a memorandum from the Ministry for Foreign Affairs from August 2025 on the course of the accession application. The National Electoral Commission has stepped decisively onto the political stage, he says, and the question is whether its representatives are fit to remain in office.
art.726.title: The left must say no to the EU
art.726.summary: The author says the EU is a machine that transfers power and wealth from the public to bureaucratic and economic elites, and that the four freedoms lead to the harmonization of wages and working conditions between countries. In Brussels, a bureaucracy with a major democratic deficit has been built up, where public-interest organizations have little power against lobbyists.
art.727.title: Submitted article: Steingrímur J.'s personal experience of EU talks speaks volumes
art.727.summary: Guðni refers to an article by Steingrímur J. Sigfússon about his experience of the accession negotiations in 2009 and urges sceptics who want to "look inside the package" to read it. He says it is astonishing that Þorgerður Katrín claims Iceland can secure full control over fisheries and agriculture.
art.728.title: Submitted article: Is there demand for 40% unemployment and a 50% loss of purchasing power with EU membership?
art.728.summary: The author says the government's journey into a “technically bankrupt” Europe is a march toward ruin, and that Iceland is one of the world's three highest-quality-of-life countries, all of which stand outside the EU and the euro. NO on 29 August is the only right answer.
art.729.title: Submitted article: Is a seat at the table enough?
art.729.summary: The MP points out that although Iceland would keep its seat on the Arctic Council within the EU, the Union would hold the negotiating mandate in areas such as the protection of marine resources, as it does for Sweden and Finland. What matters most, he says, is that the mandate behind the seat is Icelandic and that the voice is our own — that position should not be given up under any circumstances.
art.730.title: Submitted article: Iceland’s self-confidence and the politics of fear ahead of the EU referendum
art.730.summary: The former President of the EFTA Court says it is hard to see any convincing arguments for Iceland joining the EU; the EEA/EFTA model is a workable arrangement that provides broad access to the internal market while preserving control over fisheries, agriculture, and the currency. The campaign for membership risks becoming fear-based politics because the positive arguments are weak.
art.731.title: Submitted article: Let’s take no risks with the EEA Agreement!
art.731.summary: The MP says the undisguised propaganda by EU supporters against the EEA Agreement has become apparent in the run-up to the vote; it is falsely claimed that Iceland is already, for the most part, inside the EU. European parliamentarians repeatedly tell her that Iceland gets a great deal for very little through the EEA Agreement.
art.732.title: Submitted article: A Viðreisn engineer spoils the parade
art.732.summary: Guðni compares the EU debate to the emperor’s new clothes and refers to an engineer’s summary of the consequences of membership, which gives him a chill to read. He also refers to a meeting between Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson and Carl Baudenbacher on the transfer of Iceland’s sovereignty.
art.733.title: Submitted article: Is no risk really being taken?
art.733.summary: The former Prime Minister rejects the claim that new accession talks carry no risk; they would take several years regardless of the outcome and require agreement in Alþingi. He fears that EEA cooperation could be seriously damaged in the meantime because the administrative system would be preoccupied with the negotiations.
art.734.title: Submitted article: The euro, happiness, and fear
art.734.summary: The professor compares Finland and Iceland: the Finnish economy is grappling with low growth, high unemployment, and public debt of around 90% of GDP, and GDP per capita has grown much less in Finland than in Iceland since the adoption of the euro in 1999.
art.735.title: Submitted article: Why is the government not doing anything?
art.735.summary: The author asks what explains the government’s inaction on inflation, which measured 5.3% in July and could trigger contingency clauses in wage agreements. He cites voices from the business community asking whether a government that wants to “force us into the EU” is neglecting economic management.
art.736.title: Submitted article: What lessons can be drawn from the events in Ceuta?
art.736.summary: Erna discusses the mass crossing of people at the Ceuta border in late July and says the events raise questions about border control, Schengen cooperation, and the EU’s responsibility when pressure is high. She asks which constitutional framework best serves the interests of a small state.
art.737.title: Submitted article: The EU is a bureaucracy, but Iceland is a unique diamond
art.737.summary: The author says the EU is a centrally controlled military and customs union that limits individual freedom through heavier regulation, and recounts Iceland’s history of independence from 1874 to the founding of the republic in 1944.
art.738.title: Opinion piece: What exactly keeps the door open?
art.738.summary: The author turns the “look inside the package” argument on its head: outside the EU, Iceland keeps both options open, joining or staying out, and that is the most open position imaginable. It is a no that keeps the door open, not a yes.
art.739.title: Opinion piece: Why doesn’t the government want to lower interest rates?
art.739.summary: Guðlaugur Þór recalls that the governing parties promised lower inflation and lower interest rates, and that the prime minister had intended to “nail down interest rates”, yet in August 2026 inflation is still far above target and the policy rate is 7.75%.
art.740.title: Opinion piece: What is right should be right
art.740.summary: The author says the debate on the transfer of sovereignty has gone off the rails: until now, it had been undisputed that EU membership would require the transfer of part of Iceland’s sovereignty, but that now seems to have changed in the run-up to the referendum.
art.741.title: Opinion piece: Animal health as a foundation of the food economy
art.741.summary: Erna discusses the EU screening report on Chapter 12 of the negotiations on food safety and animal health; Iceland considered it necessary to maintain special rules on protection against animal diseases, and the issue remained unresolved when the talks were halted in 2012. She asks whether legislative changes upon accession would increase operational risk in the food value chain.
art.742.title: Opinion piece: Not in step on the involvement of foreign politicians?
art.742.summary: The author compares the prime minister’s remarks that she wants no foreign interference in the referendum with the conduct of the foreign minister, who is said to have invited five foreign ministers from EU states to Iceland this year, where they spoke in favor of membership at meetings and in the media.
art.743.title: Opinion piece: More on the extensive transfer of power to the EU
art.743.summary: The former Speaker of Parliament argues that legal discussion over the past 35 years has shown broad agreement that EU membership would require a transfer of powers in all branches of state authority and that constitutional amendments would be needed before accession.
art.744.title: Opinion piece: We do not negotiate the fundamental rules
art.744.summary: The author says he will vote no, not out of opposition to European cooperation but because accession talks are fundamentally about an applicant state adopting the EU acquis; only transition periods, safeguard clauses, and special arrangements within that framework can be negotiated.
art.745.title: Opinion piece: We already know more than enough
art.745.summary: The former permanent secretary says there is already ample information about what EU membership would entail; control over resources is a fundamental issue. He cites an IMF forecast that GDP growth in the EU will be only about 1.44% per year in 2027-2031, and even lower in the euro area.
art.746.title: Opinion piece: Why, then, was the alleged agreement needed?
art.746.summary: The author says the foreign minister’s claims that the talks are not about adaptation run counter to the EU’s own negotiating framework, which states that the talks are about adapting to the Union’s rules and administrative system.
art.747.title: Opinion piece: Information chaos from the “let us see” camp
art.747.summary: Birgir criticizes advertisements such as “May I see … whether my children can get lower interest rates?” and says accession talks will not produce any new information on such matters; nothing indicates that the government intends to present specific demands in these areas.
art.748.title: Opinion piece: The gulf between the truth and supporters of the European Union
art.748.summary: The author recalls that Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson referred to a gulf between parliament and the nation, and says the arguments for membership are economic, about interest rates and currencies, and about security — the security argument can be dismissed offhand with minimal knowledge. No company makes an investment decision without a risk assessment.
art.749.title: Opinion piece: It matters on what basis talks are resumed
art.749.summary: Erna points out that guidance material from the National Electoral Commission says there are differing views on whether “resuming accession talks” means continuing the negotiations from 2010 or starting a new accession process, and asks whether Iceland’s negotiating framework from 2010 still applies sixteen years later.
art.750.title: Opinion piece: Finland in rapid decline after joining the EU
art.750.summary: The author says Finland is grappling with economic stagnation, with over 10% unemployment, over 30% youth unemployment, and public debt approaching 90% of GDP, after joining the EU in 1995 and adopting the euro in 1999.
art.751.title: Opinion piece: The euro does not fix traffic
art.751.summary: The author says the rightward swing this spring in the municipal elections can largely be traced to traffic congestion costing society two to three percent of GDP — a problem the euro will not solve.
art.752.title: Opinion piece: Relative stability does not guarantee control over fishery resources
art.752.summary: The managing director of SFS says that claims that Iceland would retain full control over its fishery resources and that the rule of relative stability would protect Iceland’s interests cannot both be true: if Iceland needs the rule, the country is already subject to the Common Fisheries Policy.
art.753.title: Opinion piece: With EU membership, Iceland loses control over the country’s fishing grounds
art.753.summary: The author says accession agreements to the EU are overwhelmingly legal in nature, and that talk of a permanent exemption from the fisheries policy overlooks that the issue is about law, not politics.
art.754.title: Opinion piece: Fisheries and sovereignty in the European Union
art.754.summary: The author refers to the experience of the British, who did not realize the transfer of legislative and judicial powers until after joining. Under the current rules, Icelandic fishing companies would receive about 70% of the current catch and Iceland’s highest courts would become European; after accession, there would be no turning back.
art.755.title: Opinion piece: Icelanders, think twice
art.755.summary: The British author says a yes to talks may seem like a cautious step, but much is at stake; the EU has shown persistence in keeping states inside, as repeated referendums in Denmark and Ireland show, and invested heavily against Brexit in 2016.
art.756.title: Opinion piece: Now Iceland’s ballast as an independent nation-state is being tested
art.756.summary: The former minister recounts a quarter-century history of the EU debate and calls the 2009 membership application a major undemocratic mistake supported by the leadership of VG contrary to party resolutions. The referendum now, he says, has been driven by Viðreisn.
art.757.title: The euro and emigration
art.757.summary: The professor says having its own currency is an important economic policy tool for a narrowly based economy like Iceland; in a monetary union, adjustment to shocks is shifted onto the people themselves in the form of unemployment and emigration.
art.758.title: National referendum in August
art.758.summary: The MP says it is strange to insist that no good agreement can come out of negotiations; options are valuable, and it is natural to see the agreement and then assess whether membership brings more advantages than disadvantages. According to polls, just over half the nation is in favor of saying yes.
art.759.title: Submitted article: Laws could not be passed that conflict with EU rules
art.759.summary: The author points out that EU applicant countries are not permitted to pass laws that are incompatible with the Union’s rules while the application process is underway, since the process is primarily about adapting the applicant country to the rules.
art.760.title: At the beginning, one should consider the end
art.760.summary: The author says there is a risk that the advocates of membership who have gone furthest in claiming there will be special arrangements will want to show they have lived up to their bold promises, and that the leaders of the government could be tempted to do the same even if the outcome of the negotiation process were poor.
art.761.title: What would be the fate of Iceland’s fisheries within the European Union?
art.761.summary: The author says EU membership would pose enormous risks to the fisheries sector; the British experience of “exemptions” from the Common Fisheries Policy has been disastrous because other EU states have found ways around them.
art.762.title: The message from Rubio
art.762.summary: A former ambassador discusses the greetings sent by Marco Rubio on National Day, in which it was reiterated that the United States will continue to foster defense cooperation with Iceland on the 75th anniversary of the defense agreement, and says there is reason to give this full attention in the EU debate.
art.763.title: Submitted article: “You know perfectly well what is in the package”
art.763.summary: The author quotes Uffe Ellemann-Jensen as saying that the EU is not a sealed package — states know what they are getting into — and says there is no need to embark on an extensive, costly, and time-consuming application process to find out what is already known.
art.764.title: Caution is advised in the presence of cliffs
art.764.summary: The former chairman of the Central Bank’s supervisory board says having one’s own currency matters because the exchange rate can absorb part of the shock when setbacks occur; the floating exchange rate of the króna better safeguards the economy’s competitiveness. The article is a response to an article by Þröstur Ólafsson.
art.765.title: Submitted article: Is there reason to celebrate today?
art.765.summary: The chairman of Miðflokkurinn writes on National Day that prosperity carries the risk that people forget what was required to achieve success, and asks whether some Icelanders now have less confidence in the nation’s abilities than when a poor nation fought for independence.
art.766.title: Young people’s housing difficulties within the EU
art.766.summary: The author reviews a Eurofound report from December that paints a bleak picture of the housing crisis within the EU; many young people cannot afford to move out despite having jobs, and homelessness has increased in many of the Union’s member states.
art.767.title: Submitted article: A referendum on negotiations
art.767.summary: The author says Iceland has previously been in talks for months without getting any closer to a result; in reality, negotiations are conducted with individual member states that have veto power — with Spain over the fish — and the Central Bank would lose its risk buffers in foreign exchange matters.
art.768.title: Opinion piece: Correct premises, wrong conclusions
art.768.summary: A former ambassador says it appears that no formal position has been obtained from the U.S. authorities on whether Iceland’s special status in security and defence matters would remain unchanged upon EU membership; the 1951 defence agreement is bilateral, and changed circumstances for one party may have an impact.
art.769.title: Opinion piece: The EU’s economic decline
art.769.summary: The professor says the EU’s share of global output has shrunk substantially since around 1990 and that the Union’s economic performance has been weak compared with other countries of the world, according to World Bank statistics.
art.770.title: Opinion piece: The euro and the risk
art.770.summary: The professor says the euro is intended to ensure stability, low inflation and low interest rates, but inflation varies greatly among euro-area countries, and some of them have inflation almost as high as Iceland’s.
art.771.title: Opinion piece: Will the government have to resign after losing the EU referendum?
art.771.summary: The author discusses Eiríkur Bergmann’s criticism of Kristrún Frostadóttir and considers the political consequences for the government of losing the referendum.
art.772.title: Opinion piece: The issue is about the right to govern
art.772.summary: The author points out that the Treaty of Lisbon provides for full EU authority over the conservation of marine resources and that only the Union may legislate on them; discussion of ownership of natural resources changes nothing about the right to govern them.
art.773.title: Opinion piece: The króna is not flawless, but the euro is not a magic solution either
art.773.summary: The chair of Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn says debate about the króna regularly flares up when inflation is high and interest rates bite, since the currency affects people’s daily lives, but the euro is no magic solution.
art.774.title: Opinion piece: The euro is no windfall
art.774.summary: The professor says the report by the foreign experts on Iceland’s currency options does not conclude that adopting the euro would be beneficial for Iceland; its main message is that adopting the euro entails both advantages and disadvantages.
art.775.title: What does it mean that the application is “still in effect”?
art.775.summary: Erna asks what constitutional status is being described when it is said that the 2009 membership application is “still in effect”, and outlines Iceland’s formal accession process within the EU institutional system from 2009–2010.
art.776.title: Question for Kristrún Frostadóttir
art.776.summary: Guðni asks the Prime Minister to answer whether she has familiarised herself with the available data on the effects of EU membership on agriculture, including the report Sveitalíf 2025, which predicted a rapid decline in the number of dairy producers upon accession.
art.777.title: Well, that was strange
art.777.summary: The former ambassador uses the Humpty Dumpty rhyme as a metaphor for the republic and discusses its position in the run-up to the vote.
art.778.title: We would effectively have joined the EU
art.778.summary: The author says that if restarting the application process were approved, with the accompanying full alignment to EU rules and administration alongside the negotiations, Icelanders would in effect have materially joined the Union before any agreement was in place.
art.779.title: Sovereignty clearly no obstacle
art.779.summary: The author responds to an article by economist Pétur J. Eiríksson and criticises the fact that sovereignty apparently poses no obstacle in the eyes of those who call joining the EU "participation in cooperation among democratic nations".
detail.varnarsamningur.0: The NO side argues that Iceland’s security is already ensured by the 1951 bilateral defence agreement with the United States and its membership of NATO; EU membership would add nothing in that regard, as the Union has no independent military capability to defend Iceland.
detail.varnarsamningur.1: Gunnar Pálsson, former ambassador, has written that participation in the EU’s security and defence policy could complicate or even put the defence relationship with the United States at risk, and international relations scholar Albert Jónsson points out that the United States will continue to defend Iceland because of its own interests, regardless of EU membership.
art.780.title: ▶ Voices from the founding meeting: why yes
art.780.summary: Interviewees at SJÁ’s founding meeting want to see an agreement, let the nation decide its future, and believe the EU offers opportunities for young people.
art.781.title: ▶ Let’s say yes and see what comes of it
art.781.summary: Interviewees say there is no way to determine what membership would look like unless the talks are completed; that it would be crazy to close the window that is now open.
art.782.title: ▶ Don’t say no to an unwritten agreement
art.782.summary: Young people at SJÁ’s founding meeting say the EU is a major opportunity and want to make an informed decision once an agreement is on the table instead of rejecting it unseen.
art.783.title: ▶ I want to see what’s on offer
art.783.summary: Interviewees say they intend to vote yes in order to see what is on offer and make an informed decision on that basis.
art.784.title: ▶ Want to see an agreement and a stronger currency
art.784.summary: Interviewees want an agreement on the table before a position is taken, and one wants a stronger currency that does not collapse in place of the króna.
art.785.title: ▶ An informed decision for future generations
art.785.summary: Interviewees say it is irresponsible to throw opportunities away; with a yes vote, people get to see what is on offer for future generations.
art.786.title: ▶ Curiosity is the foundation of progress
art.786.summary: Interviewees say curiosity is a virtue, want to see the final agreement and opportunities for young people — and cheer for lower interest rates.
art.787.title: ▶ The exchange-rate spread eats your money
art.787.summary: It is shown how a 1,000-króna note shrinks by 500 krónur simply by exchanging krónur into euros and back again because of the exchange-rate spread.
art.788.title: ▶ Does Sigmundur Davíð know better than the Danes?
art.788.summary: Polls are cited in which 75–91% of Danes, Irish people and Swedes say they are better off within the EU, and it is asked whether Sigmundur Davíð knows better than the residents themselves.
art.789.title: ▶ Customs clearance is a hassle for everyone
art.789.summary: A story is told about a freight carrier who does not want a customs union because customs clearance is a source of income; the narrator does not think that is a good reason to maintain inconvenience for others.
art.790.title: ▶ Will Iceland stop being Iceland?
art.790.summary: It is pointed out that Finland, Italy and Denmark retain their culture within the EU, and Iceland could therefore continue to be proud of its own.
art.791.title: ▶ A vote on talks, not membership
art.791.summary: It is explained that the vote is about starting negotiations; if an agreement is reached, there will be another vote on the agreement itself.
art.792.title: ▶ What do Putin and Halla have in common?
art.792.summary: A map of Europe is reviewed and it is pointed out that only Belarus, Russia and Iceland remain outside EU ties; Iceland belongs alongside Europe’s democracies.
art.793.title: ▶ Living with your parents until 30?
art.793.summary: Young people cannot get into the housing market, and the question is raised whether lower interest rates are possible; that is why the narrator wants to see the agreement.
art.794.title: ▶ Would you say no to Kylie Jenner?
