art.794.summary: A dating analogy: on 29 August, Iceland is not marrying the EU, only getting to know it and seeing what might come of it.
art.795.title: ▶ Wouldn’t you open the lucky sweater?
art.795.summary: An analogy about a lucky sweater: no one throws away a package unopened, so it should be opened and examined to see what is inside.
art.796.title: ▶ 100–150 thousand krónur more per month
art.796.summary: It is claimed that Icelandic households pay 100–150 thousand krónur more per month on their mortgage than a comparable European family, and that is why the narrator wants to see the agreement.
art.797.title: ▶ Is Iceland losing its sovereignty?
art.797.summary: What is described as a misunderstanding is corrected: on 29 August, the only decision is whether to talk to the EU, and no sovereignty would be lost by doing so.
art.798.title: ▶ 370 thousand people without a seat at the table
art.798.summary: At a time of Russia’s invasion and the United States’ withdrawal, Europe stands together, but a small nation like Iceland does not even have a seat at the table.
art.799.title: ▶ The young people’s vote on Iceland’s future
art.799.summary: Young people are encouraged to go to the polls; the only way to get the information is to vote yes, get the agreement and assess its pros and cons.
art.800.title: ▶ Króna or euro?
art.800.summary: It is pointed out that those who use the euro pay lower interest rates and that the information needed to make a decision can only be obtained through a fully completed agreement.
art.801.title: ▶ What is the cost of changing nothing?
art.801.summary: The cost of completing the talks is weighed against paying mortgage loans at the highest interest rates in Europe for life.
art.802.title: ▶ Learn from Brexit — young people, show up
art.802.summary: It is recalled that young people in Britain opposed Brexit but did not turn out to vote; young people should decide their own future and vote on 29 August.
art.803.title: ▶ Everything on the table for an informed decision
art.803.summary: Passers-by say they want everything put on the table and to make an informed decision on membership once an agreement is in place.
art.804.title: ▶ Dating costs money, but knowledge is power
art.804.summary: The talks are compared to dating: the cost is not money wasted because the information strengthens Iceland’s position, and it is better to understand than to argue.
art.805.title: ▶ You try on the sweater before you buy it
art.805.summary: The vote on 29 August is about getting an agreement on the table, reading it, and making an informed decision.
art.806.title: ▶ How can you afford to live here?
art.806.summary: Passers-by describe the high cost of living, seven-thousand-króna hamburgers, and say there is nothing to lose by looking at what membership would entail.
art.807.title: ▶ Advance voting has begun
art.807.summary: It is pointed out that it is possible to vote in advance as early as today, and people are encouraged to vote yes in order to see an agreement.
art.808.title: ▶ No major decision without information
art.808.summary: The speaker says they would never make an important decision about work, studies, or housing without information, and that on 29 August people are voting on whether to get an agreement on the table.
art.809.title: ▶ Bubbi: children deserve a bright future
art.809.summary: Bubbi Morthens says he intends to vote yes for his children, who deserve a beautiful future.
art.810.title: ▶ Akureyri: yes to seeing the agreement
art.810.summary: Interviewees at a SJÁ event in Akureyri want to see the agreement instead of saying no to something that no one knows what is.
art.811.title: ▶ Stability, opportunities and the facts on the table
art.811.summary: Interviewees in Akureyri want to know whether membership would increase stability in the banking system, get the facts on the table, and seize the opportunities in the solidarity of European nations.
art.812.title: ▶ Let’s lay the ghost to rest once and for all
art.812.summary: Villi vandræðaskáld says the EU ghost will never be laid to rest unless the nation gets to know what is on offer and then takes a position.
art.813.title: ▶ Iceland’s A-team in the negotiating committee
art.813.summary: There is trust that the government will appoint the best possible negotiators, including foreign ones if necessary, if the matter goes further.
art.814.title: ▶ May I invite you in to take a look?
art.814.summary: Shop metaphor: major decisions are difficult, but even more difficult if one refuses to look at what is on offer.
art.815.title: ▶ Decisions the children will live with the longest
art.815.summary: A child does not want to open a package, and it is pointed out that adults are now making decisions that shape the future of those who are younger and will have to live with them the longest.
art.816.title: ▶ The world’s smallest currency carries a risk premium
art.816.summary: It is explained that interest rates and prices are higher in Iceland because banks add a risk premium to the world’s smallest independent currency — a premium no one voted for.
art.817.title: ▶ Would you pay for the same milk three times?
art.817.summary: Indexation is described as a uniquely Icelandic arrangement in which inflation is added to the principal; in euro countries inflation is lower and indexation is almost unknown.
art.818.title: ▶ Norwegians got an agreement and said no
art.818.summary: It is pointed out that Norwegians twice rejected an accession agreement in a referendum without consequences; a yes on 29 August would not mean membership, but rather that the nation votes again on the agreement itself.
art.819.title: ▶ Hard to choose without taking a look
art.819.summary: Restaurant metaphor: there is no need to decide anything right away, only to look at the options on offer.
art.820.title: ▶ Frugal and looking forward to lower interest rates
art.820.summary: A couple describes how they can afford to live in Iceland and looks forward to paying lower interest rates.
art.821.title: ▶ Cheaper to live in the Netherlands than in Iceland
art.821.summary: A man living in the Netherlands says that no one there takes out car loans and that higher income is needed in Iceland to maintain the same standard of living.
art.822.title: ▶ Believe in the dialogue even if the goals are unclear
art.822.summary: The interviewee says he will vote yes because he believes in the dialogue; it would be absurd to walk away from the table and not have the option, even though the negotiating goals could be clearer.
art.823.title: ▶ But what about our fish?
art.823.summary: Refers to remarks by the EU fisheries director in the Financial Times about room for special arrangements for Iceland and the precedent of Malta with a 25-mile zone.
art.824.title: ▶ Finnish farmers receive basic support from the EU
art.824.summary: Corrects the claim that the Finns pay their farmers themselves: basic support of 875 million euros comes from the EU, and support for Icelandic farmers could also come from Europe.
art.825.title: ▶ Information can only be obtained with a yes vote
art.825.summary: Passers-by say they will vote yes because no decision can be made without the information that can only be obtained by completing the negotiations.
art.826.title: ▶ Control over the resource would be guaranteed
art.826.summary: Replays older remarks stating that the application made clear that Iceland would not join the union unless control over the resource was clearly guaranteed.
art.827.title: ▶ Why not try and see?
art.827.summary: A fishing metaphor: whoever does not dare cast will never catch fish; try, look, ask questions, and then decide.
art.828.title: ▶ Voted yes at Kringlan
art.828.summary: An amusing story about a man who voted early at Kringlan because he wants to see and inspect the agreement.
art.829.title: ▶ Whose interests does the króna serve?
art.829.summary: Professor Guðrún Johnsen points out that the króna’s high-interest-rate environment is extremely convenient for capital owners, who can earn high returns risk-free in deposit accounts.
art.830.title: ▶ An independent nation sits at the table
art.830.summary: National Day message: an independent nation should sit at the table where decisions about it are made.
art.831.title: ▶ Iceland’s negotiating objectives read aloud
art.831.summary: Detailed negotiating objectives were read aloud on control over energy and fishing resources, protection of agriculture, regional funding, and remaining a country without a military.
art.832.title: ▶ Kristrún: let’s see the agreement and the opportunities
art.832.summary: Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir says she intends to vote yes; the decision belongs to the nation, and those who want increased competition, exchange-rate stability and lower tariffs should want to see the agreement.
art.833.title: ▶ Guðni: sovereignty evolves and changes
art.833.summary: Former President Guðni Th. Jóhannesson says Iceland is a free and sovereign state, not despite international cooperation but because of it.
art.834.title: ▶ Is your opinion based on having examined the issue?
art.834.summary: Guðni Th. says that before forming an opinion, one should examine the matter itself; it is far too common for people to form opinions without informing themselves about the issues.
art.835.title: ▶ The EU protects working people better
art.835.summary: Steinar Harðarson says that almost all progress in occupational health and safety has come through EU directives dealing with the safety and health of working people.
art.836.title: ▶ Opponents can also say yes
art.836.summary: It is pointed out that even opponents of membership can vote yes, because the vote is about accession talks, not final membership.
art.837.title: ▶ Yes opens opportunities, no closes them
art.837.summary: Passers-by mention a bright future for young people, the ability to afford housing, stability, and that there is nothing to lose by holding accession talks.
art.838.title: ▶ There is no European army
art.838.summary: Claims by the NO side that membership would force Iceland into a European army are described as falsehoods; there is no European army, and defence matters remain under the authority of each member state.
art.839.title: ▶ NATO does not protect subsea cables and energy security
art.839.summary: The defence agreement and NATO are sufficient in the event of an invasion, but today security also concerns energy, cyber and infrastructure security, where full EU membership would increase Iceland’s security.
art.840.title: ▶ Conservatism or liberalism, 29 August
art.840.summary: The debate is framed as a classic clash between conservatism and liberalism: liberal forces see opportunities in increased competition, the euro, and security ties with Europe.
art.841.title: ▶ We share values with Europe
art.841.summary: Sólveig Arnarsdóttir says she realized in Berlin how important it is to strengthen ties with Europe because Icelanders share values with the continent.
art.842.title: ▶ Accession talks or Eurovision — which is more expensive?
art.842.summary: The cost of accession talks, 1.9 billion, is put in context with pizzas, Eurovision, and other expenses; a good agreement would last forever.
art.843.title: ▶ Snærós: lies and half-truths from the NO side
art.843.summary: Snærós Sindradóttir says the NO side is lying about the vote being on membership, about Iceland’s cost burden and lack of influence, and never looks at the nation’s overall benefits.
art.844.title: ▶ An interest rate hike costs you 108 thousand a year
art.844.summary: An interest rate increase to eight percent is said to cost a household with a 50 million loan an extra 9,000 krónur per month; with the euro, the economy would be more stable and predictable.
art.845.title: ▶ What, then, was the struggle for?
art.845.summary: An excerpt from the opening meeting of Áfram Ísland, asking on behalf of vanished generations what the struggle for independence was for if sovereignty is to be handed over.
art.846.title: ▶ Europe’s richest nations outside the EU
art.846.summary: It is argued that Iceland rose from poverty to the front ranks outside the EU, and that three of Europe’s five richest nations — Norway, Switzerland, and Iceland — are outside the Union and without the euro.
art.847.title: ▶ Young people: Interests better served outside the EU
art.847.summary: A young interviewee says the EEA Agreement provides access to the internal market with the main benefits of membership without the drawbacks, and that the vote is about the future of young people.
art.848.title: ▶ Guðni Ágústsson: Let us defend freedom
art.848.summary: Guðni Ágústsson says people are being misled by talk of taking a look inside the package; Iceland is far better off as an independent nation, and the EEA Agreement is the best part of European cooperation.
art.849.title: ▶ We decide our own affairs
art.849.summary: The interviewee does not want to transfer part of sovereignty to Brussels, says living standards are better in Iceland than in Europe, and that the króna is not the cause of high inflation and interest rates.
art.850.title: ▶ The focus should be here at home
art.850.summary: It is argued that voters are being asked to grant a mandate for a costly and time-consuming process lasting many years, one that would divert energy and resources away from living standards and economic issues at home.
art.851.title: ▶ The regulatory burden would grow even heavier
art.851.summary: A young voter says burdensome regulation comes from the EU via the EEA and that it would increase even further with membership; the same cause must be fought for as the generations that secured independence.
art.852.title: ▶ Young people against the EU: Read up
art.852.summary: The chair of Ungir gegn ESB says the vote is about whether to hand over decision-making power that previous generations fought for, and urges young people to familiarize themselves with the process itself on the EU’s website.
art.853.title: ▶ Former ESA employee says no
art.853.summary: An interviewee who worked for ESA in Brussels says judicial and legislative power should remain with Icelanders and sees the referendum as the first step toward joining the Union.
art.854.title: ▶ Not a left-right issue
art.854.summary: An interviewee says accession talks and membership are not separate matters; joining would mean transferring legislative power, losing an independent monetary policy, and losing undivided control over resources.
art.855.title: ▶ Icelanders should govern Iceland
art.855.summary: A young woman says the vote is about protecting sovereignty, the króna, and the currency; 27 nations have gone through the accession process and none received a special agreement.
art.856.title: ▶ A yes means an application for membership
art.856.summary: An interviewee says power should be as close to the people as possible; a yes vote would set an application process in motion that must ultimately entail membership, and he does not believe in exemptions.
art.857.title: ▶ 0,1% voting weight in the Council
art.857.summary: An attendee cites a speech by Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson: the sovereignty won through the independence struggle would be transferred to 70.000 officials and lobbyists in Brussels, and Iceland would receive only 0,1% voting weight in the Council.
art.858.title: ▶ Villi: All of this can be done here at home
art.858.summary: Villi says indexation, usurious interest rates, and the financial system are man-made and that Icelandic politicians can fix them themselves without transferring sovereignty to Brussels.
art.859.title: ▶ Decisions made in Iceland
art.859.summary: Valdís says the fundamental question is where decisions about Iceland’s future should be made — by people who know Icelandic conditions and are accountable to the nation.
art.860.title: ▶ Chat Control: The EU monitors messages
art.860.summary: It is claimed that new EU legislation (Chat Control) authorizes the scanning of private messages without a court order and that the majority vote in the European Parliament was ignored in its handling.
art.861.title: ▶ Villi: Courage to make our own decisions
art.861.summary: Villi says indexation, usurious interest rates and the financial system are man-made and can be fixed at home; politicians should not leave the nation facing a surrender of sovereignty to Brussels.
art.862.title: ▶ Let us learn from the 2009 application
art.862.summary: The interviewee says the 2009 application was made with a weak democratic mandate and swallowed up the energy of the administrative system until the government fell; he fears the same process will repeat itself step by step.
art.863.title: ▶ Kerecis became big because Iceland is small
art.863.summary: Guðmundur Fertram says Kerecis would not have become a bigger or better company within the EU; it became international precisely because of Iceland’s small size.
art.864.title: ▶ Farmer: Agriculture is better off outside the EU
art.864.summary: Oddný Steina, a farmer and consultant, says agriculture and food production in Iceland are better off outside the EU and wants Icelanders to continue producing their own food.
art.865.title: ▶ Iceland’s small size is a competitive advantage
art.865.summary: Guðmundur Fertram says it has never proved a disadvantage to be Icelandic; small size is a competitive advantage that should not be surrendered to the European Union.
art.866.title: ▶ Entrepreneur: Opportunity in smallness
art.866.summary: A company founder says Icelanders’ interests are better served outside the union from a business and operational perspective; the country’s small size creates closeness and opportunities for innovation.
art.867.title: ▶ Switzerland bows to no one
art.867.summary: It is claimed that nations do best when they do not seek shelter with the big powers; Switzerland preserves its independence and goes its own way outside alliances.
art.868.title: ▶ Farmer: Let us protect agriculture
art.868.summary: Margrét Hrund, a farmer, says she intends to vote no in order to protect Icelandic agriculture and calls for unity behind it.
art.869.title: ▶ Iceland’s future in the hands of Icelanders
art.869.summary: Anton Berg says earlier generations fought for Iceland’s right to stand on its own feet; the current generation should preserve that freedom rather than hand it over to others.
art.870.title: ▶ Europe’s debt problem falls on young people
art.870.summary: Anton Berg says France has run deficits since 1974 and Italy and Spain almost continuously for half a century; with joint EU bonds, the accumulated debt problem of the major states would fall on future generations of Icelanders.
art.871.title: ▶ Iceland’s seat at the table: 0.1%
art.871.summary: It is pointed out that voting weight in the EU Council follows population size and that Iceland would have about 0.1% weight in the vast majority of decisions.
art.872.title: ▶ A footstool, not a seat at the table
art.872.summary: It is argued that 6 members of parliament out of 720 and about 0.1% weight in the Council provide Iceland with no real influence; it would be more accurate to speak of a footstool than a seat at the table.
art.873.title: ▶ The President’s referral power would be narrowed
art.873.summary: It is explained that EU regulations would apply directly in Iceland and would not go to the President for confirmation; the President’s referral power and the people’s final say would therefore extend to fewer decisions than today.
art.874.title: ▶ EEA: We get the most, give the least
art.874.summary: It is argued that Iceland is not alone at all: the EEA Agreement provides access to the internal market without sacrificing free trade agreements, resources and self-government, whereas accession would mean 0.1% weight and that regulations from Brussels would automatically take effect.
art.875.title: ▶ 800 billion euros in military build-up
art.875.summary: It is pointed out that the EU’s Readiness 2030 plan amounts to 800 billion euros in defence spending; with membership, Iceland would have to take part in the Union’s common budget and pay for weapons purchases.
art.876.title: ▶ Three reasons to say no
art.876.summary: Three reasons are given: Iceland has never done better than as a sovereign nation, power should be close to citizens rather than with a union of 450 million, and Icelandic agriculture would not withstand the competition, with the associated risk to food security.
art.877.title: ▶ EU regulation drives entrepreneurs away
art.877.summary: It is argued that European companies begin their journey in the United States or Asia because Europe’s burdensome regulatory framework holds back creativity and the freedom of entrepreneurs.
art.878.title: ▶ On our own terms
art.878.summary: Brief statement: the interviewee wants Icelanders to continue shaping society on their own terms, based on Icelandic conditions and interests.
art.879.title: ▶ A land of resources and unspoiled nature
art.879.summary: The interviewee says Iceland is a land of resources and unspoiled nature, with agriculture at the forefront; the opportunities should be used on our own terms and the benefits from them enjoyed.
art.880.title: ▶ Iceland through the eyes of young people in the EU
art.880.summary: It is pointed out that unemployment is low, GDP per capita is among the highest in the world, and that more young people own housing in Iceland than in most of Europe; this success is explained by the fact that Icelanders themselves have made the decisions that suit Iceland.
art.881.title: ▶ Stefán Pálsson: Change from within
art.881.summary: Stefán Pálsson says it is good neither for individuals nor for nations to expect change to come from outside; Icelanders can engage with the wider world on their own terms and change what they themselves choose.
art.882.title: ▶ Helga Kristín: An independent country going forward
art.882.summary: Helga Kristín wants to continue living in an independent country where Icelanders make decisions about domestic affairs and natural resources, for themselves and for future generations.
art.883.title: ▶ A nation without an army, not militarisation
art.883.summary: Sunna Björg says Iceland is a proud nation without an army and should work for peace on the international stage rather than take part in increased militarisation.
art.884.title: ▶ Young people pay Europe's debts
art.884.summary: It is argued that Europe is ageing and debts are growing; pensions are mostly paid by current taxpayers, unlike the Icelandic funded pension system, and pressure for joint EU spending will fall on future generations.
art.885.title: ▶ What is likely in negotiations?
art.885.summary: It is argued that poorer member states are unlikely to accept that one of Europe’s richest nations would take more from EU funds than it pays in, and that 27 nations with 450 million inhabitants would grant a nation of 400,000 people permanent exemptions from their rules.
art.886.title: ▶ What future is being offered?
art.886.summary: It is pointed out that the purchasing power of young people in Iceland is 35% higher than that of their peers in the EU, unemployment is lower, and home purchases happen earlier in life; young people’s future is said to be better protected under their own control than under officials in Brussels.
art.887.title: ▶ Do you know what EU membership costs?
art.887.summary: Passers-by are asked what EU membership costs per year; few know the answer, which is said to be around 50 billion krónur a year.
art.888.title: ▶ Birkir: The future in our hands
art.888.summary: Birkir says the future of young people is better safeguarded in the hands of Icelanders than within the European Union.
art.889.title: ▶ Dóra: Control of natural resources here in Iceland
art.889.summary: Dóra Tómasar says it is good for young people that control of natural resources remains here in Iceland.
art.890.title: ▶ Árni Daníel: Democratic tradition strengthened
art.890.summary: Árni Daníel says he was raised in a democratic tradition with deep roots in Icelandic history and culture, and wants that tradition to be reinforced and strengthened.
art.891.title: ▶ Birgitta: An independent country for the children
art.891.summary: Birgitta says our parents handed down to us an independent country; it is our responsibility to do the same for our children.
art.892.title: ▶ The organisational chart grows with accession
art.892.summary: Nations’ decision-making power is compared to an organisational chart that grew with accession to the EU: politicians could hide behind rules from Brussels, and the public lost the ability to hold decision-makers accountable in their own local communities.
art.893.title: ▶ Ágústa: Let’s not give away our resources
art.893.summary: Ágústa says natural resources are an important foundation of prosperity and innovation in Iceland and must not be given away.
art.894.title: ▶ Berglind: Let’s solve the problems ourselves
art.894.summary: Berglind says she believes in Iceland and that Icelanders can solve their own problems themselves, as they have always done throughout history.
art.895.title: ▶ Where do the 50 billion come from?
art.895.summary: It is explained that member states pay around 1% of national income to the EU, which would amount to about ISK 50 billion a year for Iceland — equivalent to the operating costs of all the country’s upper secondary schools; only part of it would come back, and then with conditions attached.
art.896.title: ▶ Bjarnheiður: What are we seeking?
art.896.summary: Bjarnheiður Hallsdóttir says Iceland ranks among the leading European nations on measures of prosperity, wellbeing, equality and human rights; the path to membership would be burdensome, costly and time-consuming, and the EU would not solve the temporary problems of the Icelandic economy.
art.897.title: ▶ Bjarnheiður: EEA benefits without EU domination
art.897.summary: Bjarnheiður says the EEA Agreement brings Iceland enormous benefits; joining the EU could shut off other trade agreements, and the country would come under the domination of the Union instead of controlling its own resources.
art.898.title: ▶ ISK 50 billion a year — no one guessed right
art.898.summary: Passers-by guess the annual cost of EU membership; no one lands on the figure, said to be ISK 50 billion a year, and the question is asked whether the money would not be better used to strengthen the country from within.
art.899.title: ▶ Young people: Better circumstances in Iceland
art.899.summary: Young interviewees say the position of young people in Iceland is much better than in Europe and that the future is better secured in their own hands; Iceland has done well over the past 80 years.
art.900.title: ▶ Arna: No uncertain journey to Brussels
art.900.summary: Arna Páls does not want a years-long uncertain journey to Brussels; the government should focus on the tasks it was elected to carry out — lowering interest rates, bringing down inflation, and strengthening the education system.
art.901.title: ▶ Daníel: Smallness is a strength
art.901.summary: Daníel says the small size of Icelandic society is its greatest strength: everyone is close to those in power, there is less bureaucracy, and lines of communication are shorter.
art.902.title: ▶ Hilmar Veigar: The decline of the EU in numbers
art.902.summary: Hilmar Veigar Pétursson argues that the EU fell from being the world’s largest economy in 2014 to behind the United States and China; productivity per hour worked grew by 7% over a decade compared with 18% in the United States and 12% in Iceland, and the EU’s share of the world’s 100 largest companies fell from 20% to 8%.
art.903.title: ▶ Georg: Regulatory burden hampers innovation
art.903.summary: Georg, who describes himself as an internationalist, believes the EU is on the wrong path because of increasing regulation that weighs on innovation; he says the focus should now be on bringing down inflation and interest rates and using artificial intelligence to create value at home.
art.904.title: ▶ Guðmundur: Let’s take no risks
art.904.summary: Guðmundur says Icelanders have done extraordinarily well as an independent nation, both in prosperity and rights, and does not want to take any risks by pushing for EU membership.
art.905.title: ▶ The EU decides who may fish
art.905.summary: It is claimed that the EU decides who may catch fish from the sea and can at any time change the rules on the allocation of fishing quotas; Western European nations have centuries of fishing experience in Icelandic waters and could therefore seek catch quotas off Iceland.
motrok.tollfrelsi.0.title: The fish could leave the country unprocessed — the examples already exist
motrok.tollfrelsi.0.text: Sigurjón Þórðarson, MP for Flokkur fólksins, turns the full-processing argument on its head: “Under the current rules and with accession to the European Union, foreign food chains such as Unilever could very easily buy up the largest seafood companies and move the fish abroad unprocessed for processing there.” He says these are no ghost stories — Vinnslustöðin has closed its saltfish processing in the Westman Islands while expanding saltfish processing at its company in Portugal, and accession would open the way for the sale of fishing companies and fishing quotas to foreign parties.
motrok.tollfrelsi.1.title: The EEA provides the access — the price of tariff-free trade is control
motrok.tollfrelsi.1.text: Þórir Garðarsson points out that Iceland already has “broad access to Europe’s internal market” through the EEA, but that “the European Union’s common fisheries policy is, however, specifically excluded from the EEA Agreement” — Iceland therefore retains control over fisheries management itself and imposes limits on foreign ownership. With membership, that would change: in earlier talks, the European Commission considered Icelandic restrictions on foreign investment in fisheries incompatible with the regulatory framework, and a larger pool of buyers could raise quota prices and tempt family-run fishing companies to sell their rights abroad.
motrok.tollfrelsi.2.title: “Isn’t that enough?” — unrealistic to give up control for tariffs
motrok.tollfrelsi.2.text: Sigurður P. Sigmundsson responds by asking: “Iceland has a good EEA agreement that provides access to the EU internal market and the so-called four freedoms. Isn’t that enough?” Why should Iceland enter talks about reducing its authority over fisheries and agriculture — authority that would be transferred “to a large extent” — when it is “unrealistic wishful thinking” that Iceland would obtain special arrangements and permanent exemptions of any real significance, and all the main interest groups in those sectors have opposed negotiations.
motrok.varnarsamningur.0.title: Gauti B. Eggertsson: The 1951 agreement is worthless without NATO
motrok.varnarsamningur.0.text: Gauti B. Eggertsson, professor of economics at Brown University, says the 1951 defence agreement has no value if NATO falls apart — and the environment for free trade has already collapsed with Trump’s tariff war. Instead of relying on pillars that may fail, Iceland best protects its sovereignty among a group of states that respect the sovereignty of others, and there are major interests at stake in joining the EU customs union.
motrok.varnarsamningur.1.title: Davíð Þór: The defence agreement stands and falls with NATO
motrok.varnarsamningur.1.text: Davíð Þór Björgvinsson, former judge at the European Court of Human Rights, points out that the 1951 defence agreement entails that the United States defends Iceland on NATO’s behalf; if NATO were to come to an end, all the legal foundations of the agreement would collapse — “if NATO goes down the drain, the defence agreement with the United States is broken”. The United States’ unpredictable conduct means that the pillars of Icelandic security must be reassessed rather than taken for granted.
motrok.varnarsamningur.2.title: EU membership does not complicate anything — 23 of 27 EU states are in NATO
motrok.varnarsamningur.2.text: Davíð Þór Björgvinsson rejects the claim that EU membership would put defence ties with the United States at risk: 23 of the EU’s 27 member states are in NATO, the EU treaty explicitly provides that the Union’s policy shall respect member states’ commitments to NATO, and the United States itself has bilateral defence agreements with individual EU states such as Spain, Greece and Poland — EU membership and bilateral defence cooperation with the United States therefore go hand in hand in practice.
art.906.title: A person alone is but half a person – with others, they are more than themselves
art.906.summary: Traces the history of Iceland as a nation that from the outset chose to connect with European culture and society while also preserving its own identity. Points out that the sea is no longer a defence against modern threats and asks whether it is not wiser to stand not alone but within a community that places peace and security at the forefront.
art.907.title: When Path Dependence Becomes an Argument for Saying No
art.907.summary: Responds to an article by Smári McCarthy and defends the arguments of Carl Baudenbacher. Says the EEA is based on a two-pillar system in which legislative power is not transferred to supranational institutions and that the adoption of acts requires the consent of the EFTA states. EU membership, by contrast, would bind Iceland to decisions made by qualified majority in far more areas, including fisheries, agriculture, and trade policy.
art.908.title: National sovereignty and individual freedom
art.908.summary: Says individual freedom is curtailed by usurious interest rates and inflation associated with the króna; young people cannot afford to leave home and companies cancel investments. Sovereignty is described as a tool that Iceland has used through participation in NATO, the EEA, and Schengen, and the same thinking should apply to the currency.
art.909.title: “The will to join the European Union”
art.909.summary: Quotes Professors Maximilian Conrad and Magnús Árni Skjöld Magnússon, as well as a former EU enlargement commissioner, saying that the accession process is driven by the will to join. There is no such thing as just taking a look inside the package; the EU’s negotiating framework for Iceland states that the shared objective of the talks is accession.
art.910.title: To understand, or not understand, the debate
art.910.summary: Says it is understandable that the owners of large companies and the media they own argue for NO because the króna protects them from foreign competition operating in a stable currency. Questions the political judgment of Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson, who opposed EFTA, NATO, and the EEA, all of which later proved beneficial for the nation.
art.911.title: NO! An assault on democracy and the stripping away of voting rights
art.911.summary: Calls referendums the crown jewel of democracy and says organisations, interest groups, and a former president are trying to sabotage the vote with deception and fake news claiming it is about membership. Reminds readers that the same forces fought against the EEA Agreement, which most people believe was decisive for living standards.
art.912.title: What do the other 20,000 companies say?
art.912.summary: Says SA’s survey was presented misleadingly because only 388 companies out of about 2,000 responded negatively, less than 20% of members. Small and medium-sized companies face enormous financing costs and the volatility of a micro-currency, and the króna is said to be one of the biggest obstacles in the day-to-day operations of retail and service companies.
art.913.title: Is Marta Kos misleading people too?.. but misleading people is not allowed
art.913.summary: Questions the credibility of Marta Kos, the EU’s enlargement commissioner, by referring to writings about her alleged cooperation with the Slovenian intelligence service. Says she speaks with two voices: to Icelanders she says no adaptation takes place in the talks, but in an interview with NRK she said the process largely concerns adapting the applicant country’s legislation.
art.914.title: Sovereignty, supranational institutions, and the basis of equality in Europe
art.914.summary: A professor of political science at HÍ says the NO side’s sovereignty arguments are largely symbolic and exaggerated. A substantial transfer of decision-making power has already taken place through the EEA Agreement, under which Iceland implements a large share of EU rules without participating in the decisions.
art.915.title: Where does a nation of 400,000 people have the greatest influence?
art.915.summary: He says that independence and influence are not the same thing, and explains how NATO membership strengthened Iceland’s position in the Cod Wars. A small nation has the most influence when it has a seat at the table, and he cites Guðni Th. Jóhannesson as saying that sovereignty is not carved in stone.
art.916.title: The Moral High Ground
art.916.summary: He points out that the fishing industry, heavy industry, data centres, energy companies, airlines and tech companies all settle accounts in foreign currency because the króna does not suit them. The króna is thus intended only for the general public and those companies that cannot escape it, with the associated Iceland premium and high interest rates.
art.917.title: Save Billions
art.917.summary: A city councillor for Miðflokkurinn says there is no majority for joining the EU, neither in Alþingi, in the business community nor among the public, and that permanent exemptions in key policy areas are unrealistic. A YES would cost billions, or tens of billions, in talks that would inevitably run aground.
art.918.title: Why accession talks?
art.918.summary: He says the vote is about completing the talks and obtaining the treaty terms for the nation to approve or reject, not about membership. Most counterarguments, such as concerns about fisheries and agriculture, are in fact demands to be addressed in the treaty, and the only way to get answers is to finish the talks. Iceland already adopts a large share of EU rules without voting rights.
art.919.title: What was adapted?
art.919.summary: A satirical piece about the “Spectre of Alignment”, which he says is a ghost story told by opponents of accession talks since 2009. He cites Vísindavefurinn as saying it is undisputed that there was no need for alignment and that it had been agreed that no legislative or institutional changes would be made until after the referendum had been concluded.
art.920.title: Referendum: The Status Quo is Path Dependent
art.920.summary: He responds to Carl Baudenbacher and says that the status quo is also a path: the EEA entails the continuous adoption of EU legislation without a seat at the table and an ever-deepening lock-in year by year. A NO is a bet that the world of 1994 will endure, and delay means Iceland will later face the same choice with less bargaining power.
art.921.title: Promises That Do Not Hold Up
art.921.summary: He rejects claims that prices of goods would fall by 25% upon accession and points out that wages make up about half of costs in the restaurant sector. The only real reduction would be in imported agricultural products from the EU, which would put domestic agriculture under tough competition, while other goods could rise in price because of the EU’s tariff barriers against the rest of the world.
art.922.title: When the Counterarguments Become Endorsements
art.922.summary: He reads SFS’s statement of reasons against membership as an argument for it: Iceland has a strong negotiating position to secure special arrangements in fisheries. Membership would mean complete tariff-free access for products regardless of processing stage, access to EU investment funds and to regional development funds that could support fishing communities.
art.923.title: Spliff, Donk & Gengja in Alþingi
art.923.summary: He says the government has broken its promise that the EU process would not begin until the end of the electoral term. EU exemptions will be few, small and temporary, and no human power can absolutely guarantee that they will be permanent.
art.924.title: Icelandic Milk Production Is Not Bargaining Currency in Brussels
art.924.summary: The chair of Nautgripabændur BÍ asks what would happen to agricultural agreements, milk quotas and tariff protection upon accession; the EU abolished its milk quota system in 2015. Uncertainty alone reduces investment and new recruitment in agriculture, and imported food is not Icelandic food security.
art.925.title: Referendum: What Is Path Dependence?
art.925.summary: The former President of the EFTA Court says that although the vote is only on resuming negotiations, a YES result would create an institutional process with its own internal logic, in which later decisions would appear as follow-on decisions. The EU’s powerful promotional machinery would frame the question as whether Iceland is finally ready to take its natural place in Europe.
art.926.title: What European Union Are We Voting On?
art.926.summary: A lawyer points out that the EU itself now considers its current structure inadequate, citing the Draghi report and the European Parliament resolution from November 2025 on more efficient decision-making. It is unclear what kind of European Union Iceland would be joining: how many states it would include, which decisions would be taken by expanded majority voting, and which responsibilities would have shifted from the member states to the Union.
art.927.title: Does Anyone Believe in Top Lists?
art.927.summary: Responding to Hilmar Veigar Pétursson’s criticism of the EU’s competitiveness, the author says that rankings by companies’ market value say little about what those companies deliver to society. The Nordic countries are among the most competitive regions in the world, with strong welfare systems, the lowest income inequality, and a robust innovation environment, unlike the United States, where there is no statutory paid leave nationwide.
art.928.title: “Do You Want to Come Out and Play?”
art.928.summary: The writer says the debate is a repetition of the doomsday predictions made in 1993 about the EEA Agreement, none of which came true; today everyone agrees on the progress it brought. Most of Iceland’s advances have come from outside, from the herring boom to NATO, EFTA, and the EEA, and now the nation itself has the chance to answer whether it wants to come out and play.
art.929.title: The Interest-Rate Serfs and the Others
art.929.summary: The author says the nation is divided into two groups: 260 companies that keep their accounts in euros or dollars and obtain cheap financing abroad, and the young people who bear the interest burden in a closed krona economy. Privileged groups that thrive under the current system, the author argues, see everything wrong with exploring the possibility of the euro and dress up their opposition in the language of sovereignty.
art.930.title: Are 72% of Europeans Really Content in the European Union?
art.930.summary: The author criticizes Evrópuhreyfingin’s use of the 72% figure from Eurobarometer and points out that respondents were only asked whether their country had benefited from membership, without a neutral response option. In a comparable question with a neutral option, only 58% said membership was good, and the author cites scholars who believe Eurobarometer presents an overly flattering picture of public opinion.
art.931.title: The EEA Lifeline Is Beginning to Fray
art.931.summary: The article traces how attitudes in the Nordic countries were turned upside down after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine: Finland and Sweden joined NATO, and Bondevik, the former leader of Norway’s NO movement, now wants a referendum on EU talks. Norway’s farmers’ association is preparing for EU membership to return to the forefront, because security issues could trump other interests.
art.932.title: Medicines and the EU
art.932.summary: For 30 years, Icelandic pharmaceutical legislation has been based on EU rules that Iceland implements through observer participation but without a seat at the table. There are only about 3,000 medicines authorized for the market here, compared with about 10,000 in the other Nordic countries, with frequent shortages and high prices, and full membership would increase the chances of solutions such as participation in a larger pharmaceutical market and joint EU drug procurement.
art.933.title: Labour Market Parties Would Continue to Conclude Collective Agreements Within the EU
art.933.summary: The author says there is no basis for the claim that Iceland would have to change its system of collective bargaining if it joined the EU; the Union only requires minimum wages where no collective bargaining framework exists. With the adoption of the euro, workers would be guaranteed real value in exchange for their labour instead of constantly seeking ever higher pay rises to keep up with inflation in the volatile krona.
art.934.title: Let’s Not Close the Door
art.934.summary: The author says the vote is about examining the outcome of negotiations and lists negotiating objectives on control over resources, fisheries, and agriculture. Citing a report showing 70% correlation in Iceland’s and the euro area’s business cycles, the author says euro adoption would lower interest rates, abolish indexation, and improve the position of the younger generation.
art.935.title: Innovation in Europe: The Bigger Picture Hilmar Leaves Out
art.935.summary: Responds to an article by Hilmar Veigar Pétursson on the EU’s competitiveness problem and says it tells only half the story. Reviews progress in European innovation: the research and development share up to 2.24% of GDP, more than 140 unicorns at the end of 2024, and a tenfold increase in startup investment over five years, along with Horizon Europe, the world’s largest research programme.
art.936.title: Great-grandmothers want to see – from Flatey to The Hague
art.936.summary: Two great-grandmothers, one aged 79 in Flatey and the other 27 in The Hague, say they do not know how they would vote on a final accession agreement but want to see what Iceland would be offered. The younger has benefited from European study grants but wants to move home and asks about interest rates and housing; the older does not want to close doors that the next generation might wish to walk through.
art.937.title: What would a yes mean for farmers?
art.937.summary: A dairy farmer says there is no pressing need for membership, as Iceland’s interests are well protected by the EEA Agreement. Many years of uncertainty during an accession process would reduce investment in agriculture and make it all but impossible for farmers to sell their holdings; significantly lower product prices due to increased imports could leave farms unable to service their debts.
art.938.title: Who fears the European Union?
art.938.summary: Asks who has the most to lose from EU rules on transparency, competition and common ground rules. Describes how tougher EU rules on money laundering, tax avoidance and the registration of beneficial owners coincided with Brexit, and suggests that powerful vested interests in Iceland suddenly become preoccupied with popular sovereignty whenever the EU is mentioned.
art.939.title: We are in a plastic boat on rough seas
art.939.summary: Compares policy-rate responses in Iceland and the euro area to three external shocks, COVID, Russia’s invasion and the war in the Middle East; the difference is 2.5 to 5.75 percentage points, and the real interest-rate gap is now about 3.4 percentage points. Likens the króna to a plastic boat with a small engine on rough seas and says the nation needs a bigger ship.
art.940.title: The nations’ purchasing power in Europe’s Champions League
art.940.summary: A professor corrects misleading claims about purchasing power using Eurostat measurements of the purchasing power of disposable income: Iceland ranks 9th in Europe in 2024, just above the euro-area average, not with the highest purchasing power in the world. In 2014, Iceland was at the bottom among the top twelve countries after purchasing power fell more here than elsewhere in the financial crisis.
art.941.title: My NO people, you are so sweet when you obey
art.941.summary: A satirical piece that compares NO voters to a herd voting the way their father and grandfather voted. It says sovereignty shows itself in milk prices twice as high, housing loans three times as large, and a króna that dances like a drunken sailor, and reminds readers that the vote is only about talking to neighbouring nations, not joining anything.
art.942.title: No plan, no sledgehammer
art.942.summary: The chair of UVG says Kristrún Frostadóttir’s plan and sledgehammer against interest rates and inflation have not worked, and now the nation is supposed to choose for the government. It would be irresponsible to devote the government’s efforts in the coming years to accession talks instead of prioritising living standards; a no vote would send a clear message about priorities.
art.943.title: Why I’m going to say YES
art.943.summary: The chair of Uppreisn, Viðreisn’s youth movement, wants a more stable economic environment through adopting the euro and says the króna is not a defence against the problem but the problem itself. In a world of rising tariffs, an import-dependent small nation needs unrestricted access to the internal market and should not adopt rules without electing the representatives who set them.
art.944.title: On monetary sovereignty and its transfer
art.944.summary: An academic discussion of monetary sovereignty with reference to Bodin, Mundell and Zimmermann. Says it is clear that by adopting the euro following entry into the EU, Iceland would transfer a substantial part of its sovereign authority, not only in monetary matters, to the European Central Bank.
art.945.title: What do the oligarchs want you to vote on 29 August?
art.945.summary: Says a small state needs strong ties with countries that share common values in a world where great powers respect neither sovereignty nor borders, while the United States is now undermining NATO and cooperation among European states. Criticizes Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson’s advice to cultivate ties instead with MAGA members of Congress and tech oligarchs, and asks what oligarchs fear the nation might see if it votes yes.
art.946.title: Yes, for science, innovation and culture
art.946.summary: A minister says Iceland’s contributions to EU cooperation programmes, around 34 billion for 2021–2027, return 1.7 krónur for every króna invested. Larger programmes lie ahead: the €175 billion Horizon Europe, an expanded Erasmus+, and a €234 billion competitiveness fund, and full membership would mean having a seat at the table when participation in them is negotiated.
art.947.title: Do you want lower inflation and lower interest rates?
art.947.summary: Says inflation has risen and interest rates have increased since the government’s first budget, citing Kristrún Frostadóttir’s words that people want to join the EU when inflation and interest rates are high. The government therefore has a political incentive for the economic situation not to improve, and the only way to lower interest rates is to take the EU off the agenda with a no vote.
art.948.title: The Prime Minister’s sledgehammer struck the bell
art.948.summary: Attributes the year’s third policy rate hike, to 8%, to overheating and the government’s inaction; inflation is home-grown, driven by housing and labour costs. A yes vote changes nothing about the task of bringing wage developments and public spending into line with value creation; adopting the euro would not remove the need for restraint, only shift where it is applied.
art.949.title: The euro at their own discretion? No, Þórður Snær. Financial reporting doesn’t work that way.
art.949.summary: Responds to an article by Þórður Snær Júlíusson and says large companies do not get to choose the euro for themselves: under IAS 21 and the Annual Accounts Act, companies must report in the currency that carries the greatest weight in their operations. Notes that Síldarvinnslan reported in dollars from 2009–2025 and Landsvirkjun still does; the story that the fishing industry ‘fled the króna’ does not hold up under accounting rules.
art.950.title: How do we improve quality of life in the last 20–30 years of life?
art.950.summary: Discusses the ageing of the nation and the need for a new service society that supports the independence, activity and dignity of older people. Asks why a nation of 400 thousand people should develop every solution on its own, and whether full EU membership could open the way to more structured cooperation, research, innovation and project funding in this field.
art.951.title: When Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson points the way
art.951.summary: Reviews the career of Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson, who is urging a no vote, and asks whether that career gives reason to make his judgment a guiding light. Points out that his conventional political career was much shorter than his standing in the debate suggests: about ten years as an elected MP and just over two and a half years as a minister.
art.952.title: SFS analysis: What is the fear?
art.952.summary: Says SFS analyses claiming that foreign parties would buy up fishing quotas are fearmongering; nothing happens automatically upon accession, rather fisheries management and ownership are negotiated. The current quota system protects a closed private-rights system for a handful of large fishing companies, while only 1.4% of the catch is fully processed in Iceland; membership and a stable currency would provide tariff-free market access and incentives for full processing.
art.953.title: You do not have to be pro-EU to say yes
art.953.summary: Says the question on the ballot is limited: whether to return to the negotiating table, not whether to join the EU. While talks are under way, no power is transferred to the EU, Alþingi can break them off at any time, and membership would require a constitutional amendment approved by two parliaments; undecided voters can therefore say yes.
art.954.title: The same vision for the future in Reykjavík and Brussels
art.954.summary: Points out that Iceland’s industrial policy to 2035 and the EU’s competitiveness policy, shaped in the wake of the Draghi report, emphasize the same priorities: productivity, innovation, simpler regulation, skills and market access. The EU’s Union of Skills plan on education and mobility of professional qualifications fits well with Icelandic goals for jobs in high-productivity sectors.
art.955.title: The European Union and healthcare - together we would be stronger
art.955.summary: The Minister of Health points out that health emergency preparedness falls outside the EEA Agreement, meaning Iceland is not on equal footing with EU states when crises strike. During the pandemic, the Swedes were allowed to purchase vaccines for Iceland through the EU, but there is no guarantee that will happen again; preparedness cooperation must be secured through a bilateral agreement or membership.
art.956.title: What really matters to the people of this country
art.956.summary: Says that each percentage point in the interest-rate gap with the euro area costs society around 120 billion a year, and that euro adoption could save families tens of thousands or more than a hundred thousand krónur a month on mortgage payments. Through the EEA, Iceland already adopts a large share of the regulatory framework without having a say; the talks are about getting the agreement on the table.
art.957.title: Something of a problem child
art.957.summary: The parliamentary group chair of Viðreisn quotes Guðni Th. Jóhannesson’s words that the króna is something of a problem child: wonderful to have, terrible to owe. A household paying 300 thousand a month on a mortgage pays just over 200 thousand in interest, and the state’s interest costs are around 100 billion a year; lower interest rates would quickly wipe out the alleged 50 billion cost of membership.
art.958.title: Choosing the euro for themselves but the króna for the rest of us
art.958.summary: The executive director of Samfylkingin’s parliamentary group points out that the owners of Morgunblaðið, the main owners of Ísfélagið, refinance the company’s debts in euros on terms unavailable to households while the paper fights against any discussion of the euro. He asks why big companies may escape the króna while the public remains stuck with 9–10% mortgage interest.
art.959.title: The option that is not on the ballot
art.959.summary: Examines the Prime Minister’s argument that a yes vote “preserves options” and points out that a no vote also preserves options; the issue was closed twice in fifteen years and reopened both times. A voter who wants to stay outside the EU but inside the EEA, the position of about half the nation according to polls, finds that option nowhere on the ballot, and nothing has been set out about what happens if no prevails.
art.960.title: “You’re going to need a bigger boat”
art.960.summary: Rejects the claim that a yes vote is equivalent to membership and points out that the Norwegians twice completed negotiations and rejected the agreement in a referendum, and that Britain left the Union. In a turbulent world, membership offers economic benefits and greater security, including the EU’s mutual defence clause, which obliges member states to assist a state that is attacked.
art.961.title: Prices could fall sharply in Iceland
art.961.summary: An economics professor shows, using Eurostat data, that prices in Iceland are 62–73% above the EU average and 24–31% higher than high wages can explain, the largest deviation of any country in the comparison. The purchasing power of an hour of work drops from 2nd place to 9th when price levels are taken into account, and the experience of EEA countries that joined the EU suggests that a substantial part of the price premium could recede with membership.
art.962.title: A job interview with the EU?
art.962.summary: Turns the YES side’s analogies about going to a job interview, viewing a property, and trying on a hat on their head: no one goes to a job interview for a job they do not want. The EU regulatory framework is available and can simply be looked up; examples of permanent exemptions, such as the special rules of Åland, are of an entirely different nature from the exemptions from fisheries and agricultural policy that YES supporters talk about.
art.963.title: Buying the nation’s vote
art.963.summary: Points out that according to Meta’s ad library, Áfram Ísland spent about ten times more on advertising on Facebook and Instagram than Já til að sjá, and that the movement’s domain is registered to the advertising agency Pipar\TBWA. It asks who is paying and what interests lie behind it, and compares the fearmongering and information disorder to the 2016 Brexit vote.
art.964.title: The future: bright or bleak?
art.964.summary: Says the EU has moved from cooperation among sovereign states toward a federal state in which a supranational governing system gains ever more power. Mentions that the Germans blocked exports of medical supplies during COVID and warns of unfunded pension liabilities in France, Italy, Germany, and Spain, while Iceland benefits from a funded pension system.
art.965.title: Why are Icelandic startups incorporated in Delaware?
art.965.summary: Says foreign venture capital funds invest in the United States, the United Kingdom, the EU and Switzerland, but Iceland is not on their lists; Icelandic entrepreneurs must register their companies in Delaware and minimise ties to the Icelandic economy to obtain funding. The króna, indexation and the history of capital controls are an insurmountable topic of conversation with investors, and Iceland ranks 37th on StartupBlink’s list of startup ecosystems, far behind comparable countries in the EU.
art.966.title: The króna is the valve holding back Icelandic business
art.966.summary: Compares the króna to a half-closed valve in the pipeline of an open market: currency risk deters foreign investors from small and medium-sized enterprises and makes capital more expensive. With the euro and membership in the customs union would come lower risk, increased foreign investment, cheaper financing, access to EU grants and greater competition in oligopolistic markets.
art.967.title: The EU multiplies the influence of small states: The example of Cyprus
art.967.summary: Reviews the experience of Cyprus, which has less than 0.25% of the EU’s population yet nominates a commissioner, sits on the Council of Ministers and has six Members of the European Parliament, proportionally more than its population would suggest. A blocking minority normally requires four states, and Cyprus held the Presidency of the Council of Ministers in the first half of 2026; membership gives a small state influence far beyond its size.
art.968.title: Let us vote YES to strengthen our freedom and sovereignty
art.968.summary: Says economic issues are not the most important matter, but rather security and democracy at a time when dictators are on the march; it is urgent to strengthen ties with nations guided by democracy, the rule of law and solidarity. Membership would involve limits on the exercise of sovereignty, but not its surrender; the EU is a union of sovereign states, and any change into a federal state would require the consent of all member states.
art.969.title: Grand Fenwick by Faxaflói
art.969.summary: Compares the security arguments of the YES side to the novel The Mouse That Roared: seeking shelter in an alliance that has no army and has never flown a fighter jet under its own flag. Article 42 of the EU Treaty states that for NATO states, NATO remains the foundation of collective defence; Iceland has been in NATO since 1949 and has had a defence agreement with the United States since 1951, and security issues are a fallback argument because the older arguments have proved difficult to carry.
art.970.title: Back and forth down a blind alley
art.970.summary: A former parliamentary group chair of Samfylkingin recounts the history of Iceland’s international cooperation and says the EEA pillar will not stand forever, among other things if Norway takes the step to full membership. The euro could reduce the public’s interest burden by up to 30% and save hundreds of billions in interest costs. The only way to resolve disputed issues is to complete the negotiation process.
art.971.title: How much is Iceland sacrificing now through reduced FREEDOM?
art.971.summary: The author asks how free Iceland really is: outside the customs union, without voting rights on the rules of the internal market, and with a micro-currency carrying exchange-rate risk. He wants to complete the negotiations, compare the agreement with the EEA and the króna, and reject it if it proves worse. A YES on 29 August is a step toward negotiating and seeing the agreement.
art.972.title: Word on the Street: Trump intends to annex Greenland — so is Iceland next?
art.972.summary: The column says Trump’s statements about annexing Greenland show that Iceland cannot remain passive. Iceland does not enjoy the same protection from the EU as Denmark, and therefore closer cooperation with European states, including on defence matters, is vital. The first step is to vote yes on 29 August.
art.973.title: One spoke first — the other now wants to settle the matter
art.973.summary: Þorsteinn recalls that Ragnhildur Helgadóttir was the first to raise the idea of full membership in Alþingi in 1990 and says Þorgerður Katrín is now following the same fundamental policy. Turning 75% membership through the EEA into full membership rests on the same ideology as Iceland’s foreign policy for nearly eight decades. A NO would increase the risk that Iceland will not itself decide what community of nations it ends up in.
art.974.title: Word on the Street: A knife-edge contest and the no side is using deception — yet the yes camp is gaining confidence
art.974.summary: The column says the no movement is better funded and that its advertisements claim, without supporting assumptions, that membership would cost 50 billion a year; Morgunblaðið then mentioned 90 billion. Despite these deceptions, the contest is on a knife edge and the yes side is gaining ground.
art.975.title: A seat at the table...
art.975.summary: The author says the claim by YES supporters about having a seat at the table is plainly wrong; the seat is of little use if the person sitting there sleeps through the meetings, as Icelanders have allegedly done regarding EU regulations. He also doubts that Iceland would ever get the euro and points out that Romania had not met the conditions nineteen years after joining.
art.976.title: We are not voting on membership on 29 August!
art.976.summary: Davíð Þór says the vote is only about reopening negotiations, not about membership. Undecided voters can safely vote yes because they can say no later when an agreement is on the table. Claims that talks would automatically mean a loss of sovereignty and a grab of natural resources are false or misleading.
art.977.title: Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn is no longer on the beaten path
art.977.summary: A former MP criticizes Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn for putting forward the Swiss lawyer Carl Baudenbacher as its main speaker against negotiations. He asks why the party is so strongly opposed to membership that it does not even want to let the nation explore what it might have to offer.
art.978.title: The bill always lands somewhere
art.978.summary: The author links the year's third policy rate hike, to 8%, to the vote and says the level of interest rates and the EU issue are the same problem seen from two sides. The economy is cooling, defaults are rising and inflation is 5.3%; the cost of the króna always falls on the public.
art.979.title: Word on the Street: Bændasamtökin and farmers are showing voters the utmost disrespect
art.979.summary: The column accuses Bændasamtökin and farmers of lies and fake news in the run-up to the vote. A sector that receives 30 billion krónur a year in public support should show voters courtesy rather than spread deceitful propaganda.
art.980.title: Word on the Street: What interests are being defended, and why?
art.980.summary: The column says the Central Bank's rate hike tangibly highlights the drawbacks of maintaining an independent currency in a micro-economy. Interest rates in Iceland are many times higher than in the euro area, and the increase will be grist to the mill of YES supporters.
art.981.title: Svarthöfði writes: Barely literate people publish golden-age prose
art.981.summary: Svarthöfði mocks NO supporters who suddenly posted polished text on social media and suspects that campaign groups provided them with ready-made posts. Distortions of fact and misrepresentations, he says, characterize the writing on the NO side.
art.982.title: 29 August is Icelanders’ biggest interest-rate decision day
art.982.summary: Sigmundur Ernir echoes Guðmundur Andra Thorsson’s words that election day will be Icelanders’ biggest interest-rate decision day. The króna is a tiny currency that mainly benefits the wealthy, while the public is left with usurious interest rates, high prices and inflationary pressure.
art.983.title: Do MPs see further than the nation – 30 years into the future?
art.983.summary: The author lists ten reasons to vote yes for the sake of children and grandchildren and points out that no MP can see 30 years into the future. A yes is not approval of membership, but approval of exploring the option, defending Icelandic interests in negotiations and allowing the nation to make the final decision.
art.984.title: The damn tub can leak – just don’t rock it
art.984.summary: The entrepreneur says Icelanders curse inflation, usurious interest rates, oligopoly and the quota system, yet sanctify the system whenever change is mentioned. He wants to test fisheries, agriculture, currency issues and special arrangements in negotiations and compare the result with the real Iceland of the króna, indexation and debt-burdened households.
art.985.title: Word on the Street: The thunderous speech and the speech that did not move the room
art.985.summary: The article recalls a 2014 speech by Hilmar Veigar Pétursson of CCP in which he said the króna fostered a victim mentality among Icelanders and that the plan was to join the EU. According to the article, his stance has now changed because of his substantial wealth and state support for CCP/Fenris.
art.986.title: The opposition’s record
art.986.summary: Kolbrún says the NO campaign is marked by distortions and spin, comparing it to the opposition’s record filibustering during the fishing fee debate. Dire predictions of misery did not come true then, and the argument being made now is of the same kind.
art.987.title: Islands, outermost regions, special arrangements and exemptions
art.987.summary: The managing director of Bændasamtakanna says Article 349 TFEU on outermost regions is not a realistic precedent for Iceland; the provision applies only to regions of France, Spain and Portugal with GDP below 75% of the EU average. Ireland, Malta and Cyprus received no permanent exemptions from the Common Agricultural Policy, only support within it. The Finnish model was conditional on production not increasing beyond the 1991-1993 reference levels.
art.988.title: We certainly can do this ourselves
art.988.summary: A Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn MP recalls the prime minister’s pre-election words that the EU would not be a priority issue and would not fix the poor economic situation. The years 2014-2020 show that Icelanders are fully capable of managing economic affairs themselves, with price stability and reasonable interest rates. An exploratory trip to Brussels is neither free nor risk-free while the home-grown inflation problem remains unresolved.
art.989.title: Þorgerður Katrín is not telling the truth in interviews
art.989.summary: The Supreme Court attorney says the foreign minister is making false claims: exports to the EU are 50%, not 70%, and talk of a total accession cost of 13-15 billion is imaginary. Félag skattgreiðenda estimates gross payments at 43-53 billion a year and net costs at around 34 billion. Real interest rates in Iceland are not glaringly out of line with those in France and Italy.
art.990.title: Main pillars on shaky foundations
art.990.summary: The lawyer and former permanent secretary says the leading states, France and Germany, are grappling with economic problems and growing political uncertainty; AfD is polling as Germany’s largest party and Le Pen has a realistic chance of the presidency. To seek shelter in the EU under these circumstances is to seek shelter in a wasteland. Iceland is a North Atlantic state with growing alignment with the United States, Canada, Britain and Norway.
art.991.title: Walling yourself in when the world is open
art.991.summary: A former Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn MP says no one applies to join an organisation just to peek inside the package; a YES vote is a declaration of support for entry involving a major transfer of sovereignty. Accession talks create prolonged uncertainty that delays investment and costs the public growth and jobs. In a customs union, free trade agreements with China, India and more than 40 countries would lapse, and negotiating authority would shift to Brussels.
art.992.title: EU membership – major opportunities in trade with China would be lost
art.992.summary: The chairman of the Icelandic-Chinese Chamber of Commerce says the 2014 free trade agreement with China would lapse upon EU membership; China has likely become Iceland’s second-largest trading partner. EU tariffs on Chinese cars are 17-35%, and on clothing up to 70%, which would raise prices and inflation. Direct flights to Beijing from October would create tariff-free export opportunities for fresh seafood that would be lost within the EU.
art.993.title: EU enlargement and the YES side – a shared goal
art.993.summary: A former minister describes the interaction between the foreign minister and the EU enlargement commissioner from January 2025: the Commission interprets the 2009 application as still valid, and POLITICO reported on the August vote before it was announced at home. Iceland is to be used by von der Leyen and Marta Kos to prove a new fast track in enlargement policy. The government is asking for an unconditional mandate without negotiation objectives, which Brussels already knows how to use.
art.994.title: The freedom to move forward
art.994.summary: The foreign minister writes in Morgunblaðið that the vote is not about membership but about whether to sit down at the negotiating table; the final decision will always belong to the nation in a second vote. Internal market rules are having an ever greater impact on Iceland, while our influence on shaping them is limited. The figure of 50 billion in annual costs is a gross figure and part of an information muddle; the IMF points out that closer linkage to the euro could lower capital costs.
art.995.title: The blind spot
art.995.summary: Iceland’s former ambassador to the EU says that, for the first time, the Union is now a direct party to armed conflict in Europe, and that its militarisation has shifted the power of initiative from elected representatives to unelected officials. War spending is draining resources from infrastructure and welfare, while energy costs, economic contraction and mounting debt are battering the Union. The EU itself has changed, even though the authorities speak only of a changed world situation.
art.996.title: What is in these 100 documents that I am not allowed to access?
art.996.summary: A former foreign minister says the Ministry for Foreign Affairs is denying him access to around 100 documents on its communications with the EU from his time in office. The 2009 application forms the basis of the process that the current foreign minister intends to complete, even though it is claimed that the vote is not about the application. He asks whether something in the documents could disrupt the package game.
art.997.title: Before "whether" becomes "how"
art.997.summary: Heimssýn says the question of whether Iceland should join the EU is being replaced by a question about an exploratory journey back to the negotiating table. Referring to Carl Baudenbacher’s article on path dependence and framing, it argues that a YES vote would set in motion a process in which the administration, experts and interest groups begin preparing for membership as an accepted reality. The later decision would therefore not be taken under the same circumstances as the first.
art.998.title: Ministry-related work would move abroad with EU membership
art.998.summary: The blog republishes a section from a Morgunblaðið article by lawyer Tryggvi Axelsson arguing that Iceland’s vote in the Council of Ministers would never matter in the adoption of legislation except as a declaration of support. Council meetings take place for two days almost every week, and two to three ministers would have to attend them, with the resulting absences and an increase in staff in the Prime Minister’s Office and ministries. The constitution would be amended, and the country’s system of government would undergo a fundamental change.
art.999.title: RÚV covers the very serious debt position of the EU states
art.999.summary: Heimssýn points to a RÚV news analysis on an IMF expert report about Europe’s financial strains: public spending across the continent will rise by almost five percent of GDP by 2040 due to ageing, the energy transition and defence. The report’s authors say the European social model is at risk. A state of disintegration lies ahead in the Union that is supposed to draw Iceland in.
art.1000.title: Hilmar Veigar Pétursson says NO on 29 August!
art.1000.summary: The blog recounts a speech by Hilmar Veigar Pétursson at an Áfram Íslands meeting: in 2007, 46 European companies were among the 100 most valuable in the world, but now only 16 are, and 41 unicorn companies moved their headquarters out of the EU in 2008-2021. Around €300 billion flows annually from Europe into investment in the United States. Iceland is already in a stronger position in productivity, and the figures call for a NO vote.
art.1001.title: Jón Baldvin, DV and Douglass North
art.1001.summary: Heimssýn explains Douglass North’s concept of path dependence: once talks resume, an institutional process is created with its own logic, expectations and expert networks, making later decisions seem like a natural continuation. The EU’s propaganda machine would kick into gear with information campaigns, grants and conferences. A mandate that could formally be revoked might develop into a self-reinforcing process.
art.1002.title: Central banks and financial supervisors reiterate the trouble with the EU’s regulatory burden
art.1002.summary: The blog says the Central Bank of Iceland and Nordic financial supervisors have repeatedly called for the EU’s regulatory burden to be eased, and refers to Draghi’s report on the Union’s sluggishness. Innovation is delayed and entrepreneurs give up on Europe. Hilmar Veigar Pétursson, previously positive towards the EU and the euro, now intends to say NO.
art.1003.title: What would happen to the Icesave judgment under EU membership?
art.1003.summary: Heimssýn reviews an article by Carl Baudenbacher, president of the EFTA Court when the Icesave judgment was delivered in 2013: membership would not invalidate the judgment, but would render it obsolete for the future. The EU Deposit Guarantee Directive from 2014 has not been incorporated into the EEA Agreement, but would become binding upon membership, under the supervision of the European Commission and the jurisdiction of the Court of Justice of the European Union. The legal position that made Iceland’s victory possible within the EEA would not remain in place within the EU.
art.1004.title: An Icelandic resource – but who enjoys the returns?
art.1004.summary: Drawing on a new legal opinion by three law professors for the Prime Minister’s Office, the blog discusses foreign investment in fisheries under membership. Iceland has an exemption in the EEA that permits restrictions on foreign ownership, but the Court of Justice of the European Union rejected British nationality requirements against quota hopping in Factortame II. Real economic links to Iceland are not the same as Icelandic ownership, and the returns could flow out of the country.
art.1005.title: Daði Már’s currency report failed the IMF test
art.1005.summary: The blog presents a memorandum by Jón Helgi Egilsson and Erna Bjarnadóttir comparing the finance minister’s currency report with criticism from the Central Bank and the latest IMF assessment. The IMF considers the króna no more volatile than comparable currencies and emphasizes the exchange rate as an adjustment tool in response to Iceland-specific shocks. The Prime Minister’s Office’s claim that the costs of the króna outweigh the benefits is not based on a comprehensive analysis by the report’s authors.
art.1006.title: Anne Sibert wanted us to guarantee Icesave – does not seem to be following developments
art.1006.summary: Heimssýn criticizes writings by Anne Sibert, a former member of the Central Bank’s Monetary Policy Committee, who says it is right to adopt the euro even if the European Central Bank’s monetary policy suited Iceland poorly. Sibert is said not to have followed monetary policy developments since 2012.
