She had also believed that Icelanders should guarantee Icesave, but the nation rejected that twice and the EFTA Court ruled in Iceland’s favor.
art.1007.title: Icelanders have many reasons to revive their journey toward EU membership
art.1007.summary: The former Prime Minister and Foreign Minister of Sweden writes that solitude is rarely reassuring in an unstable world; the unpredictable policy of the Trump administration and its designs on Greenland have made Iceland more vulnerable, and being outside the customs union leaves the country defenseless in trade wars. Full membership would strengthen sovereignty because it would bring participation in decisions that Iceland already implements through the EEA. After Brexit, Iceland shares no maritime border with any member state, and there is therefore room for compromises on fisheries, just as Sweden and Finland obtained special rules for northern agriculture.
art.1008.title: A thought on the EU, the ATAD directive, and why the moneyed interests want us to say NO on 29 August
art.1008.summary: A user points out that the Brexit campaign intensified after the EU introduced the ATAD directive against tax avoidance by large corporations and asks whether the same pattern can be seen in Iceland. The strongest opponents of membership are the moneyed interests: the large fishing companies, CEOs, banks, and the power elite. The resistance may be more about transparency and tax loopholes than about fish.
art.1009.title: When claims meet reality
art.1009.summary: Screenshot comparison: mbl.is quotes CCP CEO Hilmar Veigar as saying that no one believes in Europe, while Viðskiptablaðið simultaneously reports that billions are flowing back into European stocks and that European corporate profits are headed for 22% growth. The author asks whether people are being subjected to propaganda.
art.1010.title: Concerts in the EU
art.1010.summary: A user lists world-famous musicians who have played in EU countries in recent years but skipped Iceland, and says that a common market area would make it cheaper for artists to perform here. He himself half-jokingly calls these wishful claims, as a response to false claims from the NO side.
art.1011.title: The EU is building an army
art.1011.summary: A short post sharing material about the EU’s military build-up, arguing that it is a governing authority that builds an army, not a trade association. The EU has therefore become something different from, and more than, economic cooperation.
art.1012.title: ▶ Young people, let’s show up and vote
art.1012.summary: Young people are urged to go to the polls on 29 August; the vote concerns the next 30–40 years, housing issues, and the future of those who will live longest with the outcome.
art.1013.title: ▶ Quiz: lower interest rates, yes please
art.1013.summary: A light-hearted quiz celebrating lower interest rates and describing indexation as cold; a yes vote in August would not mean joining the EU, only looking into the possibilities.
art.1014.title: ▶ Nonsense that there is nothing to negotiate
art.1014.summary: A response to the claim that everything about the EU can be read online: no one knows what Icelandic special arrangements might be available until we sit down at the negotiating table, for example on fisheries and agriculture.
art.1015.title: ▶ Nonsense about the influx of foreigners
art.1015.summary: The claim that foreigners would flood into the country upon accession is dismissed as nonsense; free movement has applied since 1994 through the EEA, and the Danes themselves have the strictest immigration rules in the EU.
art.1016.title: ▶ Quiz: yes on 29 August
art.1016.summary: Light-hearted quiz; lower interest rates get a yes please, indexation is called ice-cold, and the interviewee intends to vote yes on 29 August.
art.1017.title: ▶ Nonsense that unemployment would rise
art.1017.summary: The claim that unemployment would increase upon accession is dismissed as nonsense; countries such as Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Ireland experienced lower unemployment after joining the EU.
art.1018.title: ▶ Nonsense that sovereignty would be lost
art.1018.summary: The claim that sovereignty would be lost is dismissed as nonsense; the 27 EU nations have not lost their sovereignty, and with membership Iceland would finally gain representatives instead of accepting EEA rules without influence.
art.1019.title: ▶ Nonsense that no opt-outs are available
art.1019.summary: The claim that no permanent opt-outs are available is dismissed as nonsense; Denmark has a permanent opt-out from the euro and Finland in agricultural matters.
art.1020.title: ▶ A football contract explains the yes vote
art.1020.summary: A former professional compares the vote to an offer from Hammarby in 1995: voting yes only means hearing what is on offer, and a final agreement would then go back to a referendum.
art.1021.title: ▶ Lárus Welding: lots of upside, no downside
art.1021.summary: Lárus Welding says the yes option has far more upside than downside; Iceland should be part of the conversation in light of world affairs, and any agreement would in any case go back to the people.
art.1022.title: ▶ Sovereignty is strengthened by a seat at the table
art.1022.summary: Sovereignty is described as twofold: Iceland would continue to govern its internal affairs, but today follows EU rules without influence; with membership it would gain a seat at the table and sovereignty would increase.
art.1023.title: ▶ Treasury interest burden comparable to Greece
art.1023.summary: Ásgeir Brynjar, PhD in finance, says the Treasury pays a similarly high share of expenditure in interest as Greece because of the high-interest-rate environment of the króna; with an application and ERM shelter, stability would be gained.
art.1024.title: ▶ The Draghi report paints a dark picture
art.1024.summary: The Draghi report on Europe’s competitiveness is said to show that the continent is falling behind and that complex regulation is holding companies back; the wrong time for Iceland to bind itself more tightly to the system.
art.1025.title: ▶ Ísak: we are doing better outside the EU
art.1025.summary: Ísak points out that Iceland ranks at the top on measures of living standards and economic performance and asks why it should join the EU when the country is doing better than the member states.
art.1026.title: ▶ Selma: let future generations govern the country
art.1026.summary: Selma says she believes in Iceland’s opportunities for the future and wants future generations to be free to govern the country without constraint.
art.1027.title: ▶ Georg: the EU is on the wrong path
art.1027.summary: Georg says he is an internationalist but believes the EU is on the wrong path, especially because of the regulatory burden on innovation.
art.1028.title: ▶ Jóhann: no foreign master
art.1028.summary: Jóhann says he neither wants nor needs a foreign master and refuses to give up Icelandic jurisdiction, currency, or natural resources.
art.1029.title: ▶ Jóhann: we can solve these issues ourselves at home
art.1029.summary: Jóhann says Iceland is the best country in the world and that Icelanders can solve themselves at home any issues that need fixing.
art.1030.title: ▶ Bingo: isn’t this enough?
art.1030.summary: A bingo-style run-through of the list against membership: chat control surveillance, 0.08% voting weight, the common fisheries policy, the customs union, and 15 billion in annual expenditure.
art.1031.title: Accession talks are not a trial subscription
art.1031.summary: Guðbjörg Oddný, MA in international relations, says accession talks are not a trial subscription but require enormous time, funding and work across the entire government system. The direct cost of resumed talks is conservatively estimated at around ISK 1.9 billion, and the process would create prolonged uncertainty for businesses and investors. Iceland is in a strong position through the EEA and does not need another round.
art.1032.title: Trump should not be the reason
art.1032.summary: Friðjón says uncertainty on the international stage because of Trump is a hasty and poor reason to vote yes; a yes vote amounts to a declaration of willingness to join the EU, not merely to have a look inside the package. Trump is a temporary variable in the international system, and it is short-sighted to let reactions to one president determine a long-term decision about Iceland’s position.
art.1033.title: How do interest rates fall with euro adoption?
art.1033.summary: Professor of economics Gauti B. Eggertsson explains that long-term interest rates fall as soon as a credible plan to adopt the euro is in place, as happened in Italy and Spain where rates fell toward German rates years before the euro was adopted. Croatia entered the exchange rate mechanism in July 2020 and adopted the euro on 1 January 2023; claims of a 19-year adoption process are a misleading average calculation.
art.1034.title: Older people should absolutely not vote no
art.1034.summary: Björn, a director and producer, says membership could mean a brighter future for younger generations and that older people should not use their vote to close off young people’s opportunities. He notes that 94% of Maltese people believe EU membership has worked out well and that more than 70% of Britons believe Brexit was the wrong decision.
art.1035.title: More options and a stronger position if we say yes
art.1035.summary: Ragna, a Samfylkingin MP, says Iceland has more options and a stronger position if it enters negotiations. It is expensive to maintain an independent micro-currency; the króna is a high-interest currency, and the borrowing costs of the state and municipalities are much higher than they need to be. It is less risky to enter talks with Iceland’s interests as the guiding principle than to shut the door immediately.
art.1036.title: Open the door to infrastructure investment across the country
art.1036.summary: Minister Logi Einarsson says EU membership could significantly expand Iceland’s financing options for infrastructure development; Iceland would become a full participant in the European Investment Bank and gain access to European grant and guarantee schemes. Icelandic authorities and municipalities would continue to prioritise projects, and the EU might have covered a large share of the costs arising from the volcanic activity near Grindavík.
art.1037.title: The unfortunate Ólafur Ragnar
art.1037.summary: Lúðvík recounts that Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson fought against EFTA membership in 1970, opposed NATO and voted against the EEA Agreement, yet his dire predictions did not come true. Now he is using the same warnings against EU talks; it would be better to negotiate, see what is on offer, and let the nation make an informed decision.
art.1038.title: Iceland, Europe and the spheres of influence of great powers
art.1038.summary: Þorsteinn says the biggest question in the referendum concerns Iceland’s position in a world where great powers divide the world into spheres of influence and the liberal international order is breaking down. He recounts examples of pressure by great powers on small states, including when the Vice President of the United States thanked Iceland for rejecting the Belt and Road even though the Icelandic government had made no such decision.
art.1039.title: What does uncertainty about an EU accession treaty mean?
art.1039.summary: Jón says EU membership would entail a fundamental change from the EEA, as customs, currency, foreign affairs and defence, and several other policy areas would come under EU authority. It is far-fetched to think that Iceland, as the 28th state, would secure permanent exemptions from the Union’s fundamental rules in fisheries and agriculture. It is better for Icelandic politicians than the EU to handle these policy areas.
art.1040.title: Referendum: Gratitude and Outlook from the Swiss Substitute
art.1040.summary: Carl Baudenbacher, former President of the EFTA Court, sums up eight points and asks whether Iceland would gain any real benefit from joining or give up proven institutional independence. The EEA is neither a relic nor a waiting room, but Europe’s alternative institutional framework, and Iceland’s security rests on NATO and the defence agreement with the United States, not the EU.
art.1041.title: Is 532 billion a smaller number than 245 billion?
art.1041.summary: Egill responds to an article by Konráð Guðjónsson and says the profits of banks and real estate companies more than doubled during the inflation period, from 245 billion in 2016–2020 to 532 billion in 2021–2025. He points out that Gauti B. Eggertsson responded to the Áfram Ísland report with an 82-page memorandum showing 30 examples of misleading presentation.
art.1042.title: Low interest rates and low consumer prices?
art.1042.summary: Reynir reviews the main arguments for membership and finds that they do not withstand scrutiny; the purchasing power of wages is high in Iceland by international comparison even though consumer prices are high. Having its own currency enables countries to manage their economy better and deal with local fluctuations, as was seen in the 2008 banking collapse.
art.1043.title: Unsure about the EU? Say no
art.1043.summary: Jón Ívar, a doctor, says a narrow yes would set off years of conflict, while a narrow no would allow the nation to focus on urgent tasks at home. Accession talks cost a great deal of money and political energy, and major decisions on sovereignty should rest on broad consensus, which is not in place. No today is not no forever.
art.1044.title: The three groups that say YES
art.1044.summary: Rúnar divides the pro-YES camp into three groups and says the talks are genuine accession negotiations involving further alignment with the union’s rules while they are under way, not exploratory talks. Currency, lending terms and prices are not negotiating items, and full control over resources was not accepted in previous negotiations with applicant countries.
art.1045.title: Just say no to the salesman
art.1045.summary: Egill likens the “yes to see” argument to a sales pitch where the foot is already in the door and complicated issues are discussed at the very end. The structure of the EU is clear, there is no reason to assume that a microstate would receive much consideration in decisions on further integration, and the talks would drain valuable energy from other policy areas.
art.1046.title: History repeats itself
art.1046.summary: Daði Már, Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs and Deputy Chair of Viðreisn, recounts how opponents’ dire predictions about NATO, EFTA and the EEA did not come true; rather, decisions to increase international cooperation proved fortunate for the nation. The same voices of objection about sovereignty and resources are now being heard; when an agreement is on the table, the nation will make an informed decision in a second referendum.
art.1047.title: In the grip of the króna
art.1047.summary: Jón Bragi, cand. oecon and MBA, says the layoffs of 1,100–1,400 tradespeople are almost entirely confined to companies financing projects in Icelandic krónur, while companies outside the króna economy continue their projects. The króna is a currency with an inbuilt drive toward self-destruction, and stability will be achieved by saying yes.
art.1048.title: Landsvirkjun, “all of Iceland” and the uncertainty over EU membership
art.1048.summary: Þorgrímur, an MP for Miðflokkurinn, says that before deciding on accession talks it must be clearly established what room the authorities would have to use Landsvirkjun as a tool for regional viability, job creation and energy security. It must be ensured that the right to utilise and dispose of energy resources remains with the nation for all time; until then, the answer is no.
art.1049.title: A changed world picture
art.1049.summary: Sigurgeir describes how Icelanders used a “changed world picture” in the 20th century to advance: sovereignty in 1918, independence in 1944 and the extension of territorial waters in the Cod Wars. He considers it unconvincing that a changed world picture should now lead to joining the EU, and that the circumstances should instead be used to advance on Iceland’s own terms, as previous generations did.
art.1050.title: Had enough of the debate about the EU?
art.1050.summary: Diljá Mist, MP for the Independence Party and 2nd Deputy Chair of the Foreign Affairs Committee, says the vote is on whether to continue Iceland’s application to join the EU and that a yes would mean a long, strict and costly process. Claims that the vote is about “seeing lower interest rates” are false, and Iceland’s voting weight within the EU would be 0.08%.
art.1051.title: We have nothing to lose – that is why I say yes
art.1051.summary: Sindri says yes means wanting to see what is on offer and lists examples of special arrangements for member states: Ireland outside Schengen, Malta’s 25-mile protection zone, Denmark’s summer-house exemption and Sweden’s exemption for oral tobacco. The argument that permanent special arrangements are not available therefore collapses under its own weight; claims about selling off resources have no basis.
art.1052.title: Pinocchio and the golden promises
art.1052.summary: Kristín compares promises of EU membership to Pinocchio’s Toyland, where the price tag only became clear later. The EU will not fix Icelandic economic management, will not build housing, and the euro is not a magic wand; lower interest rates and lower inflation are achieved through responsible economic management at home. The package is not unknown, since the Union is built on common treaties.
art.1053.title: The Spanish want Icelandic fisheries
art.1053.summary: Gunnar Bragi, former Minister for Foreign Affairs, Fisheries and Agriculture, says a permanent exemption from the free movement of capital and investment in fisheries would not be approved; the Spanish made that clear in the summer of 2009 and the Dutch did so recently. If investment is allowed, there will be a scramble to acquire Icelandic fishing companies in order to gain access to the resource.
art.1054.title: The people or the money?
art.1054.summary: Yngvi Ómar states that the share of the population living in owner-occupied housing fell from 87% in 2005 to 61% in 2025, and that housing prices rose by 103% in real terms over ten years compared with 24% within the EU. He says the no movement has far more capital behind it, that Áfram Ísland may have 200–300 million krónur at its disposal, and urges people to review official information at þjóðaratkvæði.is.
art.1055.title: Stand guard over... what?
art.1055.summary: Ingibjörg Rósa describes how runaway inflation, indexation and debt weighed heavily on the lives of her parents in agriculture, and that the loans she took over were many times higher than the original loan amounts. She says Iceland is still struggling with inflation and interest rates that never fall except briefly, and asks whether the time has not come to think outside the box and try something new.
art.1056.title: Sovereignty, what sovereignty
art.1056.summary: Ólafur says claims that Iceland would not lose sovereignty upon joining are wrong; the transfer of powers would be so extensive that the constitution would have to be amended. The claim that Iceland is already 75% in the EU is misleading, since a review by the Ministry for Foreign Affairs up to the end of 2016 showed 13.4% of the total body of rules. Iceland would enter the EU customs union and lose its current free trade agreements, including with China.
art.1057.title: No is okay
art.1057.summary: Ágúst compares wages and housing prices in Iceland and Poland and says average wages in Iceland are 913 thousand krónur compared with 291 thousand in Poland; the ratio of apartment prices to annual wages is higher in Poland. The situation in the EU is deteriorating, with increased military spending, ever-rising debts of member states and persistent unemployment.
art.1058.title: What if?
art.1058.summary: Pétur, an employee of the Viðreisn parliamentary group and a substitute MP, asks what happens if interest rates and inflation fall, indexation disappears, the grocery basket becomes cheaper, and Iceland gains influence over the rules it already adopts through the EEA. The vote is about entering negotiations and obtaining an agreement for the nation to decide on; if it is not good enough, no will be said in a later vote.
art.1059.title: Mortgage rates do not fall automatically with the euro
art.1059.summary: Magnús says the claim that mortgage rates automatically fall with the euro confuses the symptom with the disease; inflation causes the high rates, and it is homemade. The pension system’s return benchmark and banks’ interest margin also keep rates high, and both are Icelandic choices that the euro would not change.
art.1060.title: Will the EU help with road construction in Iceland?
art.1060.summary: Jón Þorvaldur says EU membership would help build infrastructure, both through direct grants from the CEF fund, from which Ireland has received 1.6–16 billion per year, and through low-cost financing from the European Investment Bank. The real interest rate on EIB loans is about 1%, compared with 2.75% on Icelandic government funding, which could reduce tolls or shorten the repayment period for road projects.
art.1061.title: We are at the party but not allowed to choose the song
art.1061.summary: Árni Páll, a lawyer, says he trusts Iceland to negotiate as it has done on fish stocks, EFTA, the EEA and defence matters. Iceland is already at the EU party through the EEA, follows the house rules but is not allowed to choose the song; real sovereignty means having a seat at the table. The vote is about being allowed to see the agreement, and then the nation will decide.
art.1062.title: With all due respect?
art.1062.summary: Steingrímur uses sarcasm against opposition to talks and writes as if speaking for those who do not talk to foreigners; in that way, the nation would never get to know what is on offer or what the sacrifices would be. He recalls that the EEA Agreement was never put to the nation in a referendum and that foreigners in Brussels already control an astonishing amount in Iceland through it.
art.1063.title: The first stone from the wall – why I say yes
art.1063.summary: Brynhildur recounts the story of the Norwegian captain who paid workers in Siglufjörður directly in 1903 and says that the opening of Iceland, free trade, EFTA and the EEA have always met resistance from those who did best within the closed system. She says she is voting yes because no means closing the door without even looking out through it; the position is personal and not a conclusion by Viska.
art.1064.title: Fearmongering and the facts about energy resources
art.1064.summary: Jóhann Páll, Minister for Energy, says a well-funded advertising campaign is fuelling fear that Iceland will lose control over its resources. Under Article 194 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, decisions on the use of energy resources rest with the member states themselves, and the EU cannot force through an interconnector. Entering talks transfers no powers, and no agreement would take effect unless the nation approves it.
art.1065.title: What, then, was the struggle for?
art.1065.summary: Jón Pétur, an MP for Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn, says earlier generations fought for independence and sovereignty, and that Iceland already has close cooperation with Europe and access to the internal market, while also being able to make its own free-trade agreements outside the EU’s trade policy. An agreement would inevitably involve transferring part of decision-making power, and for that reason people should vote no.
art.1066.title: A sensible order of things
art.1066.summary: Jón Steindór, a lawyer, says the question is clear: yes means Iceland sits back down at the negotiating table and gets a clear picture of the terms of possible membership. If an agreement is reached, it will be put to the nation in a separate referendum; a yes is therefore not a final decision but the first step toward an informed decision.
art.1067.title: Do companies profit from inflation?
art.1067.summary: Konráð, an economist, responds to Egill Almar Ágústsson and says the calculations on ríkissjóður.is and verðtrygging.is are unrealistic; the net interest payments of the national economy are around and below 50 billion a year, not a possible saving of 250 billion. Inflation reduces companies’ profitability rather than increasing it, because interest on non-indexed debt and operating costs rise as well.
art.1068.title: What is it that we still have left to see?
art.1068.summary: Gunnar says the first yes is not a neutral search for information but the start of a formal accession process; the EU’s basic framework is known and only the details, transition periods and possible special arrangements are unknown. An opinion by three law professors shows that decision-making power over the conservation of fish stocks and total allowable catch would pass to the EU upon accession.
art.1069.title: Opportunities for Icelandic agriculture in the EU
art.1069.summary: Svavar says the biggest opportunity for Icelandic farmers within the EU lies in exports and marketing; the Union runs one of the world’s most extensive promotional and marketing systems for food under the slogan Enjoy, it's from Europe. It is realistic that hundreds of millions of krónur per year could be obtained for marketing Icelandic products, in addition to broader protection of origin such as PDO and PGI.
art.1070.title: The interests of Reykjavík residents and the elephant seal in City Hall
art.1070.summary: Pétur, a city councillor, says the EU’s principle of subsidiarity would ensure that the day-to-day running of municipalities would remain at City Hall, but points out that interest-bearing debt in the Reykjavíkurborg group amounts to around ISK 400 billion. A modest 2% interest-rate reduction would mean annual savings of ISK 3.6 billion for the A-section and ISK 30–40 billion for the group over a single electoral term.
art.1071.title: Which negotiating framework applies?
art.1071.summary: Erna points out that the EU adopted a revised accession-negotiation methodology in 2020, with six thematic clusters instead of individual chapters, and asks which negotiating framework would apply if talks were resumed. When the talks were halted in 2013, Iceland’s most important interest chapters, fisheries and agriculture, had not been opened, and the authorities have not answered this fundamental question.
art.1072.title: The golden donkey
art.1072.summary: Guðjón Þórir, an engineer, asks whether Iceland’s independence is being properly valued and whether one of the richest nations in the world needs to place its resources in the hands of others for distribution. Last time, he says, the answer was stop when Brussels demanded distribution of the country’s resources.
art.1073.title: Negotiations on European Union membership: yes or no?
art.1073.summary: Magnús Tumi, a professor, says there is no doubt that the best course is to find out what agreement can be reached; the EU Commissioner for Enlargement said that Iceland would not need to change any laws until a membership treaty had been approved. No EU countries have had fishing rights in Icelandic waters for half a century, and Iceland would most likely continue to manage those waters; if control of fisheries were taken over, he would say no to membership. Persistently higher inflation and interest rates weigh heavily on younger generations.
art.1074.title: SFS, interests and the truth
art.1074.summary: Þórólfur, a professor of economics, says the EU’s escalating tariffs according to degree of processing mean that around 50,000 tonnes of fish are exported each year with little or no processing, and processing plants without quotas are struggling. He cites the Norwegian negotiator Torben Foss to the effect that catch shares were specified in Norway’s 1994 accession treaty, which is equivalent to formal registration of property rights, and that Iceland would not lose disposal rights over its resources.
art.1075.title: Vanity
art.1075.summary: Haukur, an engineer, says it is astonishing that those who claim there is nothing in the package do not want to open it and expose their opponents. If the package is not opened, disputes will continue over what would have been in it; the best course is to say yes to talks and, if necessary, no to an agreement, thereby making an informed and lasting decision.
art.1076.title: We can do this ourselves – but who profits from it?
art.1076.summary: Margrét describes the Icelandic economy as a goldfish on the inflation-and-interest-rate merry-go-round, with the Central Bank’s key rate now at 8%. She points out that the interest one person pays is another person’s income; high interest rates are not bad for everyone, and capital owners profit from the interest-rate spread while indebted households and young people bear the burden.
art.1077.title: Do you need five university degrees to say yes?
art.1077.summary: Berglind, a board member of the organisation Sjá, asks whether Iceland could live with lower interest rates, lower inflation and greater stability, and says one should not need expertise in European law in order to be allowed to say yes to finding out. Before a decision on membership is taken, it is necessary to know what an agreement would actually entail.
art.1078.title: Yes, yes or no
art.1078.summary: Þorsteinn says accession talks are not contract negotiations between two equal parties but a process in which the applicant state demonstrates how it complies with the EU acquis; lower interest rates or food prices are not negotiated. The talks were based on the 2009 application, each of the 27 member states has a veto, and governments within the EU must submit their budgets to the European Commission.
art.1079.title: No to barriers - Decisions about Iceland in Iceland
art.1079.summary: Guðmundur Fertram, founder of Kerecis, says Iceland’s main competitive advantage is how close decision-making is to the people, and that progress has occurred every time decision-making power has moved closer. Cooperation and supranational administration involving the transfer of sovereignty are not the same thing; the Draghi report shows that Europe has lost competitiveness because of slow decision-making and bureaucracy.
art.1080.title: Iceland has eternal interests, but not eternal allies
art.1080.summary: Lára Herborg says the claim that Iceland is a voiceless recipient of regulation is not entirely accurate; under Articles 99 and 100 of the EEA Agreement, Icelandic representatives can participate in the Commission’s expert and advisory committees when new rules are being drafted. Iceland’s representative in the European Commission would not be a representative of Icelandic interests but would work entirely in the interests of the Union.
art.1081.title: Iceland and the Faroe Islands, control over resources and sovereignty
art.1081.summary: Ásgeir compares Iceland and the Faroe Islands: the Faroe Islands’ monetary policy is determined by the Danish krone’s peg to the euro, and the Faroese alone control a much smaller share of the resources they use. He asks whether sovereignty, control over resources, and an independent monetary policy translate into better economic performance, and compares GDP per capita in the two countries.
art.1082.title: European conservatives are pro-European
art.1082.summary: Svavar, a political scientist and public administration scholar and a party-affiliated member of Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn, points out that Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn’s sister parties in the EPP, including Høyre in Norway, support their countries joining the EU. The current party leadership’s opposition to talks is a departure from the stance of European conservative parties; the vote is only about obtaining information, and the nation will have the final say on any agreement.
art.1083.title: Europe - from welfare to militarisation
art.1083.summary: Ólöf states that EU states’ military spending increased from EUR 183 billion in 2021 to EUR 408.1 billion in 2025, and that the Union supports militarisation and the arms industry through its funds. Iceland’s defence-related spending rose from 7 billion in 2024 to 10 billion in 2026, and Iceland has become involved in war in Europe through weapons purchases and military assistance.
art.1084.title: Don’t let yourself be fooled on 29 August
art.1084.summary: Sveinn Atli says the organised fear campaign by Áfram Ísland and Heimssýn is drowning out substantive debate, and reviews twelve claims that he says do not stand up to scrutiny. The EU has no common army and no power to impose conscription, and a large share of membership contributions flows back through regional development, agriculture, and fisheries funds.
art.1085.title: Who owns the fish - and where is the value created?
art.1085.summary: Baldur says an opinion by three law professors at HR indicates that local Icelandic stocks are better protected than is often suggested; the allocation of fishing rights is based on historical fishing experience, and as things stand other EU states would not gain access to them, and Iceland’s quota system would not disappear. However, the mandate to negotiate over shared stocks would pass to the EU, and he wants to see the agreement before declaring it impossible.
art.1086.title: Greenland – did you mean Iceland?
art.1086.summary: Damien Degeorges, an adviser and international relations scholar, says the EU’s financial power stopped Donald Trump over Greenland in January and thereby indirectly protected Iceland’s independence. Iceland’s security must rest on two pillars, NATO’s military strength and the EU’s financial strength, and the vote is about obtaining an offer from a security service provider.
art.1087.title: ▶ Yes to looking ahead for future generations
art.1087.summary: A series of people say they intend to vote yes to see what is on offer for future generations, trust Iceland’s negotiating position, and make an informed decision.
art.1088.title: ▶ Italians: the EU is not a burning house
art.1088.summary: Italian tourists reject the idea that the EU is a burning house, say it is important to belong to a large whole that makes nations stronger, and want Iceland to join.
art.1089.title: ▶ Swedes: too small a country for its own krona
art.1089.summary: Swedish interviewees say they absolutely do not want to leave the EU, that nations are stronger together, and that Iceland is too small a country to maintain its own krona.
art.1090.title: ▶ Queue to get in, no queue to get out
art.1090.summary: It is pointed out that none of the EU’s 27 nations is leaving, while Ukraine is trying to get in; the Union is compared to a restaurant with a queue to enter, and the narrator wants to see the menu.
art.1091.title: ▶ Doubts about the EEA proved unfounded
art.1091.summary: It is recalled that colour television, the Hvalfjarðargöng tunnel, and the EEA Agreement all met with scepticism but turned out well; whether the same applies to the EU will not be known until an agreement is seen.
art.1092.title: ▶ Special arrangements for northern agriculture
art.1092.summary: It is pointed out that Sweden and Finland secured special arrangements for agriculture in northern regions upon accession; the same arguments apply to Iceland, and this unique position is a strength at the negotiating table.
art.1093.title: ▶ Simmi Vill can’t find the arguments for no
art.1093.summary: Simmi Vill says he does not buy the exaggerations and doomsday predictions of the NO side; he wants to find out what is on offer to Iceland, especially since there are precedents for countries negotiating specific terms for their participation.
art.1094.title: ▶ Passers-by: yes, no question about it
art.1094.summary: Passers-by say they are determined to vote yes, want to see what is on offer, and take a look at the agreement out of curiosity.
art.1095.title: ▶ Vote no by advance voting today
art.1095.summary: It is pointed out that advance voting is already possible, that polling locations can be found on Ísland.is, and that voters can mark X next to no to defend sovereignty.
art.1096.title: ▶ We pay more than we get back
art.1096.summary: Passers-by say they intend to vote no; Iceland would pay more to the EU than it would get back, like giving 30 dollars, getting 20 back, and being told how to use them.
art.1097.title: ▶ Let’s write history ourselves
art.1097.summary: Independence is said to be intertwined with the nation’s history; the country was not inherited so that others could make decisions about its future, and people are urged to mark X next to no.
art.1098.title: ▶ A country with this standard of living applying?
art.1098.summary: It is claimed that, for the first time in decades, a country with a standard of living comparable to the member states would even consider applying for membership.
art.1099.title: ▶ Gross or net — control is what matters
art.1099.summary: The dispute is reviewed over whether the annual cost is 50 billion gross or 7–20 billion net; even if the net figure is lower, what matters is that Icelanders decide for themselves how the money is allocated.
art.1100.title: ▶ No free lunch in the EU
art.1100.summary: Icelanders’ tax money was said would go to infrastructure on the continent, e.g. bridges in Romania and road networks in the Balkans; Iceland would become a net contributor and should instead carry out such projects itself at home.
note: Report first prepared on 6 August 2026 and last updated on 28 August 2026. All articles about the referendum on Vísir, Eyjan (DV) and submitted opinion pieces in Morgunblaðið were analyzed, along with the websites of the movements (Evrópuhreyfingin, SJÁ, Heimssýn, Áfram Ísland, Til vinstri við ESB, Frjálst land), other media outlets (RÚV, Heimildin, Viðskiptablaðið, Bændablaðið, Skessuhorn, Austurfrétt, Feykir, BB.is, Eyjafréttir, Vikublaðið, Útvarp Saga, Mannlíf, Nútíminn), public discussion on Reddit and Facebook, and TikTok videos from the campaign movements. Neutral news coverage is not counted in the columns.
art.1101.title: What is Trump’s goodwill worth?
art.1101.summary: Says Icelanders’ choice could have significant effects on the EU debate in Norway and the position of the Nordic countries in Europe. Points out that the new U.S. national security strategy describes the EU in hostile terms and that Trump does not want a stronger, more united Europe. Asks whether Iceland’s tariff exemption this summer was linked to the Icelandic EU debate.
art.1102.title: The democracy festival 2026
art.1102.summary: Traces the history of the accession talks from 2009, their collapse, and the foreign minister’s 2015 letter on their indefinite suspension. Says NO supporters have used threats and fearmongering, while approval of the proposal would only authorize the reopening of negotiations and nothing beyond that.
art.1103.title: Young Icelanders are better off outside the EU
art.1103.summary: Says young Icelanders find it easier to save for a first home outside the EU because deposit interest rates in krónur are 7,75% compared with 1,75% in euros. Points out that only 5 of the world’s top 50 universities according to Times Higher Education are in EU countries, and that job prospects for young people are better outside the Union.
art.1104.title: Which doors do we want to keep open? The experience of Spain and Portugal
art.1104.summary: Points out that the vote is about restarting negotiations and then being able to assess the outcome, not about membership. Says the bleak picture painted of Spain’s and Portugal’s experience of EU membership does not match the development she has observed in those countries over four decades.
art.1105.title: Do you know which sirens are singing to you?
art.1105.summary: Analyzes the campaign’s rhetoric through the lens of classical rhetoric and takes the slogan “Áfram Ísland” as an example of emotional persuasion without reasoning. Says the slogan says nothing about fisheries, agriculture, the currency or sovereignty, yet still delivers a conclusion, and urges voters to ask about the arguments behind the words.
art.1106.title: There is something fishy about bananas
art.1106.summary: Recounts the story of the “bendy banana” uproar in the British press in 1994, when it was falsely claimed that the EU was going to ban curved bananas. Says the regulation nowhere mentioned that bananas were not allowed to be curved, and that Boris Johnson, one of the chief architects of Brexit, capitalized on these falsehoods.
art.1107.title: YES for the Icelandic language!
art.1107.summary: Says that in accession negotiations, efforts would be made to have Icelandic become one of the EU’s official languages, meaning that laws and regulations would be available in Icelandic and Iceland’s representatives could speak Icelandic within the Union’s institutions. Mentions Malta and Ireland as examples and says membership could open doors to cooperation in language technology.
art.1108.title: Don’t say no, say maybe, maybe, maybe
art.1108.summary: Argues that Iceland’s voice within the EU could become much louder than its population size suggests because rules are shaped in expert meetings. Points to precedents for exemptions for islands such as the Canary Islands, Madeira and the Azores, and says Iceland’s interests might be better served within the EU, provided conditions on fisheries and agriculture are met.
art.1109.title: Who do you trust?
art.1109.summary: Says the NO side’s latest weapon is to raise doubts about whether Þorgerður Katrín and Kristrún can be trusted, but that the government is simply fulfilling promises made in the coalition agreement. Recalls that in 2013 a referendum on continuing the negotiations was promised but never held, and says a special negotiating committee, not ministers, would conduct the talks.
art.1110.title: Spanish coastal fishermen to Iceland
art.1110.summary: Says the core principle of the EU’s Common Fisheries Policy is equal access for the Union’s fishing vessels to maritime areas, and that the 12-mile rule is a temporary exemption in force until the end of 2032. Argues that upon accession, coastal fishermen from all member states could establish fishing companies here and begin fishing in Icelandic territorial waters, and that it would not be possible to negotiate an opt-out from that.
art.1111.title: Halldór’s Vacuum Cleaner
art.1111.summary: Points out that the EU vacuum cleaner rules discussed in the debate apply equally in Iceland and in Spain through the EEA. Says the regulatory framework is fundamentally intended to protect the rule of law, democracy, human rights and free trade, and that lower interest rates are a likely benefit rather than a promise; we negotiate first and vote afterwards.
art.1112.title: The European Union is not built on member states agreeing. On the contrary
art.1112.summary: Describes the international system as ungoverned, where larger and stronger states call the shots when it matters. Says the EU is an experiment in which sovereign states bind themselves together through laws and common institutions, resolve disputes at the negotiating table, and where even the smallest states have a voice.
art.1113.title: Fighting for a world that was
art.1113.summary: Says he will vote yes because the world that ensured Iceland’s existence is coming to an end, and points to the actions of the Trump administration in Greenland, which is less than 300 kilometres away. Notes that within the EU it is not possible to punish a single state with tariffs because trade policy is common, and mentions inflation and the króna’s 8% interest rates.
art.1114.title: We have made many good decisions
art.1114.summary: Says Icelanders are generally much better off than EU states and that claims that the country must join the Union because matters have been badly handled do not stand up to scrutiny. Says advocates of accession tend not to talk about economic indicators other than interest rates, which are a manifestation of persistent economic stagnation.
art.1115.title: Let’s vote with an open mind
art.1115.summary: Says the vote is not on membership but on whether to resume negotiations, and that it is not timely to take a position on accession until an agreement is on the table. Warns against fearmongering by financially powerful interests and compares it to those same actors’ opposition to higher fishing fees last year, when none of the dire predictions came true.
art.1116.title: On Canada and Iceland
art.1116.summary: Compares Iceland and Canada, two resource-rich countries where independence and sovereignty matter above all, and says both countries share the conviction that small and medium-sized states can exert influence on the international stage. Says protecting small languages is vital, and that the clearer and more formal the guarantees obtained for this are, for example the right to use one’s own language in lawmaking, the better.
art.1117.title: The EU Referendum
art.1117.summary: Says he learned in his youth in Jerúsalem that everything in trade is negotiable, and that whoever does not negotiate has lost before they begin. Wants Iceland to listen and see what is on offer, then make its own demands on water, energy and fishing grounds, and only then make a decision; says the mistakes of the British should be learned from.
art.1118.title: Let’s not close our eyes to opportunities – vote yes and see the agreement
art.1118.summary: Says that a yes vote will put an agreement on the table that each person can assess on the basis of facts in a second referendum. Points out that NATO, EFTA and the EEA have all served Iceland well, and that through the EEA Iceland adopts a large share of EU legislation without having any influence on shaping it; sovereignty is strengthened by having a seat at the table.
art.1119.title: Sovereignty is not a display piece
art.1119.summary: Says sovereignty is not a display piece in a glass cabinet but a tool for safeguarding the nation’s interests, and that influence depends on knowledge and on being in the room when decisions are shaped. Says she has worked for the European Commission and seen firsthand that Icelanders are listened to; the EEA guarantees market access but not a seat at the table when rules are being shaped.
art.1120.title: Should food be cheap?
art.1120.summary: Says interest expenses have amounted to just over 10% of total income for dairy farms in recent years, and that the euro and lower interest rates would make a major difference to farmers’ livelihoods. Argues that suppliers, processing stations and retailers could also finance themselves more cheaply, and that the krona’s exchange-rate risk in the purchase of inputs would disappear with the euro, which could result in lower prices for consumers.
art.1121.title: The Battle for Iceland
art.1121.summary: Describes how Iceland emerged from poverty into prosperity by opening the country through Marshall aid, the abolition of capital controls, EFTA and the EEA. Says the krona has served its purpose but is a small and volatile currency, with the cost falling most heavily on those buying their first home or starting a business.
art.1122.title: Let’s not be small – An appeal to the younger generation
art.1122.summary: Says that tomorrow’s vote is not on membership but on accession talks, and that a yes vote would put an agreement on the table with answers to the questions that matter. Points out that Norway entered accession talks twice, obtained an agreement, and rejected it in a referendum; a yes now preserves both a future yes and a future no.
art.1123.title: Is it hard to make a decision?
art.1123.summary: Presents the choice as follows: if people want lower interest rates and a lighter debt burden, they will probably vote yes, but if they want continued indexation and an unstable krona, they will vote no. Says it is better to vote yes now and retain the option of rejecting an unfavourable agreement in the next referendum.
art.1124.title: The courage to change
art.1124.summary: Describes the work of the SJÁ civic association, founded about three months ago, as a platform for people who want to see an agreement before a final decision on the EU is taken. Says the race is very close, every yes matters, and urges people to go to the polls and mark yes.
art.1125.title: The fastest way to bring down inflation and interest rates is to vote NO on 29 August
art.1125.summary: Says the fastest way to force action against inflation and interest rates is to vote no, because the government would then face defeat and be compelled to show results before the next parliamentary elections. Refers to polls showing that over 80% of voters are dissatisfied with the authorities’ inaction on interest rates and inflation.
art.1126.title: A sausage the size of the banking system
art.1126.summary: Criticises Halldór Benjamín’s method of counting EU acts as equivalent units and concluding that Iceland adopts only one fifth of the acquis. Refers to the Norwegian Sejersted review from 2012 and the Eldring review from 2024, which found that Norway, and thus Iceland, is tied into about three quarters of the cooperation and the acquis without voting rights.
art.1127.title: Yes to see what?
art.1127.summary: Points to precedents for permanent opt-outs in the EU, such as the Finns’ Åland Islands, the Danes’ summer-house ban, and British opt-outs before Brexit, and says Iceland’s negotiating position is strong. Says the EEA Agreement is not secure forever, and that policy rates of 8% in Iceland versus 2.4% in the euro area show a striking interest-rate gap that membership and the euro would reduce.
art.1128.title: Icelandic agriculture for the future: What opportunities might European cooperation offer?
art.1128.summary: Says Icelandic farms have already become modern and robust, and that the main difference in operating conditions between Icelandic and European farmers lies in the cost of capital; within the euro area, farmers live with much lower and more stable interest rates. Argues that trade barriers on imported inputs could be reduced within the internal market, and mentions Arctic support.
art.1129.title: We can choose to stop arguing – about the krona
art.1129.summary: Says the Icelandic krona suits some business owners well, but that the labour movement spends most of its strength restoring purchasing power instead of being able to focus on housing security, working hours, lifelong learning and pay equality like its counterparts in the Nordic countries. Argues that a more stable currency could give labour negotiations breathing space.
art.1130.title: May Iceland be free while the sun gilds the sea
art.1130.summary: Criticizes the YES side for misleading information, such as claims of a 25% reduction in product prices and that Iceland is already 75% in the EU, and points out that the constitution would need to be amended because of the transfer of sovereignty that membership would entail. Likens the accession process to a sweater that turns out to be a straitjacket; once you join, your hands are tied, and he says the journey would cost billions.
art.1131.title: Is Iceland good enough for Europe?
art.1131.summary: The chair of Afstaða says the question should be what demands Europe makes of Iceland; states seeking membership must meet requirements on the rule of law, institutional independence, and the fight against corruption. External oversight could benefit Iceland’s culture of cronyism, and he says he will vote yes because he wants less corruption and wants to see what is on offer.
art.1132.title: Path Dependencies and Critical Junctures: A Response to Baudenbacher
art.1132.summary: Responds to Baudenbacher and rejects the idea that a yes vote in the referendum would create an automatic path into the EU. Points out that many hurdles would still remain along the way: the negotiations themselves, a second referendum, parliamentary elections, and the necessary constitutional amendment.
art.1133.title: The debate in the run-up to the election
art.1133.summary: Discusses propaganda techniques in the election campaign, repetition and fearmongering that appeal to emotions rather than reason. Refers to an article by Torben Foss stating that Norwegians obtained a permanent exemption for fisheries in 1994 and that Icelanders have a permanent exemption on ownership in fisheries under the EEA Agreement; the claim by SFS that no permanent exemptions are available is therefore false.
art.1134.title: Suðurlandi allt
art.1134.summary: A Viðreisn MP for the South constituency says South Iceland’s economy is built on interaction with foreign countries and that workers suffer from limited competition in banking, insurance, and grocery services. The referendum is about increasing choice and establishing whether an agreement with the EU could improve households’ position.
art.1135.title: Grandma and Grandpa, please don’t vote against us
art.1135.summary: A young author says Iceland’s prosperity has been built on decisions made at home, by Icelanders for Icelanders. With membership, the baton would be handed to Brussels instead of the next generation, and the YES campaign is putting words in young people’s mouths; most young people he knows want to govern the country themselves.
art.1136.title: Who has the final say?
art.1136.summary: The group says the YES side’s comparisons to buying real estate and reading menus are misleading young voters. Regardless of the outcome of negotiations, the final say on Iceland’s affairs would shift from Alþingi to Brussels, and Iceland’s voting weight in those decisions would be next to nothing.
art.1137.title: No to the EU is not no to Europe
art.1137.summary: Says no to the EU is not no to Europe; Iceland already participates in the internal market through the EEA, and that is the cooperation she wants to maintain. Fisheries weigh heavily in her stance; she doubts EU member states would agree to a permanent special arrangement for Iceland and does not want to take that uncertainty when the current situation serves the country well.
art.1138.title: We already know enough to make an informed decision to say No
art.1138.summary: Says that 99% of the content of membership is already set out in the EU treaties, so it is an illusion to think that something unknown will emerge in negotiations. Recounts the history of the Lisbon Treaty as an example of a democratic deficit in which voters were bypassed, says EU officials have little understanding of Iceland’s circumstances with less than 0.09% of the EU’s population, and that the customs union would reduce Iceland’s trade opportunities.
art.1139.title: No one wakes up with an interconnector in the backyard
art.1139.summary: Says that no one can lay a subsea power cable to Iceland without the approval of the Icelandic authorities, and that claims to the contrary mislead the public. Iceland already implements EU energy legislation through the EEA; with membership it would gain a seat at the table when the rules are shaped, and at a time when great powers have less respect for international law, it makes sense to deepen cooperation with an alliance built on common rules.
art.1140.title: To young people
art.1140.summary: Encourages young people to explore membership; having a seat at the table would increase sovereignty, and small nations like Malta and Luxembourg consider their influence to have grown upon joining. The euro would bring humane interest rates and a more humane housing system instead of high interest rates and indexation; if the agreement turns out to be bad, it can be rejected. Believes it is likely that the EEA Agreement will soon cease to apply.
art.1141.title: Angelica in the Cliff
art.1141.summary: Uses the story of Þorgeir Hávarsson on the cliff as an example of pride turning into self-deception. Says Iceland’s success has been built on international cooperation such as the UN, NATO, EFTA and the EEA, and assistance such as the Marshall Plan. The vote is not about membership but about getting an agreement on the table and then making an informed decision.
art.1142.title: How Did the Last Doomsday Turn Out?
art.1142.summary: Recalls MPs’ doomsday predictions about the EEA Agreement in 1993 concerning loss of independence, unemployment and poverty that did not come true; now the same record is back on the turntable. The nation is only voting on whether to begin talks; if the agreement is bad, it will say no, and voting on an agreement is an exercise of sovereignty, not a surrender of it. Mentions Icesave as an example of the nation being able to reach a different conclusion than politicians.
art.1143.title: On the Expression of Sovereignty
art.1143.summary: Says hyperactive participants in comment sections distort the concept of sovereignty and quote AfD leaders admiringly. Transferring powers in limited areas is not surrendering sovereignty but one of its clearest expressions; Iceland has already shared powers through membership in the UN, IMF, NATO, EFTA, the EEA and the European Court of Human Rights.
art.1144.title: 25.2% Success Rate
art.1144.summary: Calculates that the Icelandic authorities have met their own 2.5% inflation target in only 77 of 305 months since 2001, or 25.2% of the time, while inflation in the euro area has been below Iceland’s target 77.6% of the time. Persistent inflation is a continuing problem, and high interest rates and indexation are the price Icelanders pay for it, regardless of which parties have been in government.
art.1145.title: A Unique Opportunity to Increase Purchasing Power That We Could Miss for the Next 30 Years!!
art.1145.summary: Says accession talks and a policy aimed at adopting the euro are one of the biggest purchasing-power opportunities for the Icelandic labour market in decades; they would make it possible to tackle high interest rates, exchange-rate risk and the cost of the króna system instead of the repeated vicious cycle of exchange-rate swings, inflation and wage demands. If that path is closed now, a similar opportunity may not come again for the next 20–30 years.
art.1146.title: That Is Why We Say NO on 29 August
art.1146.summary: Says the EU has served the wealthy class from the outset, worked to lower labour costs, undermined trade unions and failed to recognise the legitimacy of collective agreements; cites the proposed EU-Inc directive as an example. Also says the EU’s leading states are fuelling the threat of war and that military build-up will come at the expense of welfare spending.
art.1147.title: I’m Voting YES! - Why?
art.1147.summary: A former mayor of Höfn says Iceland’s negotiating position is now much stronger than after the crash and that it should therefore negotiate now. The no side has grown under the shelter of fearmongering reminiscent of Brexit propaganda; Icelanders have never lost out from open international cooperation, and the United States can no longer be relied on when it really matters.
art.1148.title: Iceland’s Competitiveness
art.1148.summary: Says Iceland has fallen by seven places in IMD’s competitiveness survey and ranks 58th out of 70 in foreign investment; the króna deters foreign investors because of its small size and exchange-rate instability. The króna’s unstable exchange rate is assessed in particular as reducing Iceland’s competitiveness.
art.1149.title: Purchasing Power After Housing Costs 27% Lower Than Five Years Ago
art.1149.summary: Criticises labour leaders who oppose talks taking place and the public being allowed to vote on an agreement. States that the monthly payment burden on a 50 million króna loan rose from about 188,500 krónur per month in 2021 to about 395,300 krónur based on today’s 9.25% interest rate, and that Icelandic households have lived with a persistent interest-rate gap vis-à-vis the euro area for decades.
art.1150.title: A Stable Króna, the Abolition of Indexation, and a New Role for Iceland in the International Financial System
art.1150.summary: Says the krona is not weak because of its small size, but because indexation builds systematic inflation into the economy. Abolishing indexation and changing the price index, as was done in Norway, Denmark, Sweden and New Zealand, would lower interest rates and make the krona stable; stability is about how the system is structured, not the size of the currency.
art.1151.title: The European Union, a shelter from the United States?
art.1151.summary: Says it is an illusion to view the EU as a counterweight to US aggression; Europe is in the middle of an arms race, and military spending by EU states has more than doubled since 2021. This build-up in fact serves US interests, and it is wishful thinking to believe European states would defend Iceland against them.
art.1152.title: When the state picks up the bill
art.1152.summary: Recalls the Icesave dispute and that the European Commission took part in the case before the EFTA Court against Iceland’s position; if that interpretation had prevailed, the obligations of private banks would have been shifted onto Icelandic taxpayers. The EFTA Court rejected the claim in 2013 and Iceland won a complete victory that must not be forgotten.
art.1153.title: Failing at home, but with its mind in Brussels
art.1153.summary: A Framsókn MP says 85% believe the government has performed poorly in tackling inflation, yet it still puts an EU referendum front and centre. Iceland is already part of the internal market through the EEA while maintaining an independent policy in fisheries and agriculture; the euro would not come immediately because of the Maastricht criteria and ERM II, and Iceland would lose its independent monetary policy.
art.1154.title: Uncertainty in international affairs – What if the Norwegians get there first?
art.1154.summary: Says Iceland’s negotiating position has rarely been stronger: the British are outside the EU after Brexit, and it strengthens Iceland’s position to begin talks before the Norwegians. If the Norwegians or the British join the EU, the negotiating position would weaken significantly and the EEA Agreement could become a thing of the past; accession talks and membership are an insurance policy in an uncertain world.
art.1155.title: The Dutch mortgage
art.1155.summary: Responds to an MP’s comparison of payments on a 50 million króna mortgage in Iceland and in the Netherlands. It calculates that wages in Iceland have risen by 2.1% per year above inflation over the past 25 years, compared with only 0.3% in the Netherlands; the debt burden as a share of wages therefore falls much faster in Iceland, and over the final 20 years of the loan term it would be lower here.
art.1156.title: The EU’s war against equality and welfare
art.1156.summary: Sets out eight examples of EU institutions and the European Central Bank demanding sweeping cuts to welfare spending in exchange for assistance and emergency loans, including in Latvia in 2009, Ireland in 2010 and Spain in 2011. The EU is not a neutral alliance that protects the interests of ordinary people; banks, large corporations and financial forces wield great influence there.
art.1157.title: Yes now – so you can say no later
art.1157.summary: Says they intend to vote yes in order to get information and the necessary basis for judgment, and to be able to say no to membership later if the agreement does not stand up to scrutiny; no power will be transferred to the EU with a yes vote on Saturday. Points out that the EU treaties specifically provide for consideration of island regions, rural areas and sparsely populated areas, and that the EEA/EFTA states have little or no formal influence on the EU’s final decisions.
art.1158.title: Six exaggerations from the NO side and the YES side
art.1158.summary: Reviews six common claims from both camps about fisheries, agriculture, workers’ rights and the euro, and says neither side can state with certainty an outcome that has not been negotiated. What is needed is to negotiate, see the result, and then judge it with the future of the next generations as the guiding principle.
art.1159.title: Enough is enough
art.1159.summary: Says the EEA gives Iceland freedom and opportunities to defend its interests but no voting rights, and that the last time talks were held the nation was not asked — now it is being asked. Criticises propaganda and polarisation in the debate and votes yes out of curiosity about what can be negotiated, especially as there are many safeguards in the process that follows.
art.1160.title: An independent nation takes its seat at the table
art.1160.summary: The Minister for Foreign Affairs and chair of Viðreisn says that independence means making your own decisions and having a seat at the table where decisions are made, not being shown into a side room. Iceland adopts a large share of the internal market acquis through the EEA without sitting at that same table; a yes would only mean that Iceland sits down at the negotiating table, and the nation itself would then decide on the agreement, which matters in a time of tariff wars.
art.1161.title: The euro does not lower interest rates
art.1161.summary: Says the YES side’s interest-rate comparison is misleading because it compares nominal rates rather than real rates; the real yields on ten-year government bonds in 2001–2010 were almost the same in Iceland and the euro area. Interest rates are not the same within the euro area, what keeps rates high here is home-made, rates would have to be low already before the euro could be adopted, and the euro would only deprive Iceland of the insurance that the króna provides.
art.1162.title: Let us stand together on sacred issues
art.1162.summary: Says the term “negotiations” is misleading; the accession process takes place on the EU’s terms under Article 49 of the Treaty and concerns the conditions and timing for adopting the entire body of EU law, with alignment beginning already during the negotiation period. A yes would put Iceland on a conveyor belt toward membership; instead of independent decision-making power, Iceland would get about 0.1% population weight, less than 1% of parliamentary seats, and no veto in fisheries matters.
art.1163.title: We believe in an even bigger and stronger Iceland
art.1163.summary: Says Iceland’s success since 1918 has been built in large part on international cooperation — NATO, the defence agreement, EFTA and the EEA — and that none of those steps weakened the country. Iceland’s negotiating position has never been stronger, and there is a unique window for negotiating; the red lines are clear on control over resources, special arrangements in fisheries and agriculture, the Nordic labour-market model, and adoption of the euro.
art.1164.title: The rights are the same – but the opportunity is not
art.1164.summary: Lists examples of the weak position of disabled people, single parents and their children in Iceland, including the fact that support ends at age 18 and that HÍ registration fees have risen proportionally more for disabled people. Says EU social policy is based on the idea that equal rights on paper are not enough; barriers must also be removed so that opportunities become genuinely equal — a way of thinking that is lacking in Iceland.
art.1165.title: The small request comes first, then the big one.
art.1165.summary: Describes the “foot in the door” technique from social psychology and says “yes to see” is the small request that increases the likelihood that people will later accept the big one — membership. A yes would set a major political and administrative process in motion, followed by “escalation of commitment,” where people keep investing in a decision they have already put a great deal into.
art.1166.title: No for the coming generations
art.1166.summary: Says the YES campaign, Já til að sjá, is based on gilded promises of lower interest rates, cheaper food and lower inflation that have been disproved many times. Young people do not welcome a future in which decision-making is transferred to officials in Brussels; the authorities should focus on getting inflation and interest rates under control themselves, because no one else will do it.
art.1167.title: The scent of the lotus flower
art.1167.summary: Says the phrase “yes to see” is silly because nothing the EU shows could be permanent; mentions that a concession the Irish were promised on fishing in their own continental shelf waters was withdrawn. Any confirmation of control over resources would never be permanent, and Iceland would be stuck in Brussels for a very long time if membership came about.
art.1168.title: Am I failing my children by saying NO?
art.1168.summary: Says she is afraid of moving decision-making further away from the Icelandic public and reducing a small society’s room to respond to shocks. She wants decisions on fundamental interests to be taken as close to the public as possible and for it to be possible to hold those in power accountable and vote them out of office.
art.1169.title: The Old Covenant and the new one
art.1169.summary: Compares accession talks to the Old Covenant of 1262, when Icelanders bowed to foreign royal power in the hope of better times. Believes the problems facing Icelanders are not beyond them and that solutions exist at home if wealthy individuals keep the overall interests of society in mind.
art.1170.title: Is it better?
art.1170.summary: Asks whether it is better to import food from other countries, pay tens of billions in gross contributions to the EU, and cede part of the legislative, executive, and judicial powers with the European Court of Justice as the highest court. Says they have seen enough and will say no.
art.1171.title: The fishing-industry elite wants into the EU - I say no
art.1171.summary: Cites Kristrún Frostadóttir’s account of a fishing company owner who wants to vote yes in order to be able to sell the quota abroad and "cash out". Ireland’s experience shows that fisheries agreements do not hold unless they are embedded in the EU treaties; the Hague Preferences did not hold despite being signed.
art.1172.title: The countryside falls silent
art.1172.summary: Years of accession talks would create uncertainty for farmers, who need predictability in order to invest; no one has received an exemption from the Common Agricultural Policy. The uncertainty would arrive immediately the day after the vote if yes prevails; farmers would stop investing and younger generations would never begin farming.
art.1173.title: Before proceeding any further
art.1173.summary: The timing of the vote is unfortunate and the preparation inadequate; there is a risk that talks will begin without clear objectives. Upon accession, tariff protection against agricultural products from EU countries would as a general rule be abolished and agriculture would fall under the Common Agricultural Policy, fundamentally transforming the sector’s framework.
art.1174.title: The Danes, the EU and Iceland’s position
art.1174.summary: Says NO supporters’ claims of a cost of 50-500 billion are absurd; based on Denmark’s ratio, Iceland’s contribution could be in the range of 10-20 billion. Explains that the Danes negotiated opt-outs in justice and home affairs, defence, and the euro long after joining, showing that important issues are negotiated with individual countries.
art.1175.title: What does "it’ll all work out" cost?
art.1175.summary: Questions whether the authorities have ever really had control over the króna, which is a vulnerable floating micro-currency subject to foreign influences. Icelanders deserve borrowing terms comparable to those of other wealthy nations, and the first step is to say yes.
art.1176.title: The opportunity is now
art.1176.summary: YES keeps the nation’s opportunities open: lower interest rates and risk premiums with the euro, economic stability, and lower prices. Iceland’s negotiating position has never been better, and any accession treaty would be put to the nation in a second vote.
art.1177.title: An Iceland of 600 thousand people – are we going to build it ourselves?
art.1177.summary: Farmers have called for improvements to their operating environment, not upheaval; accession would entail a fundamental change in which the EU’s Common Agricultural Policy would become the framework and tariff protection would be abolished. There is uncertainty about the future of the CAP, including because of the possible accession of Ukraine, one of Europe’s largest agricultural powers.
art.1178.title: Billions in gains from the euro – for households, businesses, the state, the municipalities and the nation as a whole
art.1178.summary: Estimates the annual cost of the króna system at ISK 967-1,215 billion (22-27% of GDP) due to 4-5% higher real interest rates, exchange-rate risk, and risk premiums. The possible additional gain from adopting the euro is estimated at ISK 517-739 billion per year for households, businesses, the state, and municipalities.
art.1179.title: Do you want to risk complicity in genocide or warmaking for the profit of others?
art.1179.summary: Says no for peace, human rights, and international law, and calls the EU a hard-nosed trade alliance, not a benevolent association. Points to a democratic deficit: Iceland would get 6 votes out of 720 and the Commission controls what matters; Iceland recovered from the crash faster than the euro-state of Greece.
art.1180.title: Hundreds of billions in gains for people and businesses - that is why I say yes to sea
art.1180.summary: There should be no alignment during the negotiations, and the nation should vote again on a completed agreement. The interest-rate differential and oligopoly sheltered by the króna cost hundreds of billions a year, the neighboring countries remain fully sovereign within the EU, and the EU customs union provides protection when the United States uses tariffs as a weapon.
art.1181.title: The data show that Europe is by far Iceland’s most important market area
art.1181.summary: The data in the RSE report itself show that the EU receives about half of Iceland’s exports and Europe as a whole about 63%; exports to China are 1.6% despite a free trade agreement. The vote is not about membership but about dialogue with the country’s most important trading area, which already sets most of the rules for business.
art.1182.title: Interest rates, inflation, indexation, and the Icelandic climate
art.1182.summary: The vote is about negotiations, not accession; any accession treaty would go to a second referendum, and claims otherwise are information disorder. Iceland’s history has been marked by an endless struggle with inflation, interest rates, and indexation under the world’s smallest independent currency.
art.1183.title: 30 examples of misleading presentation in Áfram Íslands’s economic analysis
art.1183.summary: Documents 30 misleading presentations in Áfram Íslands’s economic analysis and says it is only natural that the organization withdraw the report. Per-capita economic growth has been lower in Iceland than in the EU, prices are 61-72% higher, and real interest rates are 4.5-5.5% versus about 0.8% in the euro area.
art.1184.title: Yes to see – a gamble?
art.1184.summary: The EU regulatory framework is not up for negotiation; only implementation, timing, and temporary exemptions are negotiated. Aligning laws and administration would take many years, put investment on hold, and he is not prepared to put sovereign powers and control over natural resources at risk for unclear benefits.
art.1185.title: These are changing times
art.1185.summary: Recalls his grandfather’s diaries as a district doctor, describing how medical services have always been built on the cooperation of the whole community. Modern healthcare, for example ECMO treatment for critically ill children, depends on collaboration far beyond a single institution and a single location.
art.1186.title: Are Icelandic fisheries and the quota system a good reason to vote yes on 29 August?
art.1186.summary: The quota system brought fisheries under control and is considered the best fisheries management system in the world; the fishing industry accounts for 40% of merchandise exports and pension funds are among the largest shareholders. In the event of accession, foreign parties could fully own Icelandic fishing companies and factory trawlers could process the catch elsewhere.
art.1187.title: If Iceland joins the European Union, I’m moving to Denmark
art.1187.summary: The vote is about reopening negotiations, not accession, and any agreement would then go to a referendum. The negotiation process itself could become the best health check of Icelandic society, as legislation, competition, prices, and institutions would be compared with Europe, policy area by policy area.
art.1188.title: The EU has strengthened profit-seeking at the expense of social solidarity
art.1188.summary: The EU has changed radically since the Maastricht Treaty and has narrowed the space for states’ independent decision-making; decisions have shifted to Brussels and the European Court of Justice always rules in favor of integration. Consumer and labor protections through the EEA do not prove that sovereignty is strengthened by membership.
art.1189.title: Who is going to keep their eye on the ball?
art.1189.summary: A policy-rate increase to 8% confirms what the no side has argued: that economic housekeeping will be put on the back burner during the accession process. It asks whether people are prepared to live with persistently high interest rates while negotiations are underway, only to end up with an agreement they will reject.
art.1190.title: These narrow-minded young farmers
art.1190.summary: Young farmers are well informed through Nordic and European cooperation; within the European Council of Young Farmers, CEJA, it is almost impossible to reach an outcome that everyone is happy with because conditions in the countries are so different. It is easier to solve the problems of young farmers with direct measures in Iceland than through the EU.
art.1191.title: The Brexit bus has arrived in Iceland!
art.1191.summary: The NO side’s ad campaign about an annual cost of 50–100 billion does not stand up to scrutiny and uses the same method as the Brexit campaigners in Britain. The Ministry for Foreign Affairs estimates direct contributions at 8–13 billion and Evrópustraumar estimates the net contribution at 6–9 billion per year, while the króna’s foreign exchange reserve costs 20–30 billion annually.
art.1192.title: The Icelandic horse and the EU: Scaremongering or a real danger?
art.1192.summary: Membership would not mean that Iceland would have to open up to imports of live horses; Iceland has maintained an import ban for three decades within the EEA, and the EU recognises the special status of island states. There is a clear legal basis for permanent exemptions when animal health is at stake; let’s finish the negotiations and vote YES to find out.
art.1193.title: Agriculture and food prices – Future developments
art.1193.summary: Icelandic agriculture will change significantly over the coming decades whether Iceland joins the EU or not; the number of dairy farms will decline and they will grow larger with increased mechanisation. The question is not whether agriculture will change but how, and poultry and pig farming already rely largely on imported feed.
art.1194.title: The application process explained for idiots
art.1194.summary: Alþingi never approved withdrawing the membership application, and a large part of the debate revolves misleadingly around an accession treaty that does not exist.
