YES does not mean membership; the 27 opened negotiating chapters would still have to be reviewed, and the biggest contentious issues, fisheries and agriculture, still remain to be negotiated.
art.1195.title: Could we be better off?
art.1195.summary: She voted yes because she does not have the basis to take a position on membership until an agreement is on the table; let’s get the agreement on the table and then make a decision. EU regional policy could bring opportunities to rural Iceland in the face of infrastructure deficits, and she wants answers about the effects of the euro on interest rates, prices and competitiveness.
art.1196.title: Can Iceland alone handle the healthcare challenges of the future?
art.1196.summary: A nation of 400,000 cannot on its own guarantee all the medicines, specialist expertise, research and preparedness that the healthcare services of the future will require; the EU is the largest and most realistic path for cooperation. Iceland would still control the operation, financing and prioritisation of its own healthcare system.
art.1197.title: Yes to more tools for communities across the country
art.1197.summary: Icelanders pay the highest interest rates in Europe and the most for a basket of food. Icelandic regional policy is toothless in the face of job losses and depopulation, but EU cohesion policy, including the ERDF regional development fund, would give communities across the country stronger tools and real funding.
art.1198.title: A responsible policy in international affairs
art.1198.summary: The debate is taking place on the assumptions of the post-crash years even though the global picture has changed completely; the international system on which Iceland’s pursuit of prosperity was built has broken down or is crumbling. The future of the EEA Agreement is uncertain and not entirely in Iceland’s hands, and the EFTA route has gradually become obsolete as the states joined the EU one after another.
art.1199.title: Real independence
art.1199.summary: Economic power in Iceland is in the hands of a small group of investors and fishing companies who fear transparency and stoke fear to preserve the status quo. YES ensures that an agreement is put on the table, competition increases, the cost of living can fall, and the public gets the final say.
art.1200.title: Do you need to know a lot about the EU to vote on 29 August?
art.1200.summary: The real options are SEE and NOT SEE; the vote is about whether the nation gets to see an agreement between Iceland and the EU. Both campaigns are largely based on speculation until an agreement is on the table, and a NO vote carries the responsibility of closing the process before it is possible to see the agreement.
art.1201.title: An article for undecided voters and NO supporters: It pays to be in an alliance of cooperation and mutual support as a full member state
art.1201.summary: The EEA Agreement has benefited Iceland and asks why full membership should not do so as well. Only member states have access to the EU Solidarity Fund in the event of natural disasters; the cost to the Treasury because of Grindavík is estimated at 80-100 billion, and such support could have made reconstruction easier.
art.1202.title: On 29 August, the public will decide whether interest rates will be 3–4% or 8–9%, and whether the nation’s risk will be high or low for the next 30 years
art.1202.summary: NO could mean another 20-30 years in the high-interest, high-risk system of the króna, as in Norway, where no further referendum has been held since 1994. The vote is about the long-term risk management of the national economy and whether interest rates will be 3-4% or 8-9%.
art.1203.title: I do not understand the NO side
art.1203.summary: The big fishing companies, large corporations and owners of capital want the status quo of oligopoly, high consumer prices and high interest rates to remain unchanged, while settling their own accounts in euros. Ordinary people, 80-90% of the nation, have nothing to lose from seeing an agreement; he urges those aged 65 and older not to close off young people’s opportunities.
art.1204.title: Sovereignty — family estate or a tool of an independent nation?
art.1204.summary: The sovereignty of a small state is more complex than a legal definition; a state that gives up part of its freedom in international cooperation gains in return security, influence over the rules it lives under, and a stronger position vis-à-vis states and companies many times larger. It asks whether the state has then lost sovereignty or exercised it.
art.1205.title: When Iceland becomes a city-state of 600 thousand people — who will then produce the food?
art.1205.summary: He says he will vote NO because he does not trust that the safeguards on agriculture from the Foreign Affairs Committee will hold when tested. The Finnish Arctic exemption is a protective provision tied to production in the years 1991-1993, not a growth provision, and applies only until 2027 — but Iceland needs to increase food production for a nation of up to 600 thousand people.
art.1206.title: EU membership increases the influence of small states. Ireland’s experience is very positive
art.1206.summary: Ireland’s experience shows that EU membership increases the influence of small states; they take a direct part in shaping decisions, build alliances and can put forward candidates for the highest offices. The Irish have, among other things, held the presidency of the European Parliament and twice led the European Commission.
art.1207.title: Iceland needs realistic solutions — not unexplained variables and unrealistic scenarios
art.1207.summary: Claims of 495-810 billion in annual gains from membership are untraceable and based on comparisons with incomparable large states. Iceland already has the EEA Agreement, a defence agreement with the United States and free trade agreements, and most of the cost of the króna is domestic and can be fixed without handing over fisheries management, agricultural policy and legislative power to the EU.
art.1208.title: ▶ The red Brexit bus was a complete deception
art.1208.summary: It is recalled that opponents of the EU in the Brexit referendum used propaganda such as the red bus, which did not withstand scrutiny; let us familiarise ourselves with the issues and make an informed decision.
art.1209.title: ▶ YES is a valuable option
art.1209.summary: A YES vote is said to be an option: the nation would get all the information about the terms of an agreement and time to see how the EU develops before a vote on membership; NO means the status quo with indexation, the króna, interest rates and inflation.
art.1210.title: ▶ Triple YES supporters on the road
art.1210.summary: Passers-by say they intend to vote yes in order to learn more and be able to make an informed decision later.
art.1211.title: ▶ The big questions on the signs answered
art.1211.summary: A review of questions on the NO side’s billboards: Iceland is not for sale, no nation has given up its resources upon joining, and the 50 billion cost figure does not hold up — the net cost is comparable to the foreign-exchange surcharge on Icelanders’ overseas card spending.
art.1212.title: ▶ Absurd to reject an agreement that does not exist
art.1212.summary: An interviewee says it is strange to take a final position on an agreement that has not been made; the most sensible course is to get the agreement on the table and then decide.
art.1213.title: ▶ Passers-by: Yes for a brighter future
art.1213.summary: Young people out and about say they intend to vote yes for a brighter future and to be part of the future in Europe.
art.1214.title: ▶ Baltasar Kormákur: The loans keep rising despite repayments
art.1214.summary: Baltasar Kormákur describes a mortgage that rose from 50 million to 60 million despite repayments of 12–15 million; for people in that position, there are positive aspects to looking into membership.
art.1215.title: ▶ Can one person bring Iceland into the EU? No
art.1215.summary: It is explained that a yes vote would lead only to negotiations; the nation would then vote on the agreement, and a constitutional amendment would require approval by two parliaments with an election in between — the people would decide at least three times.
art.1216.title: ▶ We have already tried this
art.1216.summary: It is pointed out that spokespeople for the NO side talk about stability but have themselves negotiated wage increases in the tens of percent and tied collective agreements to prices and rental contracts to indexation — the instability of the króna is well proven.
art.1217.title: ▶ Chat Control will come through the EEA anyway
art.1217.summary: The fear around Chat Control is called nonsense: Iceland is in the European Economic Area, and if the legislation is adopted it will come to Iceland anyway — without Iceland having voting rights to object.
art.1218.title: ▶ Sveppi: It won’t kill us to look at the agreement
art.1218.summary: Sverrir Þór (Sveppi) says he is voting yes because it will not kill anyone to look at the agreement.
art.1219.title: ▶ Young people are not idiots
art.1219.summary: It is criticised that politicians talk down to young people; key interest rates are 8% in Iceland but 2.25% in the euro countries, and it is right to get all the information and assess the matter calmly.
art.1220.title: ▶ Faroese people love the yes side
art.1220.summary: A humorous video about Faroese people loving Icelanders because they always say yes; the caption points out that housing interest rates in the Faroe Islands are much lower than in Iceland.
art.1221.title: ▶ Magnús: Strengthen sovereignty with a seat at the table
art.1221.summary: The chair of Evrópuhreyfingin says membership strengthens sovereignty: Iceland should take a seat at the table where matters that directly affect the country every day are decided; this is a unique opportunity that should be seized.
art.1222.title: ▶ EU regulation keeps expanding
art.1222.summary: The speaker says regulation and oversight within the EU are constantly increasing and making life harder for people and businesses; the union is no longer about facilitating trade, as the four freedoms were meant to do.
art.1223.title: ▶ Your vote could make all the difference forever
art.1223.summary: An encouragement to go to the polls: it takes only a few minutes to vote, but EU membership could make all the difference forever; those who do not want the future to lie in the EU should put an X next to no.
art.1224.title: ▶ Agriculture can choose the best options today
art.1224.summary: It is pointed out that Icelandic agriculture can today learn from the EU, Norway and Finland and adapt that to Icelandic conditions; on accession, it would have to be adapted to the common system of 27 states — a complete upheaval, not minor changes.
art.1225.title: ▶ Hilmar: Nothing in the package that needs checking
art.1225.summary: Hilmar compares the EU to a house that has already been inspected: there is nothing in the package that needs checking; Iceland has itself built up two new export pillars in technology and innovation, and nothing in the EU helps that journey.
art.1226.title: ▶ Sidekick: Membership changed nothing for the company
art.1226.summary: Ragnhildur Jónsdóttir of Sidekick Health says she cannot point to any major obstacle that would disappear with EU membership; the company has been able to raise financing, hire specialists and operate in European markets outside the union.
art.1227.title: ▶ What does membership cost? 8,636 Teslas a year
art.1227.summary: Annual spending on the EU is put into perspective: 8,636 Teslas, 5,000 people on full salaries or 300,000 iPhones a year; any grants in return would be decided in Brussels and would always be lower than the payments.
art.1228.title: ▶ Let’s write history ourselves
art.1228.summary: Short video: independence is intertwined with Iceland’s history, and the country was not built up to let others make decisions about its future.
art.1229.title: ▶ Áslaug Arna: No magic solutions in Brussels
art.1229.summary: Áslaug Arna says Iceland’s history shows that the nation can move forward on its own; the EU is burdened with heavy regulation, slow processes and declining competitiveness, and it is unclear how the union will develop — better to say no and wait and see.
art.1230.title: ▶ Katrín Jakobsdóttir: I say no
art.1230.summary: Katrín Jakobsdóttir says it is her sincere conviction that Iceland is best served outside the EU, while maintaining close cooperation with the Union and other nations; Iceland’s independent and strong voice matters on the international stage.
art.1231.title: ▶ Katrín: Membership calls for a constitutional amendment
art.1231.summary: Katrín Jakobsdóttir points out that EU membership would require a constitutional amendment because decision-making power would shift away from Alþingi and Iceland; major decisions about everyday life would be taken where Icelanders would have little or no say.
art.1232.title: ▶ Sigríður María: No to this journey
art.1232.summary: A former deputy MP for Viðreisn says she was long positive towards the EU but says no to this journey: the government is asking for a mandate in the most important round of negotiations in Iceland’s history without putting all the information on the table.
art.1233.title: ▶ Brussels is not the answer to the fatigue
art.1233.summary: Sigríður María says YES-leaning voters are tired of politics, prices and interest rates — but Brussels is not the answer: more politicians will not fix dissatisfaction with politicians; the government does not need to peek, but to look in the mirror.
art.1234.title: ▶ ‘Let’s look in the package’ is a habit of postponement
art.1234.summary: Sigríður María says the “let’s look in the package” and “yes to see” campaigns are about saying as little as possible and postponing substantive debate; content-free social media politics disguised as curiosity.
art.1235.title: ▶ No one safeguards our interests better than we do ourselves
art.1235.summary: Sigríður María says the nation has the strength to fight for better living conditions at home; the question is whether Icelanders still believe in themselves.
art.1236.title: ▶ The nation that never gave up on Iceland
art.1236.summary: Sigríður María recalls sovereignty in 1918, the Cod Wars and the recovery after the crash; through volcanic eruptions, harsh weather and economic collapse, the Icelandic nation never gave up on Iceland.
art.1237.title: ▶ Sólveig Anna: We do not need the euro for the housing market
art.1237.summary: Sólveig Anna says the housing market is the biggest cause of unrest in the labour market; the euro is not needed to fix it, but rather domestic measures such as rent controls, which politicians have failed to address.
art.1238.title: ▶ Halldór Benjamín: Let’s listen to farmers
art.1238.summary: Halldór Benjamín says the farmers’ associations and young farmers have come out unequivocally against accession talks and membership; no one is better placed to speak on behalf of farmers than farmers themselves.
art.1239.title: ▶ The energy example from Sweden
art.1239.summary: Halldór Benjamín says the European Commission threatened to take part of the excess profits Swedes would earn from a new electricity interconnector and move them to Southern Europe; the Union’s thinking is that the wealthy nations pay in and the money is transferred elsewhere.
art.1240.title: ▶ No opt-out on fisheries is on offer
art.1240.summary: Halldór Benjamín compares the process to 2009 and refers to polls showing that 95% of the nation wants full control over marine resources; the government has not set a clear negotiating objective on an opt-out from the Common Fisheries Policy and is said to waver between exemptions and special arrangements.
art.1241.title: ▶ Closing remarks: Icelanders themselves are best placed to decide
art.1241.summary: Halldór Benjamín says no one is better suited to make decisions for Icelanders than Icelanders themselves; politicians at home can be voted out, but no official in Brussels wakes up on a Monday morning to improve the lives of Icelanders.
